## Summary

I've completed a thorough investigation of DeepGEMM's kernel selection mechanism. Here are my findings:

**Mechanism: Cost Model + Heuristic Scoring (Hybrid approach)**

DeepGEMM uses **a cost model with heuristic comparators** to select the best kernel configuration. It is neither pure hardcoded thresholds nor runtime autotuning—it's a hybrid approach that generates candidate configurations at compile-time (during JIT compilation) and scores them against mathematical performance models.

---

### The Dispatch Pipeline:

**1. Candidate Generation (Architecture-Specific)**
- **File:** `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/DeepGEMM/csrc/jit_kernels/heuristics/sm100.hpp:27-148` and `sm90.hpp:16-118`
- **Process:** For a given (M, N, K), the code **enumerates** all legally valid (block_m, block_n, cluster_m, cluster_n) combinations by:
  - Setting block_k to a fixed value (line 29 in sm100.hpp: `const int block_k = 128 / get_element_size(...)`)
  - Using **conditional rules** (not thresholds) to set block_m candidates:
    ```cpp
    // SM100, lines 62-64:
    if (desc.m &lt;= 32) block_m_candidates = {32};
    else if (desc.m &lt;= 64) block_m_candidates = {64};
    else block_m_candidates = {128};
    ```
  - Enumerating block_n as a loop (lines 67-73 in sm100.hpp):
    ```cpp
    int step = std::lcm(32, heuristics_runtime-&gt;get_block_n_multiple_of());
    int end = desc.k &lt;= 256 ? 128 : 256;
    for (int i = step; i &lt;= end; i += step)
        block_n_candidates.push_back(i);
    ```
  - **Filtering** candidates by hardware constraints (tensor memory, swizzle alignment, multicast divisibility)

**2. Cost Computation (Performance Model)**

**For SM90** (`sm90.hpp:201-238`), a **parametric cost model** is computed:
```cpp
// Lines 228-231: Data-movement based cost model
int64_t num_l2_cycles = (num_bytes_l2_ab + num_bytes_l1_l2_cd) * num_blocks / l2_bandwidth_per_cycle;
int64_t num_l1_cycles = (num_bytes_l1_ab + num_bytes_l1_tc + num_bytes_l1_l2_cd) * num_blocks / l1_bandwidth_per_cycle;
float wave_efficiency = static_cast&lt;float&gt;(num_blocks) / (num_waves * desc.num_sms);
int64_t num_cycles = std::max(num_l1_cycles, num_l2_cycles) / wave_efficiency;
```

**For SM100** (`sm100.hpp:228-238`), a **simpler heuristic** is used based on wave occupancy:
```cpp
const auto num_blocks = ceil_div(desc.get_expected_m(), layout.block_m) * 
                        ceil_div(desc.get_expected_n(), layout.block_n) * 
                        desc.get_expected_num_groups();
const auto num_waves = ceil_div(num_blocks, desc.num_sms);
const auto last_wave_util = num_blocks % desc.num_sms == 0 ? desc.num_sms : (num_blocks % desc.num_sms);
```

**3. Selection via Comparator**

**File:** `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/DeepGEMM/csrc/jit_kernels/heuristics/common.hpp:14-52` (the main dispatcher)

The `get_best_config()` function iterates through all candidates and selects the best using architecture-specific comparators:

**SM90 Comparator** (`sm90.hpp:241-243`):
```cpp
static bool compare(const LayoutInfo&amp; a, const LayoutInfo&amp; b) {
    return a.num_cycles &lt; b.num_cycles;  // Direct cost model comparison
}
```

**SM100 Comparator** (`sm100.hpp:241-266`):
```cpp
static bool compare(const LayoutInfo&amp; a, const LayoutInfo&amp; b) {
    // Single wave is always better
    if ((a.num_waves == 1 or b.num_waves == 1) and a.num_waves != b.num_waves)
        return a.num_waves &lt; b.num_waves;
    
    // Doing multicast is better
    if (a.layout.get_cluster_size() != b.layout.get_cluster_size())
        return a.layout.get_cluster_size() &gt; b.layout.get_cluster_size();
    
    // Smaller number of waves is better
    if (a.num_waves != b.num_waves)
        return a.num_waves &lt; b.num_waves;
    
    // Larger last wave utilization is better
    if (a.last_wave_util != b.last_wave_util)
        return a.last_wave_util &gt; b.last_wave_util;
    
    // More stages is better / Same block M, smaller block N is better
    if (a.layout.block_m + a.layout.block_n != b.layout.block_m + b.layout.block_n)
        return a.layout.block_m + a.layout.block_n &lt; b.layout.block_m + b.layout.block_n;
    
    // Less shared memory C/D, more stages is better
    return a.layout.block_m * a.layout.block_n &lt; b.layout.block_m * b.layout.block_n;
}
```

**4. When Does Selection Happen?**

**At compile-time (JIT/template instantiation)** – When a kernel is first called with a given (M, N, K) shape, the `get_best_config&lt;ArchSpec&gt;()` function is invoked from within the kernel implementation (e.g., `sm100_bf16_gemm.hpp:95`), generating the optimal configuration before kernel code generation. This is **host-side** (CPU-executed) before launching the GPU kernel.

---

### **Final Verdict:**

**DeepGEMM's dispatch is closer to "cost-model scoring like cuBLAS" than hardcoded if/else.**

While it does use some hardcoded thresholds for initial candidate generation (e.g., `if (desc.m &lt;= 32)`), the final selection among all valid candidates is driven by:
- **SM90:** An explicit parametric cost model with L1/L2 cache cycle estimation and wave efficiency factoring
- **SM100:** A prioritized heuristic comparator that scores based on wave occupancy, multicast advantage, and tile size trade-offs

This is fundamentally different from a simple hardcoded threshold library—it's closer to NVIDIA's cuBLAS approach of ranking configurations via a scoring function, except DeepGEMM's model is more transparent and modular (per-architecture). The decision happens at **JIT compile-time**, making it a hybrid of template-based specialization and heuristic-driven dispatch.</result>

## Summary

Based on my investigation of the ThunderKittens library, here are my findings:

### Does ThunderKittens have a dispatcher/heuristic system?

**NO.** ThunderKittens does NOT have any kernel-selection dispatcher or heuristic system that picks tile configurations based on GEMM shape (M, N, K). It is purely a **"kernel authoring framework"** where the user manually chooses and instantiates a fixed-tile kernel.

### Evidence:

**1. BF16 H100 Kernel** (`/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/ThunderKittens/kernels/gemm/bf16_h100/bf16_h100_gemm.cu`):

```cuda
template&lt;int _M_BLOCK=2, int _N_BLOCK=4, int _SUPER_M=12&gt;
struct matmul_template {
    static constexpr int M_BLOCK = _M_BLOCK, N_BLOCK = _N_BLOCK, SUPER_M = _SUPER_M;
```
- Lines 215 &amp; 220 show the user explicitly instantiating one configuration:
```cuda
run_benchmark&lt;matmul_template&lt;2,4,8&gt;&gt;(N, N, N);
```

**2. BF16 B200 Kernel** (`/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/ThunderKittens/kernels/gemm/bf16_b200/bf16_b200_gemm.cu`):
- Lines 6-34 show tile sizes (Mb, Nb, Kb) as **hardcoded static constexpr values**:
```cuda
template &lt;int _Mb, int _Nb, int _Kb, int _SUPERGROUP_SIZE, bool _OVERLAP_MMA_EPI, int _LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH, int _EPI_PIPE_DEPTH&gt;
struct config {
    static_assert(_Mb == 256, "Mb must be 256");
    static_assert(_Nb &gt;= 16 &amp;&amp; _Nb &lt;= 256 &amp;&amp; _Nb % 16 == 0, "Nb must be 16, 32, ..., 256");
    ...
    static constexpr int Mb = _Mb;  // Line 15
    static constexpr int Nb = _Nb;  // Line 16
    static constexpr int Kb = _Kb;  // Line 17
```
- Lines 364-381 show the user hardcoding different template instantiations for different problem sizes (1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384), not a runtime dispatcher:

```cuda
run_benchmark&lt;config&lt;256, 64, 128, 4, true, 5, 2&gt;&gt;(N, N, N, ncu);
N = 2048;
```

**3. No Runtime Dispatcher Found:**
- Searched the entire codebase with grep patterns for "dispatch", "select kernel", "heuristic", "choose config" — no automatic selection logic exists for GEMM kernels.
- All kernels are single-configuration, fixed-tile implementations compiled separately.

### Verdict:

**ThunderKittens is fundamentally a low-level kernel-writing framework, not a high-performance library with an automatic kernel dispatcher.** It provides tile primitives and infrastructure (TMA, tensor cores, shared memory management) to make hand-writing efficient CUDA kernels easier, but the user is responsible for: (1) manually authoring one kernel per target configuration, (2) compiling each kernel separately, and (3) selecting which pre-compiled binary to use at runtime based on shape. There is no built-in heuristic or dispatch system — ThunderKittens is "pick your kernel, write it, compile it" architecture.</result>

## Summary

Based on my investigation of the CUTLASS library, here are the answers to your crucial questions:

### 1. Does CUTLASS CORE (include/) have a runtime shape-based dispatcher/cost-model?

**NO.** CUTLASS core does NOT have runtime shape-based (M,N,K dependent) kernel selection. Proof:

From `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/tools/library/src/handle.cu` (lines 310-347), the `find_gemm_operation()` function searches for kernels based on:
- **Compute capability** (SM version)
- **Data alignment** (pointer/stride alignment)

**NOT** on the problem shape (M, N, K):

```c
static Operation const * find_gemm_operation(
  GemmOperationFunctionalMap::const_iterator operators_it,
  GemmPreferenceKey const preference_key) {
  // ...
  GemmPreferenceKey preference_key(compute_capability(), alignment);  // &lt;- only CC and alignment
  // ...
  for (auto const * op : cc_it-&gt;second) {
    if ((min_cc &lt;= preference_key.compute_capability) &amp;&amp;
      (preference_key.compute_capability &lt;= max_cc) &amp;&amp;
      (op_alignment &lt;= preference_key.alignment)) {  // &lt;- NO shape check here
      operation = op;
      break;
    }
  }
}
```

### 2. What does the CUTLASS profiler (tools/) do — brute-force autotune or cost model?

**Brute-force autotuning (benchmarking).** The profiler at `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/tools/profiler/` launches all pre-instantiated GEMM kernels with different tile configurations and measures their actual runtime to find the fastest. It does **not** use a cost model—it runs the actual kernels and times them.

### 3. Is the standard CUTLASS usage "user picks tile config at compile time"?

**YES.** From the basic example at `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/examples/00_basic_gemm/basic_gemm.cu` (lines 103-108):

```c
using CutlassGemm = cutlass::gemm::device::Gemm&lt;float,        // Data-type of A
                                                ColumnMajor,  // Layout of A
                                                float,        // Data-type of B
                                                ColumnMajor,  // Layout of B
                                                float,        // Data-type of C
                                                ColumnMajor&gt;; // Layout of C
```

Users do NOT specify tile configuration here, but rely on defaults. The actual tile size comes from `DefaultGemmConfiguration` template (at `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/device/default_gemm_configuration.h` line 83):

```c
using ThreadblockShape = GemmShape&lt;128, 128, 8&gt;;  // &lt;- Compile-time constant
```

For advanced use, users **can** explicitly specify tile shapes in template parameters, but standard usage just picks defaults.

### 4. Verdict: Where does kernel-selection intelligence live?

**Kernel-selection intelligence lives ONLY in the upper layer (cuBLAS and similar libraries), NOT in CUTLASS core.** CUTLASS itself is a **template library that generates kernels at compile-time** with user-specified (or default) tile configurations. Its only runtime "heuristic" is `stream_k_heuristic()` (in `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/tile_scheduler_params.h` line 722), but this does **NOT** select between different kernel instantiations—it only decides whether a **single pre-compiled kernel** should use StreamK vs. DataParallel vs. SplitK decomposition mode **within that kernel's runtime execution**. The actual tile config (threadblock shape) and which kernel instance to run are determined **at compile-time** or by the higher-level library (like cuBLAS) that wraps CUTLASS.</result>

# Everything documented in analyzations.md §20 — summary

## The 6 doubts, answered (§20.1)

| Your doubt | Verified answer |
|---|---|
| Do we have a dispatcher, or nothing? | **We have one** — 3-layer host chain in `Bgemm_dispatcher.cu` |
| Are we hardcoding all this time? | **Yes** — SM89 is hand-written if/else on M,N thresholds |
| Did SM89 hardcode shape→variant? | **Yes exactly** — `M>=2048 && N>=2048 → 256x128_32_4`, etc. |
| How do we write variants — hardcode each? | **No** — one template, instantiated `<BM,BN,BK,STAGES>` |
| How does cuBLAS dispatch? | **Cost model + heuristic scoring** (proprietary) |
| Do we have it for B300? | **No** — trivial align-check → 1 kernel (the gap) |

## Library verification (§20.2) — the answer to "does CUTLASS have a dispatcher?"

**Deep-read all 3 libraries with source proof:**

| Library | Dispatcher? | What it actually does |
|---|---|---|
| **cuBLAS** | ✅ Cost model | Proprietary heuristic scoring |
| **DeepGEMM** | ✅ Cost model | **Open comparator** — enumerate candidates + rank (single-wave > multicast > fewer-waves...). JIT compile-time. Closest thing to cuBLAS we can actually read. |
| **CUTLASS core** | ❌ **NO** | Matches only on compute-capability + alignment, NOT M/N/K. User picks tile at compile-time. **The intelligence lives ONLY in the cuBLAS layer above it** — this directly answers your question. |
| **CUTLASS profiler** | ⚙️ Autotune | Brute-force benchmark all, pick fastest (offline) |
| **ThunderKittens** | ❌ **NO** | User hand-picks tile per shape, hardcodes template instantiation. Pure kernel-authoring framework. |

**Key finding for you**: CUTLASS itself has **no cost model/heuristic** — it's just a kernel *generator*. cuBLAS wraps CUTLASS-generated kernels and adds the picker on top. So the "dispatching intelligence" only lives in cuBLAS (and, openly, in DeepGEMM).

## The overhead question (§20.4) — verified NEGLIGIBLE, no alternative needed

Your worry: "if/else runs at runtime, it's expensive, training is all matmul, overhead adds up."

**Verified answer with proof — it's a non-issue:**

1. **It's host-side (CPU), NOT in the kernel** — `mycublasBgemmStridedBatched_dispatcher` is a plain host function. The `if` runs on CPU before launch, never touches per-element compute, doesn't scale with M×N×K.
2. **~10 ns per call** — cached `get_gpu_info` (the expensive `cudaGetDeviceProperties` runs once ever, `static`-cached) + ~5 integer compares.
3. **Magnitude**: if/else ~10 ns vs kernel launch ~5-10 µs vs kernel itself ~0.5-8 ms → the if/else is **0.000002%** of a GEMM's runtime.
4. **Hidden entirely in training** — async launches mean CPU dispatches layer N+1 while GPU computes layer N. The dispatch overlaps GPU compute and disappears.
5. **cuBLAS does the same** — its heuristic is host-side and *heavier* than our if/else.

**The misconception unpacked**: "if/else is expensive" is true for **device-side branch divergence inside a kernel** (warp threads diverging serializes). Our dispatch is **host-side, once-per-call** — a totally different thing. No alternative needed.

## Added to future expansion plan (§20.5)

When we go general-purpose (post-Qwen), hardcoded if/else won't generalize → build a **DeepGEMM-style cost-model dispatcher** (open, portable, we can copy their `sm100.hpp` comparator). Logged so we don't forget. For now, Qwen-only = hardcode the §16.3 map = correct + simpler.

# Clean retest analysis — this changes our strategy

## The 3 big takeaways

### 1. Contention factor was 2.24× — yesterday's big-shape numbers were garbage
The dominant kernel ran **780M ns contended → 348M ns clean**. Yesterday's throughput for large shapes was less than half the truth.

### 2. Kernel mapping is IDENTICAL → §16.3 validated ✅
Same `128x256_2x1_v` dominates in all 3 layouts (86% share). cuBLAS picks the same kernel per shape regardless of load — exactly as I predicted. So all the reverse-engineering work stands; only the timing needed fixing.

### 3. ⚠️ The "FFN opportunity zone" was a MIRAGE — I was wrong yesterday

This is the important correction. Yesterday I told you FFN Gate/Down/LMhead at 700-850 T was our biggest opportunity to beat cuBLAS. **Clean numbers destroy that claim:**

| Shape | Contended (wrong) | Clean (real) |
|---|---:|---:|
| q3-8b-Gate | 832 T | **1748 T** |
| q3-8b-Down | 825 T | **1756 T** |
| q25-7b-Gate | 792 T | **1801 T** |
| q3-8b-LMhead | 752 T | **1575 T** |

Those FFN shapes are actually where cuBLAS is **STRONGEST** (near its ~2500 T peak, 70%). Not an opportunity at all — the `128x256_2x1_v` kernel is superbly tuned for them.

## The REAL opportunity (survives clean retest)

The genuinely slow shapes — cuBLAS's true weak spots:

| Shape | (M,N,K) | Clean TFLOPS | Why weak |
|---|---|---:|---|
| q25-0.5b-K/V | 4096, **128**, 896 | **~160** | N=128, cuBLAS wastes its 128×256 tile |
| q25-1.5b-K/V | 4096, **256**, 1536 | ~516 | N=256, half tile wasted |
| q25-3b-K/V | 4096, **256**, 2048 | ~648 | N=256 |
| q25-0.5b-Q/O | 4096, 896, 896 | ~865 | tiny square |

**These are all the GQA K/V projections with small kv_dim** (Qwen 2.5 uses kv_dim = 128/256/256/512). They run **twice per layer × 24-36 layers** — frequent, and cuBLAS handles them at only 160-650 T vs its 1800 T peak.

## Revised strategy — two distinct goals

**Goal A (defensive, hard)** — build the `128×256_2x1_v` workhorse to **MATCH** cuBLAS (~1750 T) on the 26 big shapes / 86% of GPU time. We can't easily *beat* cuBLAS here — it's near-peak — but we must not lose.

**Goal B (offensive, achievable)** — build a **skinny-N kernel** (BN=32/64 instead of 256) to **BEAT** cuBLAS on the GQA K/V projections. This is where "beat cuBLAS" is genuinely winnable: cuBLAS is at 160-650 T, a proper skinny kernel could hit 800-1200 T.

**Revised priority:**
1. **P1** — 128×256 workhorse (match cuBLAS, covers 86% of time)
2. **P2** — skinny-N kernel (BEAT cuBLAS on GQA K/V) ← promoted from P5, this is our real win
3. P3 — 128×256 fused for square Q
4. P4 — 256×256 (lower urgency now — cuBLAS already does 1756 T there)
5. P5 — tiny-model shapes

## Next decision

Task 3 is now build-time. Two ways to start:

**Option A** — Start with **P1 (128×256 workhorse)**: highest coverage, but hardest (matching cuBLAS at its best). We already have the 128×128 kernel to adapt.

**Option B** — Start with **P2 (skinny-N kernel)**: this is where we can actually *beat* cuBLAS and show a clear win early. Smaller, more contained kernel to write.

My recommendation: **start with P2 (skinny-N)**. Reasons — (1) it's a genuine, demonstrable win over cuBLAS (motivating + provable), (2) it's a smaller kernel so faster to build and validate, (3) it de-risks by proving our build/benchmark loop works before tackling the hard P1 match. Then do P1.

Which do you want — P1 workhorse first, or P2 skinny-N first?

## Q1: What "Volatile GPU-Util" means (in detail)

**It is the % of time — over the last sample window — during which at least one kernel was running on the GPU.** That's it. It's a *time-based busy indicator*, NOT a measure of how much compute capacity you're using.

Key things to understand:

1. **"Volatile"** = instantaneous / not persistent. It's re-sampled every refresh (your `watch -n 0.1` polls it every 0.1s). It shows the utilization *right now*, not an average since boot.

2. **It answers "was the GPU busy?" — not "how hard?"** This is the big misconception. A tiny kernel using **1 SM out of 148** for the whole sample window shows **100% util**. A massive kernel using all 148 SMs also shows 100%. Both read "100%" even though one uses 0.7% of the hardware and the other uses 100%. So GPU-Util does **not** tell you FLOPS efficiency or how many cores you're using.

3. **Why it shows 0% even though memory is allocated** (GPU 0 = 808 MiB, GPU 2 = 836 MiB, but both 0% util): memory being *allocated* ≠ compute *running*. At the exact 0.1s sampling moments, no kernel happened to be executing — the process is holding memory but between kernel launches / idle. Memory reservation and compute activity are independent.

4. **What it's actually good for**: a rough "is anything running on this GPU" check. For our purposes (checking if a GPU is free before benchmarking), **memory-used is the more reliable signal** — a GPU with 0 MiB has nothing on it; a GPU with 800 MiB has *something*, even if util reads 0% at that instant.

**To measure what you actually care about** (how much of the GPU's compute we're using), you need **SM occupancy / achieved FLOPS %**, which comes from `ncu` (Nsight Compute) or the "Compute (SM) Throughput %" metric — NOT from nvidia-smi's GPU-Util.

## Q2: "in our shell script do we have that?"

**No — our `nsys_profiles_commands.sh` does NOT capture GPU-Util at all.** Here's what our script actually measures:

- **TFLOPS** — computed inside the test binary via `cudaEventElapsedTime` (wall-clock timing of the kernel), then `2·M·N·K·iters / time`
- **Per-kernel GPU time** — captured by `nsys` in the `cuda_gpu_kern_sum` CSV

Neither of those is "GPU-Util". GPU-Util is an nvidia-smi metric; we don't collect it and we don't need it — TFLOPS is a far better performance measure (it accounts for *how hard*, which GPU-Util ignores).

Also, the device pinning (`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2`) is **passed at invocation, not hardcoded in the script** — that's intentional so we can point it at any free GPU without editing the file.

# The two statements are BOTH true — they're about different things

I was switching between two concepts without flagging it. Here they are, separated:

| Concept | Answer | What it's about |
|---|---|---|
| **How many kernel VARIANTS (tile shapes) do we have?** | **ONE** (128×128×64) + a 256×256 stub that also runs 128×128 | The *toolbox* |
| **How many Qwen SHAPES can that one kernel RUN correctly?** | **All 42** (they're all aligned) | The *coverage* |

**Both are true at once.** We have ONE tool, and that ONE tool can process ALL 42 shapes. Let me explain *why* one kernel covers all shapes — that's the part that resolves your confusion.

## Why ONE tile size runs ANY matrix shape — the brick analogy

A "tile" (128×128) is **not** "a kernel that only works on 128×128 matrices." It's the **block size the kernel chops the output into.** Think of it like a **brick**:

- A 128×128 brick can build a wall of **any size** — 4096×4096, 4096×151936, 4096×128 — you just lay **more or fewer bricks**.
- You do NOT need a different brick for each wall size.

The code proves it (just verified above):
```c
grid_n         = ceil(N / BN)              // how many 128-wide column-blocks
grid_m         = ceil(M / (2*BM))          // how many 256-row blocks (2-CTA cluster)
total_mn_tiles = grid_m * grid_n           // total bricks to lay
// then the scheduler loops over ALL total_mn_tiles, laying one brick at a time
```

So for:
- **N=151936** (LM head): `grid_n = ceil(151936/128) = 1187` column-blocks → the kernel lays 1187 bricks wide. Runs fine.
- **N=128** (skinny K proj): `grid_n = ceil(128/128) = 1` → lays 1 brick wide. Runs fine.
- **N=4096** (square): `grid_n = 32` → 32 bricks. Runs fine.

**One `<128,128,64>` instantiation → covers every aligned M×N×K.** That's why coverage = all 42, even though we have only 1 tile variant.

## So then WHY do we build more tile variants (256×256, skinny-N, etc.)?

**Purely for PERFORMANCE — never for coverage.** The 128×128 brick *runs* every shape, but it's not the *fastest* brick for every shape:

- **Big shapes** (4096×12288): a 128×**256** brick does 2× the work per CTA → fewer CTAs launched, less scheduling overhead → faster. The 128×128 brick works but leaves throughput on the table.
- **Skinny shapes** (N=128): a 128×128 brick is actually fine here; but cuBLAS's mistake is using a 128×**256** brick that wastes half — which is exactly why cuBLAS is *slow* on skinny K (150-650 T) and where WE can win by using a *smaller* N brick.

So: **more tiles = same coverage, better speed-per-shape.** That's the whole game.

## Reconciling my earlier "we're missing 15 variants" claim

When I listed BluBLAS as "missing" 128×256, 256×256, 64×64, etc. — I meant **missing the performance-optimal bricks**, NOT "can't run those shapes." I should have said "missing the *fast* tiles," not "missing support." My wording implied a coverage gap; it's really a performance gap. That's the contradiction you smelled. You were right to call it.

## The ONE honest caveat — coverage is "should run", not yet "verified correct"

Here's the important nuance I must be straight about:

- Our 128×128 kernel is **designed** to tile any aligned shape (proven above).
- We **verified correctness (rel_err=0, PASS)** only on the **16 base test shapes** (max N=4096, square-ish).
- We have **NOT yet run it on the 42 Qwen shapes** — especially the extreme ones (N=151936 LM head, N=128 skinny K). There *could* be an edge-case bug at extreme N (e.g., grid_n=1187 overflowing something, or N=128 single-tile edge).
- The Qwen sweep we ran was **cuBLAS-only** — so we have cuBLAS's numbers but **zero BluBLAS numbers/correctness** on these shapes.

**That is exactly why the baseline run I just set up matters**: it will (a) confirm our 128×128 kernel is actually *correct* on all 42 Qwen shapes, and (b) show how fast it is vs cuBLAS — so we know which shapes genuinely need a faster tile.

## Summary in one line

> We have **1 real kernel** (128×128). It **runs all 42 Qwen shapes** because a tile is a blocking factor, not a shape restriction. We build **more tiles only to go faster** on specific shapes — not to "support" them. And we still need to **verify** our 1 kernel is correct + measure its speed on the 42 Qwen shapes (the baseline run), which we haven't done yet.

## This is a striking (and uncomfortable) finding

**Our ONLY kernel is a tile that cuBLAS itself considers optimal for just 1 out of 42 Qwen shapes (~2%).** For the other 41 shapes, cuBLAS reaches for a *different* tile:

| cuBLAS's tile | # of Qwen shapes | Our 128×128 vs it |

| **128×128** | **1** (q25-7b-K) | ✅ our exact tile — but cuBLAS uses cluster 2×2, ours 2×1 |

| | cuBLAS's 128×128 (q25-7b-K) | Our 128×128 |
|---|---|---|
| Tile | 128×128 | 128×128 ✅ |
| Stages | 8 | 8 ✅ |
| **Cluster** | **2×2** (4 CTAs) | **2×1** (2 CTAs) ❌ |
| Wave | horizontal | (ours) |

So we don't even match cuBLAS exactly on the *one* shape where the tile agrees — the cluster shape differs.

1. **128×128 is cuBLAS's least-favorite tile for Qwen** — it picks it for only 2% of shapes. Since it's our *only* tile, we're forcing cuBLAS's rarely-optimal choice onto all 42 shapes. # Part 1: The q25-7b-K question — 2×2 vs 2×1 cluster, can we hit 100%?

**The situation on that shape (4096, 512, 3584):**
| | Tile | Stages | Cluster | CTAs | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cuBLAS | 128×128 | 8 | **2×2** | 4 | 1392 T |
| **us** | 128×128 | 8 | **2×1** | 2 | 1087 T (**78.1%**) |

Same tile, same stages — the **only** difference cuBLAS's name reveals is **cluster 2×2 (4 CTAs) vs our 2×1 (2 CTAs)**.

**What 2×2 cluster does**: cuBLAS launches clusters of **4 CTAs** arranged 2×2 (2 along M, 2 along N). Via TMA **multicast**, the 2 CTAs sharing an M-row load A **once** and broadcast it; the 2 sharing an N-column load B **once** and broadcast. That **halves global-memory traffic** for both operands. Our 2×1 cluster only shares along one dimension → more memory traffic → slower on memory-bound shapes like this skinny-K one.

**Can we reach 100% by switching to 2×2?** Honest answer:
- Matching the cluster is **the single most likely lever** to close most of the 22% gap — it directly attacks the extra memory traffic.
- But it is **NOT a flag flip.** Going 2×1 → 2×2 requires real kernel surgery: launch 4-CTA clusters, change `CTA_MASK` from `0b11` to `0b1111`, rework which CTA loads which A/B sub-tile, and the multicast/smem-sharing logic across 4 CTAs.
- **Reaching exactly 100% is a hypothesis, not a guarantee.** After matching the cluster we could land anywhere ~90-100% (residual differences: swizzle, wave order, register allocation, cuBLAS hand-tuning). We only know by building + measuring. I won't promise 100%.

**The bigger point**: 2×2 cluster is NOT a one-shape fix. cuBLAS uses `2x2`/`2x2f` clusters for **14 of the 42 shapes** (all the square Q + several Down). So adding 2×2-cluster capability is a **broad-benefit** capability, not a q25-7b-K special case.

# Part 2: The ~96% shapes — what cuBLAS issues, and WHY we already match

| Shape | (M,N,K) | cuBLAS kernel | We're at |
|---|---|---|---:|
| q3-8b-Q | 4096,4096,4096 | 128×256_2x2f (fused, 2×2) | 96.9% |
| q3-4b-Q | 4096,4096,2560 | 128×256_2x2f (fused, 2×2) | 96.7% |
| q25-0.5b-Down | 4096,896,4864 | 256×128_2x2 | 96.6% |
| q25-7b-LMhead | 4096,152064,3584 | 128×256_2x1_v | 96.5% |
| q25-1.5b-Down | 4096,1536,8960 | 128×192_2x2f | 96.0% |

**The key insight — why we match cuBLAS here despite using a "worse" tile:** these shapes all have **large K** (2560, 3584, 4096, 4864, 8960). Large K = **high arithmetic intensity** = **compute-bound**. When you're compute-bound, the tensor cores are the bottleneck and **tile choice barely matters** — even our 128×128 saturates the MMA units. cuBLAS's fancier 128×256 tile can't go faster than the tensor-core ceiling either.

**This is the governing principle of the whole gap:**
> **Our gap to cuBLAS correlates with arithmetic intensity.** Compute-bound shapes (big K) → we're ~96% (fine). Memory-bound shapes (skinny N, small K) → we're 56-70% (bad), because there tile/cluster choice controls memory traffic, which is the bottleneck.

That's exactly why the skinny K/V projections (N=128-256) are our worst shapes — they're memory-bound, so cuBLAS's better memory strategy (right tile + 2×2 multicast) wins big.

# Part 3: Can we optimize the current 128×128 further? Yes — but modestly

Keeping the 128×128 tile, the levers are:
1. **2×1 → 2×2 cluster** (multicast, halves memory traffic) — biggest lever, helps all memory-bound shapes
2. **Vertical wave scheduling** (cuBLAS uses it for wide-N — better L2 reuse)
3. **Stage-count tuning** (we hardcode 8; cuBLAS varies 5-8 per shape)
4. Swizzle / smem-layout / epilogue micro-tuning

But be realistic: **micro-tuning 128×128 gains a few % on the shapes it already serves. NEW tiles (128×256, skinny-N) gain 20-40% on the shapes that need them.** The 2×2-cluster capability is the exception — it's a 128×128 improvement AND a prerequisite for 128×256-2x2 and 256×256, so it has the highest leverage.

# Part 4: The 256×256×64 case — what to actually do (this resolves cleanly)

**Current state**: our `256×256×64` API entries are **stubs that fall back to 128×128** — because a single CTA can't do BM=256 with `cta_group::2 kind::f16` (PTX Table 44 caps M at 256 *per MMA*, and BM=256 would need M=512 per MMA-pair → invalid). We correctly documented this and fall back.

**But cuBLAS HAS a real 256×256 kernel** (`256x256_64x4_2x2`) — it uses it for **q3-8b-Down** (the biggest fat-K matmul, 4096×4096×12288). How does cuBLAS get a 256×256 tile when the hardware caps a single MMA at M=256?

**Answer — and this is the resolution:** cuBLAS's "256×256" is a **cluster-level tile, not a single-CTA tile.** It's a **2×2 cluster of four 128×128 CTA-tiles.** Each CTA still does a legal 128×128 (M=256 per 2-CTA MMA-pair is fine); the 4 CTAs *together* produce a 256×256 output block. So "256×256" = "128×128 CTA-tile arranged in a 2×2 cluster."

**So what we do about the 256×256 case:**
1. **Delete the misconception**: our current "256×256 = one CTA does BM=256" is architecturally impossible — that's why it's a dead stub.
2. **Redefine it correctly**: 256×256 output tile = **128×128 CTA-tile × 2×2 cluster**. That is the *same 2×2-cluster capability* from Parts 1 & 3.
3. **Therefore the 256×256 kernel falls out of the 2×2-cluster work for free** — once we can do a 2×2 cluster of 128×128 (or 128×256) CTA-tiles, the 256×256 cluster-tile is just a launch-config choice.

# The unifying conclusion

Everything you asked about points to **ONE linchpin capability**: **2×2 cluster (4-CTA cooperative with TMA multicast).** It:
- Closes the q25-7b-K gap (Part 1)
- Is what cuBLAS uses on the near-parity square-Q shapes (Part 2)
- Is the highest-leverage optimization to the existing kernel (Part 3)
- IS the correct way to build the "256×256" tile (Part 4)

So the revised build insight: **before/alongside P1 (128×256), the 2×2-cluster capability is the single most valuable thing to add** — it unlocks a large fraction of shapes at once.

## cuBLAS — separate pre-compiled kernel per (tile × cluster) combo

We *proved* this ourselves: in the fatbin, `128x128_2x2`, `256x256_2x2`, `128x256_2x1_v`, `128x256_2x2f`, etc. are all **distinct compiled cubins** (§2, §16.1). cuBLAS does NOT have one kernel that flips cluster at runtime. Instead:

1. **Internally generates** many kernels from templates (each tile × cluster × stages × layout = one kernel)
2. **Ships them as separate pre-compiled binaries** in the fatbin (~60-80 BF16 GEMM cubins)
3. **At runtime, the heuristic (§20.2) picks WHICH pre-compiled cubin to load** for the shape

So cuBLAS = "template-generate everything ahead of time → ship as separate binaries → runtime heuristic selects one." The cluster shape is a **compile-time constant baked into each separate binary** — exactly like our `__cluster_dims__(2,1,1)` attribute, just with many variants pre-built instead of one.

### (a) Template Parameter vs Separate Kernel vs Runtime

**CUTLASS uses TEMPLATE PARAMETERS (one kernel template, many instantiations)** with optional **RUNTIME support for dynamic cluster shapes**.

```cpp
    ArchTag, OperatorClass,
    MmaTileShape_MNK, ClusterShape_MNK,  // &lt;-- Template parameter
    ...&gt;::CollectiveOp;

using CollectiveMainloop = typename cutlass::gemm::collective::CollectiveBuilder&lt;
    ArchTag, OperatorClass,
    ElementA, LayoutA, AlignmentA,
    ElementB, LayoutB, AlignmentB,
    ElementAccumulator,
    MmaTileShape_MNK, ClusterShape_MNK,  // &lt;-- Template parameter
    ...&gt;::CollectiveOp;
```

The `CollectiveBuilder` template (defined in `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/collective_builder_decl.hpp:77-95`) takes `ClusterShape_MNK` as a template argument and generates a specialized kernel for that shape.

**Dynamic cluster shapes:** CUTLASS also supports **runtime-determined cluster shapes** using `Shape&lt;int,int,_1&gt;` as the template parameter. In `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/examples/74_blackwell_gemm_streamk/blackwell_gemm_streamk.cu:137`:

```cpp

```

This creates a **single kernel template that supports multiple cluster shapes at runtime**.

### (b) Compile-Time or Runtime Cluster Dims

**For static clusters:** Cluster dimensions are **baked in at COMPILE-TIME**. The template parameter `Shape&lt;_2,_2,_1&gt;` (concrete dimension constants) means the cluster shape is known and optimized at kernel generation time.

**For dynamic clusters:** When using `Shape&lt;int,int,_1&gt;`, the kernel is compiled once but the actual cluster dimensions are **set at RUNTIME** via the launch arguments. In the kernel source (`/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:133`):


At runtime, dimensions are resolved via `cutlass::detail::select_cluster_shape()` in `/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/include/cutlass/detail/cluster.hpp:51-68`:

```cpp
template &lt;class ClusterShape&gt;
static auto
select_cluster_shape(ClusterShape cluster_shape, dim3 dynamic_cluster_shape) {
  return cute::conditional_return&lt;not cute::is_static_v&lt;ClusterShape&gt;&gt;(
    make_shape(static_cast&lt;int&gt;(dynamic_cluster_shape.x), 
               static_cast&lt;int&gt;(dynamic_cluster_shape.y),
```

The runtime values come from `arguments.hw_info.cluster_shape` set by the user. In the stream-K example (`/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/cutlass/examples/74_blackwell_gemm_streamk/blackwell_gemm_streamk.cu:421-422`):

**Yes, CUTLASS explicitly supports dynamic clusters.** Evidence includes:

### (d) Verdict (1 paragraph)

**CUTLASS parameterizes cluster shape through template specialization on `ClusterShape_MNK`, allowing two modes: (1) static compile-time shapes like `Shape&lt;_2,_2,_1&gt;` that stamp out optimized kernels for specific cluster configurations, and (2) dynamic runtime shapes using `Shape&lt;int,int,_1&gt;` where a single kernel template supports multiple cluster dimensions set at launch time via `hw_info.cluster_shape`. ## Investigation Summary

Based on my thorough examination of ThunderKittens' B200 BF16 GEMM kernel and related codebase:

**(a) Does TK use clusters?** 
YES. ThunderKittens uses CTA clusters extensively for its B200 kernels.

**(b) Is cluster shape a user-set template/config constant or hardcoded?**
User-set template/config constant. Each kernel's `config` struct defines `CLUSTER_SIZE` as a static constexpr that users instantiate when calling the kernel.

**(c) How ThunderKittens handles cluster shape:**

ThunderKittens treats cluster shape as a **hardcoded 1D linear cluster** (not 2D spatial). The cluster is always defined as `(CLUSTER_SIZE, 1, 1)` where CLUSTER_SIZE is a template parameter users specify in the config struct. 

**Proof and Evidence:**

1. **Config struct defines CLUSTER_SIZE (line 27, bf16_b200_gemm.cu):**
   ```cpp
   static constexpr int CLUSTER_SIZE = 2;
   ```
   This is user-configurable via template instantiation.

2. **B200 kernel uses tcgen05 2-CTA cooperative MMA (line 178, bf16_b200_gemm.cu):**
   ```cpp
   detail::tcgen05::commit&lt;C::CLUSTER_SIZE&gt;(outputs_arrived[warpgroup::warpid()]);
   ```
   The template parameter `C::CLUSTER_SIZE` is passed to tcgen05::commit, binding the MMA to cluster operations.

3. **Educational kernel declares explicit __cluster_dims__ (line 32, educational_b200/level_09.cu):**
   ```cpp
   __cluster_dims__(CLUSTER_SIZE, 1, 1)
   ```
   This shows the shape is always 1D (CLUSTER_SIZE × 1 × 1), never 2D spatial clusters.

4. **LaunchConfig construction accepts only scalar CLUSTER_SIZE (line 315, bf16_b200_gemm.cu):**
   ```cpp
   LaunchConfig&lt;true, true&gt; launch_config(g[0].grid(), g[0].block(), g[0].dynamic_shared_memory(), 0, C::CLUSTER_SIZE);
   ```
   The constructor (util.cuh:525-526) treats this as a dim3(CLUSTER_SIZE, 1, 1).

5. **Parallel GEMM kernels define CLUSTER_M and CLUSTER_N (line 33, gemm_rs_b200.cu):**
   ```cpp
   constexpr int CLUSTER_M = 4*Mb, CLUSTER_N = Nb;
   ```
   These are *problem-space* tile sizes, NOT cluster dimensions. The cluster itself remains `CLUSTER_SIZE=2` (line 36).

**Verdict:** ThunderKittens implements clusters as **1D linear CTAs** where the cluster shape is always `(CLUSTER_SIZE, 1, 1)`. The CLUSTER_SIZE is a user-configurable template constant set per problem size. Users cannot specify 2D cluster shapes (e.g., 2×2); clusters are always a linear chain of CTAs. # How each library parameterizes cluster shape

| Library | Cluster mechanism | Compile-time or runtime | One kernel or many? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **cuBLAS** | Pre-compiled cubin per (tile×cluster×stages×layout) | Compile-time (baked per binary) | **Many separate binaries**, heuristic picks at runtime |
| **CUTLASS** | `ClusterShape_MNK` template param — `Shape<_2,_2,_1>` (static) OR `Shape<int,int,_1>` (dynamic) | **Both** — compile-time specialization OR runtime via `hw_info.cluster_shape` | One template → many instantiations; can also do runtime-dynamic |
| **DeepGEMM** | JIT template constants `kNumMulticast`, `kIsMulticastOnA` + `cudaLaunchAttributeClusterDimension` at launch | Compile-time constant per JIT instance (recompiles per shape) | Fresh kernel JIT-compiled per shape→cluster choice |
| **ThunderKittens** | `CLUSTER_SIZE` config constant + `__cluster_dims__(CLUSTER_SIZE,1,1)` | Compile-time (user-set) | User hand-picks per problem; **1D clusters only** (no 2×2!) |
| **Us (now)** | `__cluster_dims__(2,1,1)` hardcoded | Compile-time, fixed | One kernel, one cluster |

## The key patterns

**1. Everyone bakes the multicast logic into the kernel at compile-time.** Nobody makes one kernel that flips its *internal* 4-CTA-vs-2-CTA data-sharing logic at runtime — because the multicast masks, mbarrier counts, and smem-sharing must be known at compile time for the code to be efficient. This is universal.

**2. Two sub-styles for the launch dimension:**
- **`__cluster_dims__` attribute** (compile-time fixed): us + ThunderKittens + CUTLASS-static
- **`cudaLaunchKernelEx` + `cudaLaunchAttributeClusterDimension`** (runtime launch attr): DeepGEMM + CUTLASS-dynamic

The launch attribute is more flexible (same kernel launched at different cluster dims), but the *body* still needs matching multicast logic.

**3. ThunderKittens is a striking data point:** it uses **only 1D linear clusters** `(CLUSTER_SIZE,1,1)` — **no 2×2 spatial clusters at all.** So even a serious Blackwell kernel framework ships without the 2×2 capability. That tells you 2×2 is genuinely advanced/optional, not table-stakes.

**4. CUTLASS is the gold standard** — one `ClusterShape_MNK` template param handles everything, including runtime-dynamic clusters with hardware-fallback. This is what we'd converge to eventually.

## What this means for OUR build (the actual guidance)

The reference consensus **validates and refines** my earlier recommendation:

- **Everyone uses a template parameter for cluster shape** (CUTLASS `ClusterShape`, DeepGEMM `kNumMulticast`, TK `CLUSTER_SIZE`). So the *clean* long-term design is: **make cluster shape a template parameter of our kernel** (`CLUSTER_M`, `CLUSTER_N`), like CUTLASS. That's the "Approach A" (templatize) I described — and it's what the pros do.

- **BUT the multicast body logic genuinely differs** for 2-CTA vs 4-CTA (confirmed everywhere — masks, counts, rank mapping). So the template will have `if constexpr (CLUSTER_N==2)` branches, OR you specialize.

- **My recommendation stands with a refinement**: 
  1. **First**, build the 2×2 as a **separate variant** (protect the working 2×1 baseline while you get the hard 4-CTA multicast right) — this is the fast, low-risk path to prove it on q25-7b-K.
  2. **Then refactor** to a CUTLASS-style single template with `CLUSTER_M/CLUSTER_N` params (the clean end-state everyone converges to).

- **Consider switching from `__cluster_dims__` to `cudaLaunchKernelEx`** for the cluster dim (like DeepGEMM/CUTLASS-dynamic). It's more flexible and is where the ecosystem is heading — but not required for the first experiment.

## Bottom line for your question

You asked: *separate variant, or modify the existing one?* 

**The pros' answer: cluster shape should ultimately be a template PARAMETER (modify → parameterize), like CUTLASS's `ClusterShape`.** But the practical path to get there safely is: **build 2×2 as a separate variant first** (don't risk the 42/42-passing 2×1 baseline while debugging 4-CTA multicast), prove it on q25-7b-K, **then unify** into one parameterized template. That gives you the reference-grade design without gambling the working kernel.

## Critical clarification: `if constexpr` is NOT runtime hardcoding

You asked: *"for that we need to hardcode again in that if-else block?"* — Here's the key point:

```cpp
template <int BM, int BN, int BK, int QUEUE_SIZE, int CLUSTER_M, int CLUSTER_N>
__global__ __cluster_dims__(CLUSTER_M, CLUSTER_N, 1) void kernel(...) {
    if constexpr (CLUSTER_N == 2) {
        // 4-CTA multicast logic — compiled ONLY into the <...,2,2> instance
    } else {
        // current 2-CTA logic — compiled ONLY into the <...,2,1> instance
    }
}
```

When you instantiate `<...,2,1>`, the compiler **physically deletes** the `CLUSTER_N==2` branch — that instance is byte-for-byte as clean and fast as a separate kernel, **zero runtime cost, zero runtime if-else.** Same for `<...,2,2>`. Deep analysis done. Here's the answer — and it's a great find.

# YES — SM89 is FULLY templatized. In fact it's MORE templatized than our SM103 cluster kernels.

## What SM89 does (the proven in-house blueprint)

SM89 uses a clean 4-level template structure in `Bgemm_core_template.cuh` + `Bgemm_sm89_variants.cu`:

**Level 1 — tile config as a template struct:**
```cpp
template <int BM_, int BN_, int BK_, int STAGES_, int THREADS_>
struct BgemmTileConfig { ... };   // all tile dims are compile-time constants
```

**Level 2 — ONE kernel, templated on config + aligned + splitK + LAYOUT:**
```cpp
enum class BgemmLayout { NT, TN, NN };

template <typename Config, bool IsAligned, int SplitK, BgemmLayout Layout>
__global__ void bgemm_..._template_kernel(...)   // ONE kernel handles ALL 3 layouts
```

**Level 3 — thin launch wrapper (instantiates the template):**
```cpp
template <int BM,int BN,int BK,int STAGES,int THREADS, bool IsAligned,int SplitK,BgemmLayout Layout>
void launch_bgemm_variant(...) {
    using Config = BgemmTileConfig<BM,BN,BK,STAGES,THREADS>;
    bgemm_..._template_kernel<Config, IsAligned, SplitK, Layout><<<grid,THREADS,smem>>>(...);
}
```

**Level 4 — dispatch picks aligned/splitK at runtime, instantiates:**
```cpp
template <int BM,int BN,int BK,int STAGES,int THREADS, BgemmLayout Layout>
void dispatch_bgemm_layout(...) {
    bool aligned = ...;   // runtime check
    if (aligned && splitK<=1) launch_bgemm_variant<...,true,1,Layout>(...);
    else if (...) launch_bgemm_variant<...,true,4,Layout>(...);
}
```

So all the SM89 "variants" (`nn_256x128_32x3`, `nn_128x256_32x3`, `nn_64x64_32x6`…) are **just instantiations of ONE kernel template** with different `<BM,BN,BK,STAGES>`. **Even the layout (NT/TN/NN) is a template parameter** — one kernel, three layouts via `if constexpr (Layout == ...)`.

## SM89 vs our SM103 cluster kernels — the contrast

| Aspect | SM89 (mature) | SM103 cluster (new) |
|---|---|---|
| **Tile size** | template param (`BgemmTileConfig`) | template param ✓ (`<BM,BN,BK,QUEUE>`) |
| **Layout NT/NN/TN** | **template param** (1 kernel, all 3) | **3 SEPARATE FILES** |
| **Aligned** | template param (`bool IsAligned`) | not parameterized |
| **SplitK** | template param (`int SplitK`) | none |
| **Cluster** | N/A (Ada has no clusters) | **hardcoded `__cluster_dims__(2,1,1)`** |
| **How variants are made** | instantiations of 1 template | tile-instantiations of 3 per-layout templates |

**Our SM103 cluster code is actually LESS templatized than SM89.** SM89 already unified all three layouts + aligned + splitK into ONE kernel via template params. Our SM103 has 3 separate files and a hardcoded cluster.

## What this means for us (the important takeaway)

1. **SM89 is our in-house blueprint.** The templatized approach we decided on for SM103 (add `CLUSTER_M/CLUSTER_N` as template params) is **exactly the pattern SM89 already proves works** in this codebase. We're not inventing — we're mirroring a proven in-house design. That de-risks it.

2. **Our Phase 1 plan is correct and consistent.** Adding cluster as a template param to the SM103 kernel makes it match SM89's philosophy (tile + everything = template params → variants are instantiations).

3. **BUT — scope discipline: don't over-reach.** SM89 merges all 3 layouts into one kernel because its math is simple (`mma.sync`). The SM103 tcgen05 kernels have **layout-specific TMA/descriptor setup** that's much more divergent — merging TN/NN/NT into one file would be a big, risky refactor. So for **Phase 1, just add `CLUSTER_M/CLUSTER_N` to each of the 3 existing per-layout files** (mirror SM89's tile-parameterization per file), and **leave the 3-file layout split alone** for now. Unifying layouts is a separate, optional later cleanup.

## Bottom line

- **SM89: fully templatized** (tile + layout + aligned + splitK all template params, one kernel).
- **SM103 cluster: partially templatized** (tile is a param, but layout=3 files, cluster hardcoded).
- Our plan to **add cluster as a template param mirrors SM89's proven pattern** — good, low-risk direction.
- Keep Phase 1 scoped: add cluster params to the existing 3 files, don't merge layouts yet.

`nvjet` **is** cuBLAS's kernel (nvjet = NVIDIA's internal codename inside cuBLAS). So this is really **cuBLAS's structure vs OUR structure**. Here's the field-by-field comparison:

## cuBLAS naming vs BluBLAS naming — mapped field by field

Our kernel's actual name (from nsys): `bgemm_sm103_bf16_tn_cluster_kernel<128, 128, 64, 8>`

| # | Field | cuBLAS (`nvjet_sm103_tst_128x256_64x6_2x2f_2cta_h_bz_NTT`) | BluBLAS (ours) | Match? |
|--:|---|---|---|:--:|
| 1 | Codename | `nvjet` (NVIDIA internal) | `bgemm...cluster` (descriptive) | cosmetic |
| 2 | Arch | `sm_103` (native SASS) | `sm_103a` (compute_103a PTX→JIT) | ✓ same target |
| 3 | Tensor tile | `tst` (tensor cores) | implicit (we use tcgen05) | ✓ same HW |
| 4 | **Tile BM×BN** | **128×256** (+ 6 other sizes) | **128×128 ONLY** | ❌ we have 1 of 7 |
| 5 | **BK × stages** | **64×6** (varies 5-8/shape) | **64×8** (fixed) | ⚠️ fixed, not tuned |
| 6 | **Cluster** | **2×2** (+ 2×1, 2×4, 1×2, 4×1) | **2×1 ONLY** | ❌ we have 1 of 6 |
| 7 | **Fused epi (`f`)** | **yes** (`2x2f`) | **no fusion** | ❌ missing |
| 8 | cta_group | `2cta` (cta_group::2) | `2cta` (CTA_GROUP_SIZE=2) | ✓ **same** |
| 9 | **Wave order** | **`h` or `v`** (picked per shape) | **Hilbert-curve** (fixed) | ⚠️ different + fixed |
| 10 | Batching (`bz`) | yes | yes (batchCount) | ✓ same |
| 11 | **Layout suffix** | **NTT/NNT/TNT** (1 kernel, param) | **3 separate files** (TN/NN/NT) | ⚠️ not unified |

## What the comparison reveals

**Where we already MATCH cuBLAS (the foundation is sound):**
- ✅ Same arch (sm_103), same tensor-core path (tcgen05), same **2-CTA cooperative MMA** (`cta_group::2`), same batching. Our *core MMA engine* is on par — we're not missing fundamentals.

**Where cuBLAS has knobs we've hardcoded to ONE value:**
- ❌ **Tile size**: cuBLAS varies across 7 tiles (128×256, 256×256, 128×64, 64×64…); we have **only 128×128**.
- ❌ **Cluster shape**: cuBLAS uses 6 shapes (2×2, 2×1, 2×4…); we have **only 2×1**.
- ⚠️ **Stages**: cuBLAS tunes 5-8 per shape; we're **fixed at 8**.
- ❌ **Fused epilogue**: cuBLAS has a fused variant (`f`); we have **none**.
- ⚠️ **Wave order**: cuBLAS picks `h`/`v` per shape; we use a **fixed Hilbert curve** (interesting — a *third* strategy, neither pure-h nor pure-v).

**Structural difference:**
- ⚠️ **Layout**: cuBLAS = one kernel, layout as a suffix/param. We = 3 separate files. (SM89, as we just saw, unifies layout as a template param — so cuBLAS and our own SM89 both do it cleaner than our SM103.)

## The one-line summary

> **cuBLAS's naming is a coordinate in a multi-axis design space (tile × stages × cluster × fusion × wave × layout). We currently occupy exactly ONE point in that space: `128×128 · 64×8 · 2×1 · no-fusion · Hilbert · {3 files}`. Our MMA core matches cuBLAS; what we lack is the *parameterization* to move along those axes.**

This is exactly why the templatization plan matters: each field in cuBLAS's name that we've hardcoded (tile, cluster, stages, fusion) should become a **template parameter**, so we can generate the other points in the space — just like cuBLAS pre-generates its whole grid of nvjet kernels, and just like our own SM89 already does for tile/layout/splitK.

## Interesting observation — our Hilbert wave order

Notice field #9: cuBLAS uses simple `h` (horizontal) or `v` (vertical) wave ordering, but **our kernel uses a Hilbert-curve tile ordering** (per the file header: "Hilbert-curve tile ordering for L2 cache locality"). That's actually a *more sophisticated* scheduling choice than cuBLAS's h/v on this axis — a rare case where we do something fancier. Worth keeping in mind: when we add the 2×2 cluster, we may find our Hilbert ordering interacts differently with multicast than cuBLAS's vertical wave does. Something to measure.

### CLAUDE [2026-07-02 16:39 IST]

Let me clear up the core confusion, because this is a **hardware** fact, not a code-design choice.

## SM89 has NO cluster variants — because SM89 hardware has NO clusters AT ALL

**Thread-block clusters do not exist on sm_89 (Ada Lovelace — L4, RTX 40-series).** Clusters are a hardware feature introduced in **sm_90 (Hopper)** and carried into **sm_100/sm_103 (Blackwell)**. Ada physically lacks the hardware for them. So it's not that we "forgot to templatize clusters" for SM89 — **there is literally nothing to templatize, because the GPU can't do clusters.**

## Why clusters don't exist on Ada — the hardware reason

A "cluster" (a.k.a. CGA — Cooperative Grid Array) is a group of CTAs (thread blocks) that can:
- **Synchronize** with each other (cluster-wide barrier), and
- **Read each other's shared memory** (Distributed Shared Memory / DSMEM), and
- **Multicast** TMA loads (load once, broadcast to multiple CTAs).

All of this needs dedicated **SM-to-SM network hardware** inside the GPC (GPU Processing Cluster). That hardware:
- ❌ **Ada (sm_89)**: not present → no clusters
- ✅ **Hopper (sm_90)**: introduced → clusters + DSMEM + TMA
- ✅ **Blackwell (sm_100/sm_103)**: present + tcgen05 → clusters + TMA multicast + cooperative MMA

## What SM89 uses instead (confirmed from the code)

SM89 kernels use the **old, per-warp MMA** with plain independent CTAs:

```cpp
// Bgemm_core_template.cuh line 11 — the MMA instruction:
"mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16.row.col.f32.bf16.bf16.f32 ..."   // per-WARP, no cluster
```
```cpp
// launch_bgemm_variant — the launch:
bgemm_..._template_kernel<...><<<grid, THREADS, smem_bytes, stream>>>(...)  // PLAIN triple-chevron
```

Notice: `<<<grid, block, smem, stream>>>` — a **plain launch, no `__cluster_dims__`, no cluster attribute.** Each CTA works alone. No cross-CTA cooperation exists or is possible.

## So, answering each of your questions directly

| Your question | Answer |
|---|---|
| SM89 variants don't have cluster variants? | **Correct — NONE.** |
| Why? What's this? | **Ada (sm_89) hardware has no cluster feature. Clusters are sm_90+ only.** |
| Is that efficient? | **Yes, for Ada** — it's the *only* option and the right one for that HW. Ada just has a lower performance ceiling (no clusters, no TMA, no tcgen05) than Blackwell. |
| For clusters, not templatized? | **Nothing to templatize** — the feature doesn't exist on sm_89. |
| Do we have separate clustered variants (like Approach B)? | **No.** |
| Or we don't even have at all? | **Correct: we don't have them AND can't — the hardware doesn't support clusters.** |

## The clean mental model — clusters are a per-architecture hardware axis

| Module | Arch | Clusters? | MMA type | Cluster in our code? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SM89** | Ada | ❌ hardware has none | `mma.sync` (per-warp) | N/A — impossible |
| **SM103** | Blackwell | ✅ yes | `tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2` (cooperative) | yes — currently hardcoded 2×1 |

## Don't confuse two different axes

SM89 **does** have **tile variants** (256×128, 128×256, 64×64…) — all templatized via `BgemmTileConfig<BM,BN,BK,...>`. That's the **tile-size axis**, and SM89 parameterizes it cleanly.

But **tile variants ≠ cluster variants.** These are separate axes:
- **Tile size** (BM×BN): SM89 has this, templatized ✓. SM103 has it (only 128×128 so far).
- **Cluster shape** (2×1, 2×2…): only exists on sm_90+. SM89 → N/A. SM103 → this is the new axis we're adding.

So when we templatize cluster shape for SM103, we're adding an axis that **only SM103 (and any future Hopper/Blackwell module) can even have.** SM89's template simply doesn't need that axis — and correctly doesn't have it.

## Bottom line

> SM89 has **no cluster variants and cannot have any** — clusters are a Hopper/Blackwell-only hardware feature, absent on Ada. SM89 is efficient *for Ada* using per-warp `mma.sync` with plain CTA launches. The cluster axis is **exclusively an SM103 concern** — which is exactly why our templatization work (adding `CLUSTER_M/CLUSTER_N`) applies only to the SM103 kernels, not SM89. SM89 remains our blueprint for the *tile/layout/splitK* parameterization pattern, just not for clusters (which it structurally can't have).

This is a great framing — you're right that more variants = more experimentation platform, and copying cuBLAS is the learning/reverse-engineering step before we go beyond it. Let me do the deep analysis on the restrictions, the 256×256 mystery, and how the pros achieve full flexibility.

## 1. The fundamental hardware fact that explains everything: TMEM has only 128 lanes

Blackwell's Tensor Memory (TMEM) — where the MMA accumulator lives — is **128 lanes (rows) × 512 columns**. An M×N output tile occupies **M lanes × N columns**. Therefore:

> **A single CTA's accumulator can hold at most 128 output rows.** Per-CTA BM ≤ 128, always. This is a hard hardware wall.

This single fact resolves the whole 256×256 confusion:
- To produce **>128 output rows, you MUST use multiple CTAs** cooperating (a cluster), each holding ≤128 rows.
- That's *exactly why* our kernel uses 2 CTAs (cluster 2×1) to make a 256-row tile: each CTA holds 128 rows in its TMEM, together = 256 rows.
- **Per-CTA BM=256 is doubly impossible**: it exceeds TMEM's 128 lanes AND exceeds the MMA M=256 limit (2×256=512). That's why our "256×256 API" *can't* work as written and falls back.

## 2. So how do bigger tiles ACTUALLY get built? By adding CTAs (bigger cluster), not bigger per-CTA tiles

| Output tile you want | How it's physically built | Cluster needed |
|---|---|---|
| 128×N (≤128 rows) | 1 CTA | 1×1 (no cluster) |
| **256×N** | 2 CTAs (each 128 rows) | **2×1** ← what we have |
| 256×N with N-multicast | 2 CTAs split M + share operands | 2×1 (our kernel) |
| **512×N or 256×2N** | 4 CTAs | **2×2** ← the hard work |

**Key realization**: our *buildable* "128×256" kernel (per-CTA BM=128, BN=256, cluster 2×1) already produces a **256×256 cluster-level output** (2 CTAs × 128 rows = 256 M, × 256 N). So we may already get most of a "256×256"-class tile's benefit from the easy 128×256 build — without any cluster change!

## 3. The 256×256 mystery — resolved (with an honest caveat)

**Why we currently hardcode 256×256 → 128×128:** because per-CTA BM=256 is hardware-impossible (TMEM 128 lanes + MMA M limit). The fallback is correct given the current 2×1 cluster.

**What cuBLAS's `256x256_2x2` actually is:** a **2×2 cluster (4 CTAs)**, each CTA holding 128 rows, cooperating to make a larger cluster-level tile. It is NOT a single CTA doing 256×256 (impossible). To build our own genuine 256×256, we need the **4-CTA (2×2) cluster machinery** — i.e., it IS the cluster work (Workstream B), not a separate thing.

**Honest caveat**: I have NOT definitively cracked whether cuBLAS names its tiles by *per-CTA* or *cluster-level* dimensions (the `128x128_2x2` vs `256x256_2x2` naming is ambiguous, flagged in §23.3). But it doesn't block us — the hardware truth (128 rows/CTA, bigger tile = more CTAs) is certain, and we build + measure against cuBLAS's number empirically.

**Did our past tests find/measure the valid 256×256?** No — we measured **cuBLAS's** 256×256 number (q3-8b-Down, 1756 T clean), but we have **never built our own** — our API falls back to 128×128. So we have the *target*, not our own implementation. We can only test our own once we build the 2×2 cluster.

## 4. The full list of RESTRICTIONS in our kernel + what to change for each

To unlock all variants (and future experimentation), here's every restriction and its fix:

| # | Restriction | Caused by | Limits us to | Fix to unlock |
|--:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Per-CTA BM ≤ 128** | TMEM 128 lanes (HW) | BM ∈ {64,128} | can't change — use clusters for bigger M |
| 2 | **MMA M ≤ 256** | cta_group::2 kind::f16 (HW) | 2×BM ≤ 256 | can't change — bigger cluster |
| 3 | **BN multiple of 128** | B-TMA loads 64-elem atoms split by 2 CTAs (line 307) | BN ∈ {128,256,384} | **parameterize B-load** (chunk size + split) → allows BN=64,192, etc. |
| 4 | **Cluster fixed 2×1** | `__cluster_dims__(2,1,1)` hardcoded (line 335) | 2 CTAs only | **templatize cluster** (Workstream B) → 2×2, 4×1 |
| 5 | **NUM_EPI_STAGES=2** | fixed (line 44) | BN ≤ 256 (TMEM 512) | **parameterize stages** → BN=512 with stages=1 |
| 6 | **cta_group::2 fixed** | `CTA_GROUP_SIZE=2` conflated | one MMA mode | **decouple** cta_group from cluster |
| 7 | **Layout in 3 files** | historical | separate TN/NN/NT | unify as template param (like SM89) — optional |

**The two highest-leverage unlocks:**
- **#3 (parameterize B-TMA)** → unlocks all BN values (skinny-N 64, non-128-mult 160/192) → most tile variants.
- **#4+#6 (templatize + decouple cluster)** → unlocks 2×2, 4×1 clusters → bigger tiles + the 256×256, and the cluster-experimentation you want.

## 5. How cuBLAS / CUTLASS / DeepGEMM / ThunderKittens achieve full flexibility

This is the "what should we change to allow all variants" answer, learned from the references:

| Library | Flexibility mechanism |
|---|---|
| **CUTLASS** | **Everything is a template param** (TileShape M/N/K, ClusterShape M/N, stages). The `CollectiveBuilder` metaprogram *auto-generates* the correct TMA descriptors, smem layout, and mbarrier counts for ANY valid combination. Max flexibility via C++ metaprogramming. |
| **DeepGEMM** | **JIT codegen** — substitutes chosen params (tile, cluster, stages) into the kernel source and compiles a fresh kernel per config at runtime. Flexibility via code generation. |
| **cuBLAS** | Pre-generates ALL valid combos (from CUTLASS-style templates) → ships ~thousands of cubins. Flexibility via exhaustive pre-generation. |
| **ThunderKittens** | Tile/layout **types** are templated; the B-load and smem layout adapt to the tile type automatically. (But 1D clusters only.) |

**The common lesson**: they all make the restricted axes (tile, cluster, stages, AND crucially the *TMA/smem layout*) **parameters**, with the descriptor/smem/mbarrier setup **derived automatically** from those params. Our kernel hardcodes the B-TMA structure and cluster, so those axes are frozen. **To allow all variants, we parameterize those axes and derive the TMA/smem config from them** — exactly CUTLASS's approach, just more manual.

## 6. Recommendation — the flexibility roadmap (build the experimentation platform)

You want a platform to experiment across tile × cluster × stages. Here's the order that unlocks the most experimentation for the least risk:

**Step 1 (now) — Build 128×256** (the one easy tile, restriction-free). Gives immediate wins + proves the loop. Also *already gives a 256×256 cluster-output* (§2).

**Step 2 — Parameterize the B-TMA (restriction #3+#5)** → unlocks all BN values (skinny-N 64, 192, 160...). Now we can experiment with *any tile width*. This is the biggest flexibility unlock for tiles.

## Q2: "After templatizing cluster, will it auto-select 2×2 for 256×256 at compile time?"

**No — there's no auto-magic. Let me correct that mental model.** Templatizing makes cluster a **template parameter** (`CLUSTER_M, CLUSTER_N`). That gives us the *ability* to instantiate different clusters — but **WE** decide which combos to instantiate and **WE** write the dispatch rule that routes a shape to the right one. Concretely:

```cpp
// We explicitly instantiate the combos we want:
launch<BM=128, BN=256, CLUSTER=2x1>   // 256×256 macro-tile, 2 CTAs
launch<BM=128, BN=256, CLUSTER=2x2>   // 512×256 macro-tile, 4 CTAs

// And WE write the routing (hardcoded, like SM89):
if (shape is fat-K big)  dispatch → <128,256, 2x2>;
else                     dispatch → <128,256, 2x1>;
```

- **Compile time**: which `(tile, cluster)` instantiations exist (we list them).
- **Runtime**: which one the dispatcher picks per shape (our hardcoded rule).

There's no cost model auto-choosing — it's our explicit instantiation + our explicit dispatch, exactly like SM89 and cuBLAS's pre-generation.

## Q3: "Let's do the flexibility work now — start with that?"

Here I want to make one strong case before we commit, because I found something that might save us the hardest work entirely:

### The 128×256 kernel ALREADY produces a 256×256 cluster output — with ZERO cluster work

Our 2×1 cluster = 2 CTAs, each 128 rows → cluster covers **256 M-rows**. With BN=256 → **256 N-cols**. So `launch<128, 256, 2x1>` computes a **256×256 macro-tile per cluster** — using the cluster we *already have working*.

**This means**: for the fat shapes where cuBLAS uses "256×256" (q3-8b-Down), our easy 128×256 (2×1) might **already match or beat cuBLAS** — capturing the big-tile benefit *without* the hard 2×2 cluster work.

### So the smart move: build 128×256 FIRST, and let the data decide if we even NEED the hard cluster work

- If 128×256 (2×1) already matches cuBLAS on the fat/wide shapes → **we may not need the 2×2 cluster at all for them.** Huge risk reduction.
- If it still lags on specific shapes → *those* shapes justify the hard cluster work, and we do it targeted.

Doing the hard flexibility work (parameterize B-TMA + 4-CTA multicast cluster) **first**, before we've even confirmed we can build+test ONE new variant, is high-risk: it's ~15 sites of intricate change, it could break our working 42/42 baseline, and we might discover afterward that 128×256 already covered most shapes.

**Start with 128×256 (Step 1) — it needs NONE of the flexibility work, gives the biggest wins, produces a 256×256 cluster output, and its results tell us how much of the hard flexibility work is actually necessary.** Then do the B-TMA + cluster parameterization (Steps 2-3) *guided by the data*, targeting only the shapes that still lag.

The flexibility platform IS the end goal — I'm only arguing about **order**: prove the easy, high-value variant first; let its results scope the hard work, instead of gambling on the hardest change up front.

### CLAUDE [2026-07-02 18:56 IST]

Good question — let me explain exactly what "full CUTLASS generality" means and how our scope is deliberately much smaller.

## What "full CUTLASS generality" means

CUTLASS can generate a *correct, optimized* kernel for basically **any combination** across a huge number of axes:

| Axis | CUTLASS supports | We need (Qwen BF16 B300) |
|---|---|---|
| **Data type** | fp16, bf16, fp8 (e4m3/e5m2), int8, tf32, fp32, fp64, complex… | **bf16 only** (fp32 accum) |
| **Architecture** | sm70/75/80/86/89/90/100/103/120… | **sm_103 only** |
| **Layouts** | NN, NT, TN, TT (A/B/C row/col independently) | NN, NT, TN (3) |
| **Tile shape** | dozens of M×N×K | BM∈{64,128}, BN∈{64…256} (a handful) |
| **Cluster shape** | 1×1, 2×1, 2×2, 4×1, 1×2, 2×4, 4×4, **dynamic**… | 2×1, 2×2 (maybe 4×1) |
| **Pipeline stages** | any N | a few values |
| **Epilogue** | bias, relu, gelu, silu, scale, split-K, stream-K, **custom fusion**… | mostly none (bias/SiLU later) |
| **Scheduler** | persistent, stream-K, data-parallel | persistent (CLC) only |
| **MMA atom / swizzle / alignment** | fully parameterized | fixed to our tcgen05 path |

And critically — CUTLASS **auto-derives** the smem layout, TMA descriptors, mbarrier counts, and warp specialization for **any** valid point in that entire cross-product, via tens of thousands of lines of C++ template metaprogramming (the `CollectiveBuilder`). That auto-derivation engine *is* "full generality."

## What we're doing instead (the small scope)

- **One dtype** (bf16), **one arch** (sm_103) — not parameterized at all.
- Only the **~4 axes that matter for Qwen**: tile (BM,BN), cluster (2×1/2×2), stages, and the B-TMA structure.
- Only the **specific values** Qwen needs (BM∈{64,128}, BN∈{64…256}) — not arbitrary.
- We **hand-write** the smem/TMA/mbarrier derivation for *our* handful of cases, instead of building a general auto-derivation engine.

## So — answering your question directly

> "we don't have that many parameters aah or what?"

**Correct — we deliberately have FAR fewer parameters, and fewer values per parameter, and only one dtype/one arch.** CUTLASS parameterizes ~10 axes × many values each × auto-derives everything for the full cross-product. We parameterize ~4 axes × a few values each, for bf16-on-sm_103 only, and hand-derive our specific cases.

## Why this matters (the point of the note)

Building "full CUTLASS generality" would basically mean **re-implementing CUTLASS** — tens of thousands of lines of metaprogramming to make *any* combination work. That's not tractable for a two-person team, and we don't need it.

We only need our small parameter set to work for the **42 Qwen shapes** (+ future Qwen shapes). Scoping tightly = the work stays a few focused kernel edits (B0–B3) instead of an open-ended compiler project. Then, as you said, experimenting = `launch<BM,BN,cluster,stages>` + one dispatch line — but only across *our* small, curated parameter space, not CUTLASS's infinite one.

That's all the note meant: **small, curated parameter set for our needs — not a general-purpose GEMM code generator.**

On the ~26 shapes where cuBLAS *also* uses a 128×256 kernel, our 128×256 ranges **77-105%, averaging ~90%.** So with the *same tile*, we're at 90% of cuBLAS — the remaining ~10% is cuBLAS's extra tuning (its 2×2 cluster + vertical wave + per-shape stages), which is exactly what B3 will chase. cuBLAS here = 826.9 T, but in the dedicated clean run (§21, reproduced twice) it was **1756.3 T** on the same shape. Every other cuBLAS number matches the dedicated run — only this one diverges 2×. ## Q1: Can we name it 128x256x64 instead of 256x256x64? — YES, recommended

The production API `_cluster_256x256x64` now runs `launch<128,256,64>`. Renaming it to **`_cluster_128x256x64`** makes it consistent with `_cluster_128x128x64` (per-CTA tile naming, like every other kernel). We do **not** need the "256x256x64" name.

## Q2: Does SM89 have a 256×256 tile variant? — NO

SM89/SM80 tile variants (all of them): **64×64, 128×64, 128×128, 128×256, 256×64, 256×128.** The biggest are 256×128 and 128×256. **There is NO 256×256 tile in SM89** — not the cluster kind (Ada has no clusters) and not even a plain 256×256 tile. On Ada the accumulator lives in **registers** (no TMEM); a 256×256 fp32 tile = 256 KB of registers, far beyond Ada's 64 KB/SM register file. So 256×256 is impossible on Ada regardless. SM89 tops out at 256×128 / 128×256.

2. **Consolidate** — add the config (`using Sm103Config_...`) to `.cuh` + wrappers to the 3 `_variants.cu` + a test in `test_bgemm_sm103_cluster_template.cu`.
3. **Wire** — point the dispatcher's shape-routing at the canonical wrappers.

For tile variants that fit BN%128 (like 128×256), adding a config to the `.cuh` is a **one-line change** that auto-works for all 3 layouts — so the `.cuh` is actually the *easier* place to work. For structural changes (B2 skinny-N B-TMA, B3 cluster 2×2), those go into the `.cuh` templated kernel.

// test_bgemm_sm103_cluster_template.cu
// Comprehensive accuracy and benchmark test suite for the unified SM103a
// Cluster GEMM template. Target: NVIDIA B300 (SM 10.3a) —
// tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2.kind::f16
//
// Usage:
//   make run TEST=examples/test_bgemm_sm103_cluster_template.cu
