what i thought to do
- our 128x256_2x2 variant still loses to cublas on the 8 target shapes and i wanted to go deep into the actual sass instructions and profiling and find the real inefficiency that is causing that gap and remove it and get us on par with cublas

what i did

today was a very heavy and hectic day and honestly i failed on almost every experiment and assumption i started with, but each failure narrowed things down and taught me something real, and by the end of the day i finally found the true reason for the gap, so i will explain the whole journey, first i did a proper instruction accounting where i mapped the sass and ptx back to our source lines using lineinfo and found the source lines that were generating the most integer and address math, like the descriptor encoding, the pipeline stage modulo, the epilogue store address and the producer smem address, and i compared our instruction mix against cublas and saw we had way more integer multiply add instructions than them, but then i caught an important mistake, that comparison was counting our whole binary which has all the template variants like nn nt tn swap and composite plus dead branches, against cublas which is one single specialised kernel, so it was not a fair one to one comparison and it had fooled me into thinking instructions were the problem

next in the morning i also went down the split-k path thinking our low k shapes were starving the gpu, but i realised that was a wrong direction because split-k is only for very skinny shapes where the gpu is truly under filled, and more importantly cublas itself does not use split-k on our 8 shapes, it runs the same plain 128x256 kernel, so there was no point in copying something cublas is not even doing, so i parked the entire split-k design as a clean future task and locked my focus back to only the 8 shapes that matter, and i stopped trusting the big 42 shape average which was mixing skinny shapes in and misleading me the whole time

then i actually went and fixed the redundant things i had found, first the index calculation, our pipeline stage counter was doing a divide by 6 modulo on every step which the compiler turns into an expensive magic multiply, and i replaced it with a simple increment and wrap, then i did the bigger one, the memory descriptor, where earlier we were rebuilding the full 64 bit descriptor from scratch on every single mma step, and i changed it so the base descriptor is built only once per stage and each step becomes just one add, using the maths that the descriptor of an address plus an offset equals the descriptor of the address plus that same offset shifted right by 4, as long as the offsets are aligned, so it stays perfectly bit exact, and both of these passed the full bit exact test suite, but the surprising part is they gave zero speedup at all, and i was really confused because removing redundant work should normally help, but the reason is that those extra instructions were never the real bottleneck, the tensor cores do the heavy matmul work asynchronously, and while they are busy on one tile the warps are just sitting and waiting for the next tile of data, so all those extra integer and address instructions were being issued during that waiting time and were completely hidden behind the wait and cost zero clock time, i also tried an l2 cache promotion hint and it moved the l2 hit metric a lot but again gave no speedup, because in a warm benchmark the data is already in l2 so there was nothing extra to save

after all these flat results i stopped guessing from static counts and profiled properly, one kernel of ours directly against one kernel of cublas, on each of the 8 shapes, and this is where i found the real thing, six of the eight shapes are already at 86 to 94 percent of cublas so they are basically fine, and the entire remaining gap is only on the two big down shapes that need more than one wave, and those are stuck around 68 percent, and the key point is that matmul at these sizes is a compute bound problem, meaning the tensor cores should be the busy bottleneck, and cublas proves it by keeping its tensor cores 82 percent busy, but ours only reach 54 percent even on a huge k of 11008, so our tensor cores are idle almost half the time, and the profiler showed me exactly why, cublas warps only stall waiting for the next data tile from shared memory which is the normal healthy behaviour for a compute bound kernel, but our warps waste around 30 percent extra time stalling on synchronization between the warps and between the tiles, and that synchronization is pure dead time where the tensor cores have nothing to do, and this overhead keeps piling up on the big multi wave shapes, so it is not a memory bandwidth problem at all, it is our own synchronization overhead that is starving the tensor cores, and this single finding cleanly explains why every instruction removal i did came out flat, i was fixing the wrong thing the whole time

so the biggest learning today is that not every redundancy costs time, if the work is hidden behind a wait then removing it changes nothing, and the only thing that actually matters is what the warps are stalled on, and for us that is synchronization, also i learnt to always compare one kernel to one kernel and not the whole binary, and to gate only on the 8 shapes and never on the mixed average, and even though the fixes gave no speedup i am keeping them because they are bit exact and cleaner and will help in cold cache and real training runs

what i will do tomorrow
- break down that synchronization stall into its exact reason like barrier or wait or fence and cut it on the two big shapes so our tensor cores stay fed like cublas, and i also found a strong future task, in mixed precision training our matmul already accumulates in fp32 internally and then we round it down to bf16 to store, and the very next operation converts it right back up to fp32, so if we directly write out the fp32 result wherever the next op needs fp32, like in the last layers and in attention, we can remove two full redundant conversions and save real time in the training pipeline

## where we are

## today's job — one clear target
**Name the exact sync stall, then cut it.** Yesterday we saw the *total* non-memory stall is 40.8% but didn't split it into which kind. That's step 1 today (fresh server, so we re-capture):

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas

nvidia-smi -lgc 1400
ncu --set full -k regex:bgemm -c 1 --cache-control none -f -o /tmp/o ./build/ncu_probe 4096 2048 11008 0 >/dev/null 2>&1
KSEL=cub ncu --set full -k regex:nvjet -c 1 --cache-control none -f -o /tmp/c ./build/ncu_probe 4096 2048 11008 0 >/dev/null 2>&1
nvidia-smi -rgc
for f in o c; do
  echo "==================== $f : warp-stall table ===================="
```

You're 100% right, bro — I overstated that. **SASS is the ground truth** — it's the *actual machine code* cuBLAS executes, nothing hidden. Not having the C++ source doesn't matter, because the source is just what *generates* the SASS. Everything cuBLAS actually *does* on the silicon is right there in the SASS, and that's literally what this whole rev-eng repo is for. Let me correct myself:

## What SASS + metrics let us fully reconstruct about cuBLAS (no source needed)
- **The mainloop structure** — how many MMAs, TMA loads, and barriers per k-iteration, and their exact ordering (this is the sync pattern we care about)
- **Pipeline depth** — count the load-buffer stages / mbarrier slots it cycles through
- **Warp specialization** — which warps do producer/consumer/epilogue (from the branch-on-warp-id + predication)
- **The barrier/fence pattern** — every `BAR`, `ELECT`, membar, `ACQBULK`, mbarrier arrive/wait is visible → this is exactly the "sync" question, provable from SASS not guessed
- **The epilogue** — how it reads TMEM, converts, stores
- **Occupancy math** — registers + smem give CTAs/SM directly

Combined with the ncu metrics (stalls, throughput, waves), **we can pin exactly where cuBLAS spends fewer cycles than us and why** — then copy that structure. That's the real path to beating it, and you're right that we already have everything we need for it.

The one honest caveat (not a blocker): SASS has no comments/symbols, so reconstructing it is *tedious* — we read it instruction-block by block and match patterns to known primitives (`UTCMMA`=tcgen05 mma, `UBLKCP`=TMA, etc.). But it's all there.

So the method locks in: **read cuBLAS's mainloop SASS side-by-side with ours, count the sync/loads/MMAs per iteration, find the structural difference — with the SASS lines as proof.**

**So the gap lives exactly where the kernel must STREAM operands from DRAM** (big shapes that exceed L2). There, cuBLAS delivers ~1.5× the memory bandwidth → keeps tensor cores at 81% while ours starve at 54%.

The dominant stall is **long-scoreboard on L1TEX = global memory** ("local, global, surface, texture"), **NOT shared-memory/sync** like I claimed yesterday. |---|---|---|---|

## The mechanism — read the stall shares carefully (this is the real insight)
This shape is **compute-bound** (arithmetic intensity ~1215 flop/byte). cuBLAS realizes it: its warps spend **89.9% of cycles waiting on global memory** (long-scoreboard on L1TEX) — that's *healthy*, it means the warps fire MMAs then wait for the next tile, and because it keeps enough memory in flight, the MMAs keep flowing → **81% compute**.

The other **40.8% of our cycles go to something else** that is **throttling how fast we issue memory requests** → so DRAM comes in slow → MMA starves to 54%. cuBLAS's "other" is only 10%.

**So the culprit is that 40.8% "other" stall — it's upstream, choking our memory issue rate.** That's the thing to name and kill.

## OURS vs cuBLAS — full breakdown (3b-Down, stable shape)
| metric | OURS | cuBLAS | what it means |
|---|---|---|---|

| Not-predicated threads/warp | 6.95 | 27.16 | same story |
| **Executed Instructions** | **4.11M** | **2.96M** | we issue **1.39× more** (proper dynamic count, single kernel) |

| Memory throughput | 914 GB/s | **1.49 TB/s** | cuBLAS 1.6× |
| **Issue Slots Busy** | **2.60%** | ~0.03 warp/sched | 🔑 **both issue <3% of cycles = latency-bound** |
| long-scoreboard stall | 22.9c (59.2%) | 40.3c (89.9%) | memory-wait dominates both |
| L2 Hit Rate | (cut) | 63.7% | — |
| Registers | 167 | 255 | — |

## The real story — 3 things now PROVEN
**1. This shape is memory-LATENCY-bound (both kernels).** Issue slots busy is only **2.6%** for us — we barely issue instructions, we sit waiting on global-memory loads (long-scoreboard). Neither kernel is near HBM bandwidth peak (914 GB/s and 1.49 TB/s are ~11% and 19% of B300's ~8 TB/s). So it's **latency**, not bandwidth.

**2. cuBLAS HIDES that latency, we don't.** cuBLAS keeps its **mem pipes 81.3% busy** — when data lands it immediately fires MMAs, so the tensor cores stay fed. Ours only reach **54.8%** — our pipe goes idle waiting. That 81 vs 55 IS the 68% duration gap.

**3. The instruction/active-thread inefficiency is REAL but NOT the wall-clock lever — and this finally explains why fix#1/#2 were flat.** We run 7.38 active lanes and 4.11M instructions (cuBLAS 31.95 lanes, 2.96M) — our single-threaded producer/consumer/scheduler warps burn issue slots on scalar address/loop work. **BUT issue slots are only 2.6% busy** — we have 97% idle issue capacity, so those extra instructions hide completely behind the memory wait and cost zero wall-clock. **That's exactly why removing them (fix#1/#2) did nothing.** ncu flags 42.9% "divergence speedup" but that's an optimistic heuristic — it's not the real bottleneck.

## So the ACTUAL lever (proven by elimination)
Not instructions, not sync, not L2 — it's **latency hiding: keep more memory loads in flight so the tensor pipe never starves.** cuBLAS does this (pipes 81% busy); we don't (55%). The knobs that control loads-in-flight: **pipeline depth** (cuBLAS name = `64x6` → 6 stages) and **registers** (255 vs our 167 → cuBLAS can hold more outstanding load state).

# ThunderKittens Blackwell (sm_100/B200) tcgen05 GEMM — Persistent Scheduler &amp; Pipeline Analysis

## TL;DR — YES, TK has a real Blackwell tcgen05 GEMM

TK ships a production BF16 tcgen05/TMA/TMEM GEMM at **`kernels/gemm/bf16_b200/bf16_b200_gemm.cu`** (1540 TFLOPs @ 4096³, per `kernels/gemm/educational_b200/README.md`). It is a **persistent kernel** whose "waves" are eliminated by NVIDIA's **hardware Cluster Launch Control (CLC)** — `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel` — *not* a manual grid-stride loop. The educational build-up (`educational_b200/level_01..09.cu`) is the same kernel minus persistence: level 09 (1285 TFLOPs) is the non-persistent 2-CTA cluster version, so comparing `level_09.cu` vs `bf16_b200_gemm.cu` isolates exactly the persistent-scheduler + cross-tile-pipelining machinery you care about.

This is directly relevant to your problem (55% vs 81% tensor-core busy, idle across wave-2): TK's design has **no per-tile/per-wave drain and no blocking cluster sync except once at kernel exit**.

---

## 1. PERSISTENT SCHEDULER — how tiles are handed out so wave-2 backfills without bubbles

**Grid = one cluster per output tile, then hardware work-stealing via CLC.** The grid is launched at full tile count (`bf16_b200_gemm.cu:50`):

```cpp
// bf16_b200_gemm.cu:50
dim3 grid() { return dim3(d.rows()/(C::NUM_CONSUMERS*C::Mb/2) * d.cols()/C::Nb); }
```

Each CTA computes an **initial** tile from `blockIdx.x`, then loops forever (`for(int task_iter=0; true; task_iter++)`) grabbing successive tiles from CLC until `try_cancel` fails:

- Initial coord: `bf16_b200_gemm.cu:122` and `:200`
  ```cpp
  int2 tile_coord = get_swizzled_2d_idx&lt;C::SUPERGROUP_SIZE&gt;(rblks, cblks, blockIdx.x/C::CLUSTER_SIZE);
  ```
- Next coord from CLC result: `:138`, `:207`
  ```cpp
  if (schedule.success) tile_coord = get_swizzled_2d_idx&lt;...&gt;(rblks, cblks, schedule.x/C::CLUSTER_SIZE);
  else break;
  ```

**The CLC mechanism** (`include/ops/thread/util/util.cuh:237-289`). A dedicated **scheduler warp** issues a hardware "try-cancel" that atomically steals a not-yet-launched CTA's tile and multicasts the coordinate to the whole cluster:

```cpp
// util.cuh:257  clc::schedule  -&gt; issues try_cancel, completes the mbarrier
"clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel.async.shared::cta.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes.multicast::cluster::all.b128 [%0],[%1];"
// util.cuh:268  clc::query -&gt; was a CTA cancelled? if so return its ctaid
"clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.is_canceled.pred.b128 ...; ... get_first_ctaid.v4.b32.b128 ...;"
```

Why this backfills wave-2 without bubbles: a CTA that finishes its tile **immediately** cancels-and-adopts a pending tile in hardware — there is no host round-trip and no wave barrier. The classic "tail effect" (partial final wave, SMs idling while others finish) disappears because finished SMs steal the stragglers' work. On your ~1.73-wave shape, this is precisely the quantization that leaves your tensor cores idle at the wave boundary.

**The scheduler runs one tile ahead.** The scheduler is a *separate warp* (warp 2 of the producer warpgroup) that pipelines the next schedule while the current tile computes:

```cpp
// bf16_b200_gemm.cu:141-153  (scheduler warp, cta_rank==0)
clc::schedule(clc_handle[...], schedule_arrived[...]);   // :146 issue next
tma::expect_bytes(schedule_arrived[...], sizeof(clc_handle[...]));  // :148
wait(schedule_arrived[...], ...);                        // :149 land it
```
and the epilogue warp reads `next_tile_coord` one iteration ahead so tile coordinates never stall the store path (`:200` init, `:202` `tile_coord = next_tile_coord`, `:207` compute next).

**Tile swizzling for L2 locality** (`include/common/util.cuh:366-402`): `get_swizzled_2d_idx&lt;SUPERGROUP_SIZE&gt;` maps the linear task id into a boustrophedon "supergroup" (serpentine) order so consecutively-scheduled tiles share A/B rows/cols and hit in L2 — reducing the memory pressure that causes your wave-2 latency stalls. `SUPERGROUP_SIZE` is tuned per shape (4 or 8, see `main()` `:370-378`).

---

## 2. PIPELINE CONTINUITY — the pipeline never drains between tiles

**This is the key technique for your gap.** The load pipeline is a shared-memory **ring buffer whose index is NOT reset at the tile boundary**, so tile N+1's loads flow into the same ring immediately after tile N's last load — no drain, no refill bubble.

Loader warp (`bf16_b200_gemm.cu:120-140`):
```cpp
int input_ring = 0;                                   // :121  initialized ONCE, before the task loop
for (int task_iter = 0; true; task_iter++) {          // :125  persistent tile loop
    for (int idx = 0; idx &lt; iters_per_task; idx++) {  // :126  K-loop
        wait(inputs_finished[input_ring], get_phasebit&lt;1&gt;(bitfield, input_ring));  // :127
        for (i&lt;NUM_CONSUMERS) tma::cluster::load_async(a_smem[input_ring][i], ...); // :130
        tma::cluster::load_async(b_smem[input_ring], ...);                          // :131
        update_phasebit&lt;1&gt;(bitfield, input_ring);                                   // :132
        input_ring = ring_advance&lt;C::LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH&gt;(input_ring);                  // :133  carries across tiles
    }
    // get next tile, no ring reset:
    wait(schedule_arrived[...]); ... tile_coord = ...;  // :135-138
}
```
Because `input_ring` and the phase `bitfield` persist across `task_iter`, the loader only ever waits on `inputs_finished` (freed by the MMA consumer). It runs `LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` stages ahead and seamlessly prefetches the **next tile's** first K-blocks while the current tile's MMA/epilogue is still draining. Contrast `level_08.cu` (non-persistent, one tile/CTA) which has no outer loop and thus fully drains per launch.

**Ring-buffer primitives:**
- Stages: `st_bf` SMEM arrays sized `[LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH]` (`:80-81`); `LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` is 4-5 in the tuned configs (`main()` `:370-378`).
- Per-slot dual semaphores: `inputs_arrived[]` / `inputs_finished[]` (`:90`, init `:102-105`) — full/empty counters.
- Phase tracking without extra registers: a single `uint32_t bitfield = 0xFFFF0000` packs 16 "arrived" + 16 "finished" phase bits (`:91`), read/flipped by `get_phasebit&lt;h&gt;`/`update_phasebit&lt;h&gt;` (`include/common/util.cuh:404-423`). `ring_advance&lt;N&gt;` is just `(ring+1)%N` (`util.cuh:425`).

**Double-buffered TMEM accumulator overlaps MMA of tile N+1 with epilogue of tile N.** `MMA_PIPE_DEPTH = OVERLAP_MMA_EPI ? 2 : 1` (`:23`). Two TMEM accumulators are allocated (`:158-163`, `:194-199`) and indexed `d_tt[task_iter % MMA_PIPE_DEPTH]` (`:173-174`), so the MMA warp can start accumulating tile N+1 into buffer B while the epilogue reads tile N out of buffer A. The handshake is `outputs_arrived[]` (MMA→epilogue, `:178`, `:208`) and `outputs_finished[]` (epilogue→MMA frees the TMEM buffer, `:169`, `:218/:234`). The MMA consumer's `input_ring` is likewise initialized once at `:164` and carried across tiles.

Net effect: at any instant the loader, the tensor cores, and the epilogue store path are all working on *different* tiles — the tensor-core feed never stops at a tile boundary.

---

## 3. WARP / WORKER STRUCTURE &amp; OCCUPANCY

**Warpgroup-level warp specialization** (`bf16_b200_gemm.cu:28-31`):
- `NUM_CONSUMERS = OVERLAP_MMA_EPI ? 1 : 2`, `NUM_PRODUCERS = 1`, `NUM_WARPS = (CONS+PROD)*4` ⇒ **8 warps** (overlap mode) or **12 warps** (2-consumer mode). Compare your 7 warps.

**Producer warpgroup** (`groupid == NUM_CONSUMERS`, `:117`) drops to **56 registers** (`warpgroup::decrease_registers&lt;56&gt;()`, `:118`) and splits its 4 warps into 3 roles:
- **warp 3 → TMA loader** (`:120-140`): issues `tma::cluster::load_async` with multicast mask `1&lt;&lt;cta_rank`.
- **warp 2 → CLC scheduler** (`:141-153`): issues `clc::schedule` / `clc::query`, one tile ahead.
- **warps `&lt; NUM_CONSUMERS` → MMA issuers** (`:154-181`): only `cta_rank==0`, `elect_leader()` issues the 2-CTA `mm2_ABt`/`mma2_ABt` then `detail::tcgen05::commit&lt;CLUSTER_SIZE&gt;` (`:178`). `mm2_*` (acc=0) initializes on `idx==0`, `mma2_*` (acc=1) accumulates thereafter (`:173-174`; defs `include/ops/group/mma/tcgen05.cuh:35,68`).

**Consumer warpgroup(s)** (`groupid &lt; NUM_CONSUMERS`, `:183`) bump to **224 registers** (`warpgroup::increase_registers&lt;224&gt;()`, `:186`, only in non-overlap mode) and run the epilogue: `warpgroup::load_async` TMEM→registers (`:213/:230`), `tensor_load_wait()` (`:215/:231`), `store` to SMEM, `tma::store_async` SMEM→GMEM with `EVICT_FIRST` cache policy (`:224/:241`).

**How latency is hidden / occupancy:** `__launch_bounds__(NUM_THREADS, 1)` (`:62`) — one huge block/SM using nearly all TMEM + SMEM rather than many small blocks; latency is hidden by the *pipeline depth* (async TMA + deep ring), not by SM oversubscription. Asymmetric register allocation (56 vs 224 via `decrease/increase_registers`) frees the register budget for the compute/epilogue warps that need it, which is what lets 224-reg consumers coexist. TMEM is explicitly managed: `tensor_allocator` `provision`/`set_addr`/`deprovision` with a `tmem_provisioned` handshake (`:87-95`, `:189-193`, `include/types/tensor/tensor.cuh:54,66,124`).

**Cluster sync only at the very end** (`:246-251`): `epilogue_group::sync(4)` then a `tmem_finished` handshake and `deprovision()` — reached *once*, after the persistent loop exits, not per tile. Your "blocking `cluster_sync` at exit" per wave is exactly what TK avoids; here it is amortized across all tiles a CTA ever runs.

**Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL)** hides *inter-kernel* boundary latency: loader calls `pdl::wait()` before starting (`:123`) and the epilogue calls `pdl::arrive()` on the final tile (`:217/:233`) — `griddepcontrol.launch_dependents`/`.wait` (`include/ops/thread/util/util.cuh:312-321`). This lets the next GEMM begin loading while this one drains its tail.

## 4. THE 2-3 CONCRETE TECHNIQUES TO ADOPT

Ranked by expected impact on your 55%→81% tensor-core-busy gap on multi-wave shapes:

**(1) Make the kernel persistent with hardware CLC, and don't reset the load ring between tiles.** This is the single biggest lever for wave-2 idle. Two parts, both required:
   - Convert to the CLC persistent loop: launch one cluster per tile, adopt the next tile via `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel`/`query_cancel` (`util.cuh:257-287`), initial tile from `blockIdx`, loop until `!schedule.success`. This work-steals the straggler tiles so no SM idles at the wave boundary. (`bf16_b200_gemm.cu:125-140`, `:165-180`, `:201-245`)
   - Keep `input_ring` + phase `bitfield` **outside** the tile loop (`:121` initialized once) so tile N+1's TMA loads issue into the same ring the instant tile N's last load completes — the pipeline never drains. This is the fix for "pipeline drains between tiles." (`:121-133`)

**(2) Double-buffer the TMEM accumulator to overlap MMA(N+1) with epilogue(N).** Allocate 2 TMEM accumulators, index `d_tt[task_iter % 2]`, and gate reuse with `outputs_arrived`/`outputs_finished` semaphores so the tensor cores start the next tile's MMA immediately instead of stalling on the current tile's TMEM→GMEM store. (`OVERLAP_MMA_EPI`, `:23`, `:158-174`, `:208-234`). Your 6-stage load pipe is deep, but if the accumulator is single-buffered the MMA still stalls on the epilogue every tile — this closes that gap.

**(3) Serpentine tile-swizzle scheduling + a dedicated scheduler warp running one tile ahead.** Use `get_swizzled_2d_idx&lt;SUPERGROUP_SIZE&gt;` (`include/common/util.cuh:366`) so consecutively-scheduled tiles reuse A/B operands in L2 (cuts the memory latency you're failing to hide), and dedicate one warp to issuing the next schedule/coordinate ahead of compute so tile-coordinate/scheduling logic never sits on the critical path (`:141-153`, `:200/:207`). Tune `SUPERGROUP_SIZE` per shape as TK does (`:370-378`).

Secondary: TK moves to **8 warps** with **asymmetric registers** (56-reg producer / 224-reg consumer via `decrease/increase_registers`, `:118`/`:186`) — worth trying vs your 7-warp/167-reg uniform layout, since it frees registers for the epilogue without starving the loader. And add **PDL** (`griddepcontrol`, `util.cuh:312-321`) to overlap this GEMM's tail with the next kernel's prologue.

## The two REAL gaps (they map exactly to our proven symptoms)
1. **Teardown blocks the wave-2 backfill** → our **22% barrier stall** (the exit `cluster_sync()`). All 4 CTAs of a cluster lockstep at exit before their SMs free → delays CLC backfilling the remaining 108 tiles. **CUTLASS explicitly fixes this**: `release_allocation_lock()` + `launch_dependent_grids()` *before* the barrier, and only a **2-CTA** barrier (not full cluster). - **Verify C: confirm our EPI_PIPE_DEPTH=2 actually overlaps MMA(N+1) with epilogue(N)** (like DeepGEMM's `kNumEpilogueStages=2`); if not, wire it up.

next i went into ncu and proved the most important thing of the day, our sm-active cycles are almost exactly equal to cublas (160k versus 156k) which means we are doing the same amount of actual work, but our tensor cores are only kept busy 54 percent of the time while cublas keeps them busy 81 percent, so the gap is not extra instructions and not extra work, it is pure idle time where the tensor cores sit doing nothing waiting for data, and this idle only appears on the multi-wave shapes where the gpu has to run a full wave of tiles and then a second partial wave, i then broke down exactly what the warps are stalling on and found our barrier stall is 40 times higher than cublas, and traced that barrier to the kernel exit teardown where all the ctas in a cluster wait for each other before releasing, this delays the second wave of tiles from starting on the freed up sms

then i found the real nature of the problem, the kernel is bimodal, the exact same kernel with no changes sometimes runs at 209us and sometimes at 147us which is basically cublas parity, and this happened on both b300 and b200, this told me that our second wave of tiles is being scheduled non-deterministically, sometimes it overlaps and keeps all the sms fed (147us) and usually it stalls with idle sms (209us), while cublas is consistently fast every single run, so the true culprit is the non-deterministic tile backfill in our persistent scheduler at the wave boundary, not a fixed overhead

to figure out the fix i did a deep research pulling apart three of the best kernel libraries we have locally, cutlass, deepgemm and thunderkittens, and they all agree on the same recipe, they keep the load pipeline running continuously across tiles without draining, they double buffer the tmem accumulator so the epilogue of one tile overlaps the compute of the next, and critically they release the tmem allocation lock early during teardown so the next tile can immediately start allocating and loading while the current one is still finishing, i checked and our kernel already carries the load ring and double buffers tmem, but we were holding the tmem allocation lock through the entire exit barrier which blocks the next wave from backfilling, i also confirmed from cutlass and deepgemm that dense bf16 needs no register juggling so our 167 registers are perfectly fine and that was never the issue, so i built the fix which adds the tmem relinquish-alloc-permit instruction at the exit before the barrier, exactly like cublas cutlass and deepgemm do

i also ran the full ~500 test case suite across every variant to check where we actually stand, and we are now beating cublas on 201 of the 519 cases with an average of 104 percent, we win very big on the small and medium shapes (up to 4x on the small tile variant) and the only two weak spots left are the beta-accumulate path (23 to 47 percent) and the skinny masked shapes (48 percent), both of which are separate future tasks and not the standard inference case, but the single most important thing i caught today is two measurement bugs that were faking our results in both directions, the first is that our build system does not recompile the kernel when only the header changes so we were repeatedly measuring the old baseline code and thinking it was our fix, and the second is that the profiler's full-metrics mode actually distorts the multi-wave timing because it replays the kernel many times and breaks the wave overlap, so from now on i force a clean rebuild, verify the change is really inside the compiled binary, and use light profiling only

so the fix is currently looking promising but not yet confirmed, on a clean a/b test the baseline never once hit the fast path while our fixed version did hit parity, which is a good early sign that the fix enables the fast backfill, but it is still non-deterministic so i cannot call it proven yet

Good question, bro. **For B300, plain `make clean && make -j$(nproc)` builds and runs fine** — the Makefile's default GENCODE is already `sm_103a`, so no override needed *to build or run*.

**But keep the GENCODE override for ONE reason: the binary verify.** Plain `code=sm_103a` embeds only SASS (no PTX), so `cuobjdump -ptx | grep relinquish` returns 0 even when Fix A is in — a false negative. Yesterday's whole disaster was *not verifying the binary*, so we don't want to lose that check. The override `code=[compute_103a,sm_103a]` embeds PTX too, so the verify actually works:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
G="-gencode arch=compute_103a,code=[compute_103a,sm_103a]"
make clean >/dev/null 2>&1
make -j$(nproc) GENCODE_FLAGS="$G" 2>&1 | grep -iE "error" | head
echo "BASELINE lib relinq: $(cuobjdump -ptx build/libmyblas.so 2>/dev/null | grep -c relinquish_alloc_permit)   (want 0)"
ls -l --time-style=+%H:%M:%S build/libmyblas.so; date +%H:%M:%S
```

So:
- **Plain `make -j$(nproc)`** = works for B300, but the PTX-verify won't (harmless, just can't prove it).
- **With `GENCODE_FLAGS="$G"`** = same sm_103a build (runs identically on B300) **+ PTX embedded so we can prove Fix A is really in the binary.**

My rec: **use the override** — it costs nothing at runtime and gives us the bulletproof verify that's the whole point today. (`-j$(nproc)` auto-picks your core count; `-j125` is fine too if the box has ~128 cores.) 👊

## 1. The regular (non-swap) MAIN M256 store path — lines 2102–2192

Note: the `swizzled_g = g ^ (r_in &amp; 7)` code you cite at ~2079 is **not** the main M256 path — it is the **Layout‑B tail piece** (lines 2076–2080, inside the `if (Config::HAS_M128 &amp;&amp; p == Config::N_M256)` branch at 1986). The **main M256 path** (2102–2192) uses `swizzled_n = n ^ (row &amp; 7)` at line 2171. Both are covered below.

### Row/col mapping (main M256 path)
- **`row`** (line 1978): `row = warp_id * WARP_THREADS + lane_id` → warp0→rows 0‑31, warp1→32‑63, warp2→64‑95, warp3→96‑127. This is the **piece-local C-row** (0..127 within the 128-row M256 piece). 4 epilogue warps × 32 lanes = 128 rows.
- **`piece_row`** (2105): `p * 128` — the piece's C-row base within the CTA tile.
- Global **C-row** = `cur_batch*M + block_row*OUT_ROWS + piece_row + row` (2143–2144).
- **`n`** = 8-column group index, `0..LOADS_PER-1`. `LOADS_PER = STORE_COLS/8 = 8` (1931–1932). So `n` sweeps the 8 groups of 8 columns that make up one 64-wide store chunk.
- Global **C-col** = `block_col*BN + chunk*STORE_COLS + n*8 + j`, j=0..7 (2142).

### (a) TMEM read — lines 2102–2115
```
tmem_row = (tmem_addr + wave_stage*ACC_COLS_PER_STAGE + p*BN) + ((warp_id*WARP_THREADS) &lt;&lt; 16);   // 2102-2104
...
for (int n=0; n&lt;LOADS_PER; ++n)
    tcgen05_ld(tmp[n], tmem_row + chunk*STORE_COLS + n*8);   // 2113-2114
tcgen05_wait_ld();                                            // 2115
```
The `&lt;&lt;16` field is the TMEM lane (datapath) base = `warp_id*32`; per the comment at 1975 the hardware auto-distributes 32 DP/warp. Each `tcgen05_ld` (32x32b.x8) returns **8 fp32** into `tmp[n][0..7]` = the 8 consecutive C-columns `chunk*64 + n*8 + [0..7]` for this thread's `row`.

### (b) alpha/beta scaling — lines 2138–2168
Three branches, per `n`:
- **beta≠0** (2141–2154): loads old C via `cp = C_in + c_row*N + c_col` (2145), reads `__nv_bfloat162 old` at `cp+i*2` (i=0..3), then `v0 = tmp[n][i*2]*alpha + old_f.x*beta`, `v1 = tmp[n][i*2+1]*alpha + old_f.y*beta`.
- **alpha==1, beta==0** (2155–2161): direct convert, no FMULs.
- **else (alpha≠1, beta==0)** (2162–2167): `tmp*alpha`.

### (c) pack fp32→bf16 — into `__nv_bfloat162 packed[4]`
`packed[i] = __float22bfloat162_rn({v0,v1})` (2153 / 2160 / 2165). `packed[4]` = 8 bf16 = 16 bytes = one `int4`.

### (d) swizzled smem address + int4 store — lines 2170–2175
```
const int swizzled_n = n ^ (row &amp; 7);                         // 2171
__nv_bfloat16 *wp = store_base
      + store_stage * Config::EPI_ROWS * STORE_COLS            // 2172-2173
      + row * STORE_COLS                                        // 2174
      + swizzled_n * 8;
*reinterpret_cast&lt;int4*&gt;(wp) = *reinterpret_cast&lt;int4*&gt;(packed); // 2175
```
Row stride = `STORE_COLS = 64` bf16 = **128 bytes**. `n` is the 16-byte group index (8 groups per 128-byte row); swizzle = `n ^ (row &amp; 7)`. This is exactly a **128B XOR swizzle** (8 groups/row, XOR by low 3 row bits).

### TMA store — lines 2178–2189
```

if (warp_id==0 &amp;&amp; elect_sync()) {

    c_col = block_col*BN + chunk*STORE_COLS;                   // 2184
    c_row = cur_batch*M + block_row*OUT_ROWS + piece_row;      // 2185-2186
    tma_2d_smem2gmem(src, &amp;C_tmap, c_col, c_row);              // 2187  ← regular path uses C_tmap
    tma_store_commit();
}
store_stage ^= 1;                                             // 2191
```

### The Layout-B tail path you cited at ~2079 (lines 1998–2080)
Different variables: `r_in = 32*(warp_id&amp;1) + lane_id` (piece-local C-row, quadrant map, 1998); `col_base = (warp_id&gt;&gt;1)*TAIL_COLS` (2004); `col_in = col_base % STORE_COLS` (2006); `g = col_in/8 + n` (2074); `swizzled_g = g ^ (r_in &amp; 7)` (2075); `wp = store_base + store_stage*EPI_ROWS*STORE_COLS + r_in*STORE_COLS + swizzled_g*8` (2076–2078); int4 store (2079–2080). Same 128B swizzle geometry, but keyed on `r_in`/`g` instead of `row`/`n`. **This path stores via `C_tmap_tail` (2095), not `C_tmap`** — a 64-row box.

## 2. Store buffer + TMA store layout / swizzle constraint

- **`store_base`** (1152–1153): `reinterpret_cast&lt;__nv_bfloat16*&gt;(smem + LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH*copy_size)` — base of the epilogue store buffer, just past the A/B load pipeline.
- **`store_smem`** (1151): `smem_ptr + LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH*copy_size` — the same address as an `int` smem offset (for the TMA `src`).
- **`store_buf_sz`** (1148–1149): `Config::EPI_ROWS * STORE_COLS * 2` bytes = 128×64×2 = **16384 bytes** — one store slot, one composite piece tall (=BM pre-B1). Double-buffered by `store_stage ^= 1`.
- **`EPI_ROWS`** = 128 (regular BM=128), **`STORE_COLS`** = 64.
- **`store_stage`** (1949): persists across CLC waves (§58 fix), selects buffer half via `store_stage*EPI_ROWS*STORE_COLS` (bf16 offset in stores) and `store_stage*store_buf_sz` (byte offset in `src`).
- **`tma_2d_smem2gmem(src, tmap, x, y)`** (690–696): `cp.async.bulk.tensor.2d.global.shared::cta` — reads the smem box at `src` and writes it to gmem tile at coords `(x=c_col, y=c_row)`. It applies the **descriptor's swizzle** when reading smem.

### Which C_tmap and what swizzle
- Regular main path → **`C_tmap`** (2187). Tail path → `C_tmap_tail` (2095). Swap path → `C_tmap` (1885).
- Encoder **`init_2d_tma_C`** (909–922): rank-2, `boxDim = {boxCols, boxRows}`, `globalDim = {totalCols, totalRows}`.
- Call sites (launcher):
  - `C_tmap`: line **2411–2413** → `init_2d_tma_C(&amp;C_tmap, C, batchCount*M, N, EPI_ROWS(=128), STORE_COLS(=64), CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B)`.
  - `C_tmap_tail`: 2417 copies `C_tmap`; if HAS_M128, 2419–2421 re-encodes with `TAIL_ROWS` box, also **`CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B`**.

**Constraint: the smem box is 128 rows × 64 bf16 (128 bytes/row) in `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` layout.** Any stmatrix rewrite MUST land bytes at exactly `row*128 + (group ^ (row&amp;7))*16` (8 × 16-byte groups per row, XOR by low 3 row bits) — identical to the current int4 swizzle `g ^ (row&amp;7)`.

## 3. The swap epilogue stmatrix path — lines 1799–1838

Preamble (per wave): `t_m128 = tmem_addr + wave_stage*BM + ((warp_id*32)&lt;&lt;16)` (1785–1786); `n128 = warp_id*32 + lane_id` (1789). `num_chunks = BN/STORE_COLS = 3` (1756). `buf = store_base + store_stage*BM*STORE_COLS` (1797); `n_base = chunk*STORE_COLS` (1796).

Chunk guard `if (n_base &lt; 128)` (1799) → M128-atom chunks (C-cols 0..127, chunks 0&amp;1); the active-warp guard `if (n128 &gt;= n_base &amp;&amp; n128 &lt; n_base+STORE_COLS)` (1809) selects the warp pair owning this chunk.

### Variable map (lines 1810–1837)
- **`pm = 2*(lane_id &amp; 3)`** → {0,2,4,6} (1810) — even C-row offset within the 8-row atom.
- **`qn = lane_id &gt;&gt; 2`** → 0..7 (1811) — C-col offset within the strip.
- **`base_n = block_col*BN + 32*warp_id`** (1812) — this warp's global C-col base.
- **`col_g = (warp_id &amp; 1)*4 + (lane_id &gt;&gt; 3)`** (1813) — the destination 16-byte group index (0..7) for stmatrix.
- **`row_m = m0 + (lane_id &amp; 7)`** (1832) — the stmatrix row (C-col in transposed output; low 3 bits drive the swizzle).

### TMEM reads (16x256b) — lines 1816–1819
```
tcgen05_ld_16x256b(v,   t_m128 + m0);                 // DP  0..15  → v[0..3]
tcgen05_ld_16x256b(v+4, (t_m128 + m0) | 0x00100000);  // DP 16..31  → v[4..7]
tcgen05_wait_ld();
```
The `| 0x00100000` sets DP-lane bit to reach lanes 16..31 (second half of the 32-lane atom). 8 fp32 per thread.

### alpha/beta scaling — lines 1822–1831
```
for (k=0; k&lt;8; ++k) {
   dm = pm + (k&amp;1);          // C-row  (1824)
   dn = qn + 8*(k&gt;&gt;1);       // C-col  (1825)
   x = v[k]*alpha;           // (1826)
   if (beta!=0) x += beta * __bfloat162float(C_in[(row0+dm)*N + (base_n+dn)]);  // 1827-1829
   v[k] = x;
}
```
where `row0 = cur_batch*M + block_row*BM + m0` (1820–1821).

### stmatrix store — lines 1832–1837
```
uint8_t *dst = (uint8_t*)buf + row_m*128 + ((col_g ^ (row_m &amp; 7)) * 16);   // 1833-1834
stmatrix_x4_trans(__cvta_generic_to_shared(dst),
                  pack2bf16(v[0],v[1]), pack2bf16(v[2],v[3]),
                  pack2bf16(v[4],v[5]), pack2bf16(v[6],v[7]));              // 1835-1837
```
`.trans` writes the four 8×8 bf16 tiles **column-major** — this is what makes swap-AB's transposed C land correctly. Row stride 128 bytes and swizzle `col_g ^ (row_m&amp;7)` = **the same 128B swizzle** as the regular int4 path, so the smem output is layout-identical; only `.trans` differs.

The M64-atom else-branch (1840–1867) is the scalar strip store for C-cols 128..191 and is not stmatrix.

## 4. Helper definitions

**`tcgen05_ld`** — lines 591–597:
```
asm volatile("tcgen05.ld.sync.aligned.32x32b.x8.b32 {%0..%7}, [%8];"
             : "=f"(tmp[0..7]) : "r"(addr));
```
32 lanes × 32 b32 columns, x8 → each thread loads **8 fp32** into `tmp[0..7]`. `addr` low bits = TMEM column, bits 16+ = DP/lane base.

**`tcgen05_ld_16x256b`** — lines 604–609:
```
asm volatile("tcgen05.ld.sync.aligned.16x256b.x1.b32 {%0..%3}, [%4];"
             : "=f"(tmp[0..3]) : "r"(addr));
```
16 lanes × 256b, x1 → **4 fp32/thread**. Fragment map (comment 599–603, CUTLASS copy_traits_sm100.hpp:467‑481): thread t → r0=(lane t/4, col 2*(t%4)), r1=(t/4, col+1), r2=(t/4+8, col), r3=(t/4+8, col+1). Address lane field must be 16-aligned.

**`pack2bf16`** — lines 614–617:
```
__nv_bfloat162 p = __float22bfloat162_rn(make_float2(a,b));   // round-nearest-even
return *reinterpret_cast&lt;uint32_t*&gt;(&amp;p);                       // low half=a, high=b
```
Returns one b32 (two bf16) — the stmatrix register input form. Bit-exact vs scalar `__float2bfloat16`.

**`stmatrix_x4_trans`** — lines 624–630:
```
asm volatile("stmatrix.sync.aligned.x4.m8n8.shared.b16.trans [%0], {%1,%2,%3,%4};"
             :: "r"(s_addr), "r"(r0), "r"(r1), "r"(r2), "r"(r3));
```
Writes **four 8×8 bf16 matrices column-major (transposed)** to smem in one instruction. `s_addr` = this thread's row-start **shared** address (generic→shared via `__cvta_generic_to_shared`). Each of r0..r3 = 2 bf16 (from `pack2bf16`). sm_90+.

# DeepGEMM SM100 bf16 epilogue store path — full analysis

## The headline correction (read this first)

Your premise is that DeepGEMM's **regular (non-swap-AB)** path uses `stmatrix`. It does **not**. DeepGEMM only uses `stmatrix` on the **swap-AB** path, and it is specifically the **transposing** variant `stmatrix.x4.trans`, used precisely *because* swap-AB leaves the accumulator transposed in TMEM.

The **regular, non-transposed** store helper — `deep_gemm/include/deep_gemm/epilogue/sm100_store_cd.cuh` — reads TMEM with `tcgen05.ld.32dp32b` and writes with **plain vectorized `st.shared.v4` (128-bit)**. That is the same *kind* of instruction your current epilogue uses. So for a genuinely non-transposed `D[m][n]` (m on datapaths), the "efficient DeepGEMM/cuBLAS path" is **not** stmatrix — it's a correctly-vectorized 128-bit `st.shared` into a 128B-swizzled buffer. I'll prove both paths and explain exactly why the split exists, because it determines what you should actually port.

Dispatch proof, `sm100_bf16_gemm.cuh:396-418`: `if constexpr (kSwapAB) → sm100_store_cd_swap_ab(...)` else `→ sm100_store_cd(...)`.

---

## PART A — The REGULAR (non-swap, non-transposed) path — `sm100_store_cd.cuh`

This is the one that matches your case (`D[m][n]` at `(datapath m, column n)`).

### Relevant constants (bf16, `BLOCK_M=128`), from `sm100_bf16_gemm.cuh`
- `LAYOUT_AD_M = 128` (:57) — 128 TMEM datapath rows.
- `STORE_BLOCK_M = min(BLOCK_M, 128) = 128` (:74) → `kNumUMMAStoreThreads = STORE_BLOCK_M = 128` (:76) = one warpgroup (4 warps).
- `STORE_BLOCK_N = kSwizzleCDMode / sizeof(bf16) = 128/2 = 64` (:75) (128B swizzle configured).
- `kNumBankGroupBytes = 16`, `kNumElemsPerBankGroup = 16/2 = 8` (`sm100_store_cd.cuh:30-31`).

### 1. TMEM → registers (which `tcgen05.ld`, lane→(m,n), how many regs)

`sm100_store_cd.cuh:96-98` (bf16):
```cpp
cute::SM100_TMEM_LOAD_32dp32b8x::copy(tmem_addr,
    values[0], values[1], values[2], values[3],
    values[4], values[5], values[6], values[7]);
cutlass::arch::fence_view_async_tmem_load();
```
- Variant: **`tcgen05.ld.sync.aligned.32dp32b.x8`** (32 datapaths, 32-bit elements, x8 repeat). **8 fp32 registers per lane.**
- Lane mapping (CUTLASS semantics): within an epilogue warp `W`, **lane `L` reads datapath row `m = W*32 + L`**; its 8 registers are **8 contiguous columns `n = n_base .. n_base+7`**. (Warp→datapath-group is automatic — see the note at `sm100_bf16_gemm.cuh:373-374`: "the hardware will ignore the warp index bits".)
- Key property: **each lane holds a contiguous run along N for a fixed M.** That is already row-major `[M,N]` fragment order.
- The outer loop reloads TMEM per 8-column bank-group: `tmem_addr = tmem_base_addr + w*BLOCK_N + s*STORE_BLOCK_N + i*8` (`:77-79`), `i ∈ [0, STORE_BLOCK_N/8) = [0,8)`.

### 2. Registers → shared memory: **plain `st.shared.v4`, NOT stmatrix, no transpose**

`sm100_store_cd.cuh:100-106`:
```cpp
ptx::st_shared(
    smem_ptr,
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[0], values[1]),   // r0 = bf16x2(n0,n1)
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[2], values[3]),   // r1 = bf16x2(n2,n3)
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[4], values[5]),   // r2 = bf16x2(n4,n5)
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[6], values[7]));  // r3 = bf16x2(n6,n7)
```
- `st_shared(void*, u32,u32,u32,u32)` = `st.shared.v4.u32` — a single **128-bit** store (`ptx/ld_st.cuh:147-149`).
- `cast_into_bf16_and_pack` (`common/math.cuh:73-76`) = `__float22bfloat162_rn` → one `uint32` = 2 packed bf16.
- The 4 packed regs are **8 contiguous bf16 columns (n0..n7) = 16 bytes = one bank group**, written for row `m = lane`. Contiguous-N registers → contiguous-16B smem → fully vectorized, conflict-free with the swizzle. **No `.trans`, no stmatrix — because the fragment is already in the target row-major order.**

**Why no stmatrix here:** stmatrix's register→element convention matches an *mma/ldmatrix fragment*, not a contiguous-N run. With the non-transposed accumulator you already have the ideal layout, so a 128-bit `st.shared` is optimal and stmatrix would buy nothing (and wouldn't even match the register layout without switching TMEM-load variants).

### 3 &amp; 4. Swizzle + the complete lane→(m,n)→smem-address flow

`sm100_store_cd.cuh:64-82`:
```cpp
auto bank_group_index = i + lane_idx * (kSwizzleCDMode / kNumBankGroupBytes);   // 128/16 = 8
constexpr bool kHasShortcut = (kSwizzleCDMode / kNumBankGroupBytes) == 8;       // true for 128B
auto row = kHasShortcut ? (i / 8 + lane_idx) : (bank_group_index / 8);
auto col = kHasShortcut ? (i)               : (bank_group_index % 8);
col ^= row % (kSwizzleCDMode / 16);                                             // 128/16 = 8
...
auto smem_ptr = smem_base_ptr
              + epilogue_warp_idx * 32 * kSwizzleCDMode          // warp block: 32 rows × 128B
              + row * (kNumBankGroupBytes * 8)                   // row × 128B
              + col * kNumBankGroupBytes;                        // bank group × 16B
```
For 128B swizzle, `i ∈ [0,8)`: `row = lane_idx`, `col = i`, then **`col ^= row % 8`**. End-to-end for the regular bf16 path:

- **Input**: `D[m][n]`, `m = epilogue_warp_idx*32 + lane_idx`, `n = s*64 + i*8 + (0..7)`.
- **Registers**: lane holds fp32 `D[m][n..n+7]` (`tcgen05.ld.32dp32b.x8`).
- **Pack**: 4× bf16x2 = 16 contiguous bytes.
- **smem addr** = `smem_base + warp*(32*128) + lane_idx*128 + ((i ^ (lane_idx%8))*16)`.
- **Store**: one `st.shared.v4` (128-bit).
- **Swizzle**: `col ^= row%8` = the standard **CUTLASS 128B (SW128) XOR-by-row** over an 8-row × 8-bankgroup atom. The generic modulus `kSwizzleCDMode/16` also supports 32B/64B swizzle.
- **TMA store** (`:120-131`): `SM90_TMA_STORE_2D/3D` (or `SM90_TMA_REDUCE_ADD_*` if accumulating) reads this exact 128B-swizzled smem — descriptor `tensor_map_cd` is built with the matching swizzle. `tma_store_fence()` + `NamedBarrier::sync(128,0)` before issue (`:118-119`), single elected lane issues (`:120`).

This is the layout to replicate bit-for-bit for a non-transposed C. If your current epilogue has 5.5-way conflicts and ~250× the store count, the gap is almost certainly (a) not issuing the 128-bit `st.shared.v4` (scalar/`int4`-scattered stores instead), and/or (b) a swizzle XOR that doesn't match the TMA descriptor's 128B pattern — not the absence of stmatrix.

---

## PART B — The SWAP-AB path (`sm100_store_cd_swap_ab.cuh`) — where `stmatrix.trans` IS used, and why

This is the only regular-GEMM place DeepGEMM uses stmatrix. Include it so you understand when `.trans` is the right tool.

**Why it exists:** swap-AB feeds B,A into the MMA (`sm100_bf16_gemm.cuh:326-330`), so TMEM holds **Dᵀ** — datapath axis = N, column axis = M. To write logical row-major `D[m][n]`, the datapath↔column axes must be transposed during the smem write. `stmatrix.b16.trans` does that transpose for free.

### 1. TMEM read — `.16x256b`, chosen to satisfy STSM layout (`swap_ab.cuh:86-93`)
```cpp
// Load from TMEM using `.16x256b` shape to satisfy STSM layout requirements
cute::SM100_TMEM_LOAD_16dp256b1x::copy(tmem_addr,            values[0..3]);   // lanes 0-15
cute::SM100_TMEM_LOAD_16dp256b1x::copy(tmem_addr | 0x00100000, values[4..7]); // lanes 16-31
cutlass::arch::fence_view_async_tmem_load();
```
- Variant **`tcgen05.ld.16dp256b.x1`**, issued **twice**; the `| 0x00100000` (bit 20) advances the datapath base by 16 rows so the two calls cover lanes 0-15 and 16-31. 8 fp32 regs total, packed so the register→element order feeds `stmatrix.trans`. (Contrast: the regular path's `.32dp32b` gives contiguous-N, which is what plain `st.shared` wants.)

### 2. The stmatrix write — `.x4.m8n8.b16.trans` (`swap_ab.cuh:102-106`)
```cpp
ptx::SM90_U32x4_STSM_T&lt;int&gt;::copy(
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[0], values[1]),   // r0
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[2], values[3]),   // r1
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[4], values[5]),   // r2
    math::cast_into_bf16_and_pack(values[6], values[7]),   // r3
    smem_ptr);
```
`SM90_U32x4_STSM_T` (`ptx/ld_st.cuh:66-76`) = **`stmatrix.sync.aligned.x4.m8n8.shared.b16.trans`**. 4 regs/lane, each = bf16x2 (r0,r1 from the lanes-0-15 load; r2,r3 from lanes-16-31). `.trans` transposes each 8×8 b16 tile as it stores — this is the un-transpose.

### smem address (each lane supplies its own — stmatrix semantics), `swap_ab.cuh:96-99`
```cpp
uint32_t row = lane_idx % 8;
uint32_t col = (epilogue_warp_idx % 2) * 4 + lane_idx / 8;   // warp-pair shares one 128B atom
auto smem_ptr = smem_base_ptr + row * (16 * 8) + (col ^ row) * 16;   // same 128B XOR swizzle
```
Same 128B `col ^= row` swizzle; STORE_BLOCK_N must be 128 = full warpgroup reads 128 TMEM rows (`:32`), `kSwizzleCDMode == 128` asserted (`:38`). (`sm100_fp8_fp4_mega_moe.cuh:1125-1161` is an identical `.16x256b` + `SM90_U32x4_STSM_T` pattern — corroboration.)

**FP32-output swap-AB** does *not* use stmatrix either — it falls back to per-element `st.shared` with a manual transpose (`swap_ab.cuh:72-84`). So `.trans` stmatrix is a bf16-output-only optimization for the transposed accumulator.

---

## PART C — Alpha / beta scaling

**There is none in the value path** — neither regular nor swap-AB touches alpha/beta. Confirmed: no `alpha`/`beta` symbols in `epilogue/` or `sm100_bf16_gemm.cuh` (grep returned nothing), and `EpilogueIdentity::apply_index_n` (`epilogue/transform.cuh:7-12`) is a pure *index* remap (for head-splits), not a value scale.

Two things that look like scaling but are not:
- The MMA `scale_c` predicate (`ptx/tcgen05.cuh:15-19`, `setp.ne.b32 p; ...mma... p`) is the **accumulate-enable** flag (`D = A·B + (p ? D : 0)`) across the K loop — not alpha/beta.
- `kWithAccumulation` (the "+C") is done at the **TMA store** via `SM90_TMA_REDUCE_ADD_2D/3D` (`sm100_store_cd.cuh:122-128`) — a global reduce-add `D_global += smem`, no scalar multiply, no register-level beta.

# Blackwell TMEM-load / stmatrix register &amp; lane layouts for a GEMM epilogue

Notation: `t` = lane-in-warp `threadIdx.x % 32`. All formulas below are derived by decoding the CuTe `Copy_Traits` TV-layouts in your local CUTLASS tree (the load-bearing structs quoted verbatim), then confirmed against DeepGEMM/ThunderKittens call sites. TMEM address form: bits **[31:16] = datapath lane (row m)**, bits **[15:0] = column** (`cutlass/include/cute/arch/tmem_allocator_sm100.hpp:49,53`, `DP_b = 1&lt;&lt;21`, `DP = 1&lt;&lt;16`).

## Important reality check on the premise
On Blackwell, **neither CUTLASS's SM100 collective epilogue nor DeepGEMM stores the D accumulator through `stmatrix`.** They do `tcgen05.ld` (TMEM→RMEM) → cast in registers → **plain `st.shared`** (swizzled) → TMA store:
- `DeepGEMM/.../epilogue/sm100_store_cd.cuh:89-107` — `SM100_TMEM_LOAD_32dp32b4x/8x::copy(...)` then `ptx::st_shared(...)`, no stmatrix.
- `cutlass/include/cutlass/epilogue/collective/sm100_epilogue_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:632,882` — `make_tmem_copy` T2R then an R2S atom then `SM90_TMA_STORE`.

`stmatrix` is the Hopper (SM90) accumulator path (`DeepGEMM/.../impls/sm90_bf16_gemm.cuh:338`) and the ThunderKittens register→shared path (`stsm4`/`stsm4t`). So the "16x256b → stmatrix" pipeline in your question is a *valid hand-rolled* path (the fragments are compatible, shown in Q3), just not the one CUTLASS/DeepGEMM ship. Flagging so you don't chase a nonexistent CUTLASS atom.

---

## 1. `tcgen05.ld` register/lane layout

PTX ISA §9.7.17.2.3.1 "Memory Layout" (the `.32x32b / .16x64b / .16x128b / .16x256b / .16x32bx2` subsections) and §9.7.17.8.3 (`tcgen05.ld`). Shape is `{lanes}x{bits}`; a warp accesses **32 of the 128 TMEM lanes** (its sub-partition), enforced by `((threadIdx.x/32)%4) == (((tmem_addr&gt;&gt;16)/32)%4)` (`copy_traits_sm100.hpp:402,446`).

### `.32x32b.x1..xN` (the simple, "one row per lane" case — what DeepGEMM store_cd uses)
`SM100_TMEM_LOAD_32dp32b{N}x`, `arch/copy_sm100.hpp:3378`. Each thread = one full datapath row; registers = consecutive columns:
```
thread t  -&gt;  row m = t          (lanes 0..31 = rows 0..31 of the sub-partition)
reg[k]    -&gt;  D[m = t][n = col_base + k]      k = 0..N-1
```
DeepGEMM: `SM100_TMEM_LOAD_32dp32b4x` = 4 fp32 cols/thread; `...8x` = 8. Documented in `cutlass/examples/93_blackwell_low_latency_gqa/tgv_gqa.cuh:954,999` ("every thread just holds a row of the accumulator").

### `.16x256b.x1` — the wide epilogue load (fp32). THE exact mapping
Ground truth, `cutlass/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm100.hpp:466-482`:
```cpp
struct Copy_Traits&lt;SM100_TMEM_LOAD_16dp256b1x&gt; {
  using ThrID     = Layout&lt;_32&gt;;
  using ValID     = Layout&lt;Shape &lt;_256,_16&gt;,        Stride&lt;_1,TMEM::DP_b&gt;&gt;;   // 256 col-bits, 16 rows
  using SrcLayout = Layout&lt;Shape &lt;_32,_4096&gt;,       Stride&lt;_0,_1&gt;&gt;;           // 4096 ref bits = 16 rows*256b
  using DstLayout = Layout&lt;Shape &lt;Shape&lt;_4,_8&gt;,Shape&lt;_64,_2&gt;&gt;,
                           Stride&lt;Stride&lt;_64,_256&gt;, Stride&lt;_1,_2048&gt;&gt;&gt;;
};
```
`DRegisters = uint32_t[4]` (`arch/copy_sm100.hpp:618`). Decoding `DstLayout` (thread `t = t0 + 4·t1`, `t0=t%4 ∈[0,4)`, `t1=t/4 ∈[0,8)`) against the 4096-bit reference frame (`ref_bit b → row m = b/256`, `col-bit = b%256`, `n = col-bit/32`) yields, per thread, **4 fp32 registers**:

| reg | (m, n) it holds |
|----|----|
| dst0 | `D[ t/4 ][ 2·(t%4) ]` |
| dst1 | `D[ t/4 ][ 2·(t%4)+1 ]` |
| dst2 | `D[ t/4 + 8 ][ 2·(t%4) ]` |
| dst3 | `D[ t/4 + 8 ][ 2·(t%4)+1 ]` |

So one `16x256b.x1` covers **16 rows (m=0..15) × 8 fp32 cols (n=0..7)** = 128 elems = 32 lanes × 4 regs. `t1=t/4` picks the row within a group of 8; dst0/1 hit rows 0–7, dst2/3 hit rows 8–15; `t0=t%4` picks the column pair `n∈{2t0, 2t0+1}`.

The **second half** of the 32-lane sub-partition (rows 16–31) is a second `16x256b` load with the address OR-ed by the 16-lane datapath offset — `DeepGEMM/.../impls/sm100_fp8_fp4_mega_moe.cuh:966,1129` uses exactly `tmem_addr | 0x00100000` (`0x100000 = 16 &lt;&lt; 16` = 16 datapath lanes).

Key structural fact: this per-thread pattern — **lane→row `t/4`, register→column-pair `2·(t%4)`** — is *identical* to the mma/stmatrix C-fragment. That is what makes Q3 work.

### `.16x32bx2` (`SM100_TMEM_LOAD_16dp32b*`, `arch/copy_sm100.hpp:2652`, asm `tcgen05.ld...16x32bx2...`)
The `xN` "bx2" shape reads 16 datapath rows × 32-bit, but with a **second strided copy offset by half the tile** (the "bx2" = two column strips), so a single instruction fills registers for two column blocks at a fixed 16-row height. Used for narrow-N / split accumulator tiles where a full `256b` width isn't available. The `.16x128b`/`.16x64b` families (`1248`/`1926`) are the same idea at 4/2 fp32 columns of width; ThunderKittens hand-writes `16x128b.x2` for 1- and 2-byte outputs (`ThunderKittens/include/ops/group/memory/tile/tensor_to_register.cuh:30,45`) and `16x256b.x{2,4,8}` for 4-byte (`:64,97,120`).

### `.pack::16b` variants
`SM100_TMEM_LOAD_16dp256b1x_16b` (`copy_traits_sm100.hpp:486`) splits the value mode `Shape&lt;Shape&lt;_16,_16&gt;,_16&gt;` — it packs two bf16 lanes into each 32-bit register on the way out, so the same instruction directly yields bf16x2 registers (relevant when you want to feed stmatrix without a separate pack step).

---

## 2. `stmatrix.sync.aligned.x4.m8n8.b16`, with and without `.trans`

PTX: `stmatrix.sync.aligned.x4.m8n8.shared.b16 [addr], {r0,r1,r2,r3}` (`cutlass/include/cute/arch/copy_sm90.hpp:80` `SM90_U32x4_STSM_N`) and `...x4.trans.m8n8.shared.b16` (`:140` `SM90_U16x8_STSM_T`). DeepGEMM mirrors these in `deep_gemm/include/deep_gemm/ptx/ld_st.cuh:43,54,66` (note DeepGEMM/CUTLASS put `.trans` in different token positions — both are accepted spellings). ThunderKittens: `stsm4`/`stsm4t` in `include/ops/thread/util/util.cuh:102-109`.

Each of the 32 threads supplies **4 registers, each = 2 packed b16**; `.x4` = four 8×8 b16 tiles. There are two separate mappings: an **address** mapping (which thread's `[addr]` operand names which matrix-row/col) and a **data** mapping (which (row,col) each register's b16 pair holds). Decoded from the CuTe layouts (STSM traits = the inverse of the LDSM traits, `copy_traits_sm90.hpp:73-129` → `copy_traits_sm75.hpp:76-141`):

### WITHOUT `.trans` (`SM90_U32x4_STSM_N`, reuses `SM75_U32x4_LDSM_N`)
`SM75_U32x4_LDSM_N` (`copy_traits_sm75.hpp:82-86`): SMEM side `Shape&lt;_32,_128&gt; Stride&lt;_128,_1&gt;`, register side `Shape&lt;_32,Shape&lt;_32,_4&gt;&gt; Stride&lt;_32,Stride&lt;_1,_1024&gt;&gt;`. Decoding with `t = 4·q + s` (`q=t/4∈[0,8)`, `s=t%4∈[0,4)`):
- **Register `b` (b=0..3) → matrix `b`** (stride 1024 = 1 tile).
- Within its tile, thread `t` holds **row `q = t/4`**, and the register's two b16 go to **cols `2s` and `2s+1` = `2·(t%4)`, `2·(t%4)+1`**.
- **Address operand:** thread `i` provides the base address of **row `(i%8)` of matrix `(i/8)`** (threads 0–7→matrix0 rows0–7, 8–15→matrix1, …; `DeepGEMM sm90_bf16_gemm.cuh:338` comment "only 16 lanes' addresses are used" for the x2 case).

Result in SMEM: **row-major 8×8** — element logically at `[row][col]` lands at byte `row·16 + col·2` within the tile. This is why non-trans = the natural C store.

### WITH `.trans` (`SM90_U16x8_STSM_T`, reuses `SM75_U16x8_LDSM_T`, `copy_traits_sm75.hpp:132-137`)
Register side `Shape&lt;Shape&lt;_4,_8&gt;,Shape&lt;_16,_2,_4&gt;&gt; Stride&lt;Stride&lt;_256,_16&gt;,Stride&lt;_1,_128,_1024&gt;&gt;`. Decoding with `t = ta + 4·tb` (`ta=t%4`, `tb=t/4`), register `g→matrix g`, `p∈{0,1}` = low/high b16 of the register:
- **row = `2·ta + p = 2·(t%4)+p`**, **col = `tb = t/4`**.

Compare to non-trans (`row=t/4`, `col=2·(t%4)+p`): **rows and cols are swapped.** So:

&gt; **`.trans` transposes each 8×8 b16 tile (row↔col) as it is written.** The same register content that plain stmatrix writes to `smem[row][col]` is written by `.trans` to `smem[col][row]`. Equivalently: without `.trans` a register's two b16 go to **two adjacent columns of one row** (row-major); with `.trans` they go to **two adjacent rows of one column** (the tile is stored transposed / column-major). The per-thread `[addr]` operand names a **row** start (plain) vs a **column** start (`.trans`).

---

## 3. THE KEY QUESTION — 16x256b fragment → which stmatrix variant for row-major D

Put the Q1 and Q2 tables side by side. `tcgen05.ld.16x256b.x1` gives thread `t`:
`(row = t/4, col = 2·(t%4))` and `(row = t/4, col = 2·(t%4)+1)` (plus the `+8`-row pair). Plain `stmatrix` (STSM_N) *consumes* exactly `(row = t/4, cols = 2·(t%4), 2·(t%4)+1)`. **They match.**

**Non-transposed D (C = A·B, row = m = datapath lane, col = n):**
- Downcast the two column-adjacent fp32 regs to bf16 and **pack `{dst0,dst1}` → one bf16x2 register** = `(D[m][2k], D[m][2k+1])`, and `{dst2,dst3}` → a second bf16x2 register (rows m+8).
- Feed them to **plain `stmatrix` — NO `.trans`** (`SM90_U32x2_STSM_N`, two 8×8 tiles: rows 0–7 and 8–15). Register packing rule: **register = (D[m][n], D[m][n+1])**, i.e. two column-adjacent bf16.
- Result: **row-major, row=m, col=n**, 8×8-tiled. This is precisely DeepGEMM's SM90 store — `sm90_bf16_gemm.cuh:338` packs `accum[i·4+0..1]` and `accum[i·4+2..3]` into `SM90_U32x2_STSM_N&lt;nv_bfloat162&gt;`, non-trans.

**Transposed / swap-AB case (you MMA'd `Cᵀ = Bᵀ·Aᵀ` into TMEM to avoid an epilogue transpose):** the fragment's `(row,col)` is the transpose of what you want in GMEM. Use **`stmatrix.trans`** to un-transpose each 8×8 tile back to row-major C. This is the ThunderKittens column-layout branch: `shared_to_register.cuh:167-174` dispatches `stsm4` for `rt_layout::row` and **`stsm4t` for the col layout, with the registers reordered `{tmp0, tmp2, tmp1, tmp3}`** — the x4 quadrant is a 2×2 grid of tiles, and transposing it swaps the two off-diagonal tiles (reg1↔reg2), so the register order must be permuted in addition to setting `.trans`. DeepGEMM defines the `.trans` wrappers (`ptx/ld_st.cuh:54,66`) for the swap-AB store path (`epilogue/sm100_store_cd_swap_ab.cuh`).

So: **plain stmatrix + `(D[m][2k],D[m][2k+1])` packing for the honest row-major D; `.trans` (with reg reorder) for the swap-AB Cᵀ path.**

---

## 4. TMA 128B swizzle and folding it into the stmatrix address

A 128-byte SMEM row = **8 sub-banks of 16 bytes** (16 B = one b16 8-element matrix-row = one bank group; `kNumBankGroupBytes=16`, `DeepGEMM sm100_store_cd.cuh:30`). Let `sb = (byte_off &gt;&gt; 4) &amp; 7` (sub-bank index), `r = (byte_off &gt;&gt; 7) &amp; 7` (= `row &amp; 7`, the row within the 8-row swizzle period).

**XOR permutation (all three encode the same thing):**
```
sb_phys        = sb XOR (row &amp; 7)
byte_off_phys  = byte_off XOR ((row &amp; 7) &lt;&lt; 4)
```
- CuTe `Swizzle&lt;3,4,3&gt;` = 128B (`cutlass/include/cute/swizzle.hpp:54,78`): `apply(x) = x ^ ((x &amp; yyy_msk) &gt;&gt; 3)`, with `yyy_msk = 0b111 &lt;&lt; (4+3)` = bits **[9:7]** (the `row&amp;7` field) and target bits **[6:4]** (the sub-bank field). `B=3`→8 classes, `M=4`→16-byte element kept, `S=3`→shift from bit 7 down to bit 4.
- DeepGEMM (`sm100_store_cd.cuh:65-82`, identical at `sm90_bf16_gemm.cuh:307-331`): `col ^= row % (kSwizzleCDMode/16)` → for 128B, **`col ^= row % 8`**, then `smem_ptr = base + warp·32·128 + row·(16·8) + col·16`. `col` is in 16-byte bank-group units.
- ThunderKittens (`include/types/shared/st.cuh:107-118`): `swizzle = ((addr % 1024) &gt;&gt; 7) &lt;&lt; 4; return addr ^ swizzle;` — `%1024` = 128B×8-row period, `&gt;&gt;7` extracts `row&amp;7`, `&lt;&lt;4` places it at 16-byte granularity. Same XOR.

**Folding into the stmatrix destination address:** stmatrix writes 8 rows whose base addresses come from 8 different threads, and the swizzle XOR term `((row&amp;7)&lt;&lt;4)` **differs per row** — so the address must be computed **per-thread from that thread's `(row,col)`**, not as `base + row·stride`. Concretely, thread supplying row `m`, column-group `n` hands stmatrix:
```
addr(m,n) = smem_base + m·128 + ( ((n/8_group_col) XOR (m &amp; 7)) · 16 )
```
This is exactly what TK's `dst.idx(shared_addr, {row,col})` returns before it is passed to `stsm4/stsm4t` (`shared_to_register.cuh:167-174` → `st.cuh:120`). Because each 8×8 b16 matrix-row is 16 bytes = one sub-bank, XOR-ing by `(m &amp; 7)` sends the 8 rows of a tile to 8 *distinct* sub-banks — the property that makes the subsequent TMA/`ldmatrix` reads bank-conflict-free.

## PTX ISA sections

## What this proves (undeniable now)
- **cuBLAS scales SMOOTHLY with work** — 128 tiles→73µs, 192 tiles→106µs (1.5× tiles = 1.45× time). **Linear. It backfills waves perfectly.**
- **OURS is a STAIRCASE** — ~75µs flat for *everything ≤1 wave* (32, 64, 128 tiles all ~75µs), then **JUMPS to 202µs the instant we cross into 2 waves** (128→192 tiles = 75→202µs, a **2.7× jump for 1.5× the work**), then flattens again.

## The mechanism (finally, the REAL cause of the starve)
**When we cross a wave boundary, our SMs drain wave-1 and refill wave-2 with NO overlap — a ~50µs+ bubble where the tensor cores idle.** cuBLAS overlaps the waves (as an SM finishes a wave-1 tile it *immediately* starts a wave-2 tile), so its time tracks actual work. **We don't backfill across the boundary — that's the tensor-core starvation.**

This is NOT instructions, NOT the epilogue, NOT teardown — it's **wave-boundary pipeline continuity**, and now it's *proven by a controlled experiment*, not a guess.

## And it points to the exact fix
This is the one SOTA piece §65 flagged we're missing: **CLC 2-deep prefetch.** Our scheduler keeps **only 1 CLC query outstanding** (we cut it from 2 to fix an orphaned-tile bug, line 1660) — so the producer **can't fetch the next tile's coordinates until the current tile ends → the load pipeline goes cold at the boundary → the bubble.** CUTLASS/TK/DeepGEMM keep it **2-deep** so the next tile prefetches *during* the current one → no bubble → smooth backfill (exactly cuBLAS's curve).

## So the real work now
**Restore 2-deep CLC prefetch, safely** (re-solve the end-of-grid orphaned-tile ordering that made us drop to 1-deep). This directly attacks the proven bubble. It's a real, careful change — but this time we're aiming at a **proven, measured cause**, not a guess.

### 4. The physical mechanism (why the transition stalls)
At **every tile boundary** on a multi-wave CTA, two things happen that cuBLAS avoids:
- **`sleeping`** = the compute warp waits for the next tile's loads — **the pipe drains and refills from empty** because the scheduler (CLC) only resolves the next tile *after* the current one, so its TMA loads can't be prefetched during current compute.
- **`barrier`** = the CLC + TMEM + cluster handshake at the boundary ([lines 1650-1654, 1711-1715](BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM103/Bgemm_sm103_cluster_template.cuh#L1650)).

cuBLAS keeps its pipe **full across tile boundaries** (prefetches the next tile during current compute) → never drains → stays memory-bound → 0.03 sleeping.

That's why we cut it to 1-deep.

## The bottom line
**The gap = the load pipeline drains and refills at every tile boundary, plus the boundary handshake, because our scheduler resolves the next tile too late to prefetch across the boundary.** cuBLAS overlaps the next tile's loads with the current tile's compute; we can't yet, because deepening the CLC pipe reintroduces the orphaned-tile bug.

**So the real fix is one of two, and both are real engineering (not a one-liner):**
1. **Re-solve the orphaned-tile bug** so we can run CLC 2-deep safely (e.g. drain-in-order with an explicit end-of-grid fixup for the stolen cluster) → then next-tile loads prefetch across the boundary.
2. **Decouple the next-tile load issue from the CLC resolve** — start the next tile's TMA the moment the scheduler *knows* it (before the current tile's MMAs drain), so the pipe never empties even at 1-deep.

Both target the **same root cause**: keep the pipe full across the tile boundary so the compute warp never sleeps waiting for a refill.

So even though the hardware may complete cancels out of order, the *decode/consume* order is deterministic and matches issue order. If you consume strictly in issue order and exit on the first `is_canceled == false`, you can never orphan a later success — there is no later success. Your 2-outstanding bug happened because a cancel issued *earlier* (that succeeded) had its response arrive *after* a later cancel's failure response, and you exited on the failure you saw first. The partial last wave is smoothed because CTAs that finish their share early **steal** the leftover tiles via `try_cancel` instead of sitting idle while a few CTAs finish the tail. [HIGH — this is the stated purpose of PersistentTileScheduler + clusterlaunchcontrol]

**Why a partial last wave ≠ a full wave [HIGH]:** In a non-persistent (one-tile-per-CTA) launch, the last wave's cost = the slowest single tile regardless of how few tiles are in it (hardware can't backfill across a grid-wide barrier). In the persistent + CLC model there is no wave barrier — the tail tiles are distributed to whichever CTAs are free, so tail cost ≈ (remaining_tiles / SMs) × tile_time, continuous in tile count. CLC additionally load-balances when tiles have uneven cost (K-splitting, ragged shapes). [HIGH structural; the "no grid-wide wave barrier" point is the crux]

**Maps to your kernel:** Your 67%-of-cuBLAS on multi-wave with clean single-wave is the fingerprint of wave-quantization *plus* a per-boundary bubble. Persistence alone (which you have) removes the grid barrier; the remaining 33% is the boundary bubble from Q1/Q3. Fixing (c)+(a) is what turns your quantized tail into cuBLAS-like smooth backfill.

```
if !valid:
    // DON'T break — a later-issued outstanding slot may hold a valid steal
    drain the remaining outstanding slots in issue order:
        consume slot r → (valid_r, ctaid_r); arrive clc_empty[r]
        if valid_r: do this tile's work (producer=loads, consumer=MMAs), keep draining
    break            // exit only after ALL outstanding slots drained
else:
    do tile ctaid's work; continue
```

## Correctness proof
1. **No double-compute** — uniqueness: each `try_cancel` yields a distinct CTA, so no tile is processed twice.
2. **No orphan** — completeness: at exhaustion there are exactly `DEPTH` outstanding responses; the valid ones are *exactly* the remaining unlaunched CTAs. Draining **all** `DEPTH` slots and computing every valid one processes every remaining tile. The old bug orphaned a valid because it broke on the *first* invalid before draining the later slot — drain-on-exit closes exactly that hole.
3. **No deadlock** — lockstep: every role sees the same broadcast responses and runs the *identical* deterministic drain, so all `clc_empty` arrives/phases stay in lockstep across roles and CTAs.

## The one real risk to nail in implementation
The `clc_empty`/phase bookkeeping and the exact **count** of slots to drain at exit (bounded by `DEPTH`, but the phase-flip on wrap must be exactly right) — plus every role must drain identically. That's the finicky part, and it's where I'll write the invariants explicitly and validate with 3× bit-exact on the exact 19k-tile grids that exposed the original bug.

Great catch to question it, bro — but no mistake. It's just a **badly named variable**. Let me clear it up:

## `single_wave=1` does NOT mean "run in one wave"
It means: **"don't use CLC — each cluster computes exactly ONE tile, then exits."** The name comes from its original use (grids that fit in one wave never need CLC). What actually happens when we force it on a big grid:

```
grid = 256 CTAs (ALL 128 tiles — full size, unchanged)
   ↓
wave 1: 74 clusters fit on the GPU → each does its 1 tile → EXITS
   ↓
HARDWARE sees freed SMs → launches the remaining queued 54 clusters
   ↓
wave 2: they do their 1 tile each → done
TOTAL: 2 waves of execution  →  144.8µs = 2 × 72
```

So **yes — our A/B run WAS running 2 waves**, exactly like cuBLAS (137µs = 2×68.5, grid 256, HW backfill, no CLC — remember its SASS has zero CLC ops). Same variant, same tile, same grid, same execution model now. That's precisely why it's the fair comparison — and why we jumped to ~94%.

The old (CLC) mode was **also** supposed to finish in 2 waves — one wave of clusters that then *steal* the remaining 54 tiles instead of exiting. But the steal race distributed them badly → some clusters ran 3 tiles → **3 waves** → 202µs. That was the whole bug.

**Where "single-wave" naming will bite us:** when we productize, I'll introduce a properly named flag (e.g. `use_plain_grid` / `use_clc`) so the code says what it means — the launcher decides *mode*, not *wave count*.

The remaining ~6% (144.8 vs 137) = per-wave overhead (wave-2 clusters redo the prologue: tmem alloc + pipe fill), same class as the single-wave shapes' gap — a separate, known battle (§60.22 fill floor).

Let me make it crystal clear bro — simple picture:

## The work was always the same; the DISTRIBUTION method was different

**The job (3b-Down):** 128 tiles. GPU fits only 74 clusters at once → minimum 2 rounds, no way around it.

**cuBLAS (always did this):**
```
Launch 128 clusters as a normal grid.
Round 1: 74 run, each does ITS OWN 1 tile, then EXITS.
Round 2: hardware auto-launches the waiting 54 onto freed SMs.
= exactly 2 rounds. Simple. Deterministic. 137µs.
```

**Ours (before — the bug):**
```
Launch 128 clusters, but the first 74 use CLC to STEAL the other 54's tiles
(cancel their launch, do their work ourselves, stay resident).
In THEORY: also 2 rounds.
In REALITY: the steal is a RACE — fast clusters grabbed 2-3 extra tiles,
others grabbed none → runtime = the greediest cluster = 3 rounds. 202µs.
(Sometimes the race landed even → 147µs — our old "fluke" = the lucky mode.)
```

**Ours (the A/B, now):** CLC off for this grid → identical model to cuBLAS → **2 rounds, every time, 145µs.**

So: **earlier we were NOT doing the same as cuBLAS** — same kernel tile, but different work-distribution (they: hardware backfill; us: software stealing). Neither of us was ever "single wave" here — it's 2 rounds for everyone. Our `single_wave` variable is just a badly named "CLC off" switch.

## Is it exact + permanent? Does it affect other things?
- **Exact fix for the found problem:** yes — it removes the race entirely; determinism proven by the tight reps.
- **Permanent + future-proof:** yes, because it's a **host-launcher decision** (one rule: which mode for this grid size), tile-agnostic — every current and future variant automatically gets it. Kernel code untouched, CLC path stays available where it wins, §30.12 protocol never touched.

**Do others do this? — YES, this is literally industry standard practice:**
- **cuBLAS**: its entire heuristic engine does exactly this — picks kernel/schedule per shape. We *watched* it swap 128x256→128x192 and rigid→`2x2f` as N changed. Selection-by-shape IS cuBLAS's core weapon.
- **CUTLASS**: its tile scheduler is selected per problem (DataParallel vs SplitK vs StreamK, "Heuristic" mode) — and their own docs gate stream-K on **tail-wave fullness** (<50% full → split). Same concept as our gate: choose the distribution scheme from the wave math.
- **DeepGEMM**: computes its block-grouping from **SM count** at compile time (`get_num_1d_blocks_per_group(kNumSMs)`) — scheduling parameterized by machine size, same family of idea.

What's *ours* is the specific combo: our kernel has **both** engines built in (cuBLAS's plain-grid model AND the CUTLASS/DeepGEMM persistent model), and the gate picks per shape — arguably nicer than any of them, since cuBLAS must swap whole kernels to do what we do with one flag.

**Does it affect anything?** No:
- Single-wave shapes: identical behavior to always (plain, as ever).
- 1-2 wave shapes: plain-grid — **the fix**, the only behavioral change.
- 2 waves: CLC, exactly as before §68.
- Kernel/PDL/dynamic-cluster/§30.12: untouched. `BLUBLAS_FORCE_CLC=1` still lets us A/B forever.

So: correct, near-zero cost, industry-pattern, reversible, scoped. Push + run the re-validation and let's see the three greens. 👊

## Proof 1 — cuBLAS selects scheduling per shape
**Our own ncu captures** (this session, `b300_wavesweep/c_*.ncu-rep`): same M/K, only N changes → cuBLAS swaps kernels — `128x192_2x2f` at N=1536, rigid `128x256_2x2` at N=2048, `2x2f` again at N=3072. That's shape-gated schedule selection, observed in the wild.

## Proof 2 — CUTLASS gates its scheduler on wave math (verbatim source)
[tile_scheduler_params.h:1099-1104](cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/tile_scheduler_params.h#L1099):
```cpp
// Rudimentary heuristic: prefer data-parallel decomposition if we have more than
// one wave and the tail wave is more than half full. This is subject to change.
uint64_t tail_tiles = output_tiles - (full_waves * ctas_per_wave);
if (2 * tail_tiles >= ctas_per_wave) { return 0; }
```
**CUTLASS literally computes `full_waves` and `tail_tiles` on the host and picks the distribution scheme from that comparison.** Our `grid.x <= 2*s_sm_count` gate is the same species of decision — theirs picks data-parallel vs stream-K, ours picks plain-grid vs CLC.

## Proof 3 — DeepGEMM parameterizes its scheduler on SM count (verbatim source)
[scheduler/gemm.cuh:15-21](DeepGEMM/deep_gemm/include/deep_gemm/scheduler/gemm.cuh#L15): `get_num_1d_blocks_per_group()` iterates candidates and scores them with `constexpr_ceil_div(kNumSMs, candidate)` — block-grouping chosen from the SM count.

So: **cuBLAS does it at the kernel-selection level, CUTLASS does it inside the tile scheduler with the exact same wave arithmetic, DeepGEMM bakes SM-count into scheduling.** Our gate isn't homemade weirdness — it's the standard move, and ours is backed by our own A/B measurements on top. The one thing that's uniquely ours: both execution models live in ONE kernel behind a flag, where cuBLAS needs separate kernels. That's an advantage, not a liability.
