### CLAUDE [2026-07-18 19:58 IST]

Let me break it down fully, bro — step by step, simple but technical.

## The setup: what the GPU is given

For 3b-Down we launch a **grid of 128 clusters** (each cluster = 2 CTAs working as a pair on one output tile). But the B300 only has enough SMs to hold **74 clusters at the same time**. So:

```
128 clusters in the grid
 74 fit on the GPU  → these start running immediately ("resident")
 54 don't fit       → these sit in the GPU's LAUNCH QUEUE, waiting for a free SM
```

**"Resident"** = physically living on an SM right now: its registers are allocated, its shared memory is allocated, its TMEM is allocated, its pipelines are warmed up. **"Queued"** = just an entry in the hardware's to-do list — no SM, no memory, not running, it's a *promise* of a future launch.

## What "stealing" means (the CLC mechanism)

Normally, a resident cluster finishes its tile and **exits** — frees its SM — and the hardware launches one of the 54 queued clusters onto that freed SM. That new cluster then has to **start from zero**: allocate TMEM, run the init barrier, fill its load pipeline from empty. That startup costs a couple of microseconds.

CLC (`clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel`) is a Blackwell instruction that lets a resident cluster say to the hardware:

> *"Don't launch one of those queued clusters. **Cancel it**. Tell me which tile it was going to compute — **I'll compute that tile myself**, since I'm already set up and running."*

That's the bracket, piece by piece:
- **"cancel their launch"** → the queued cluster is removed from the launch queue by the hardware, it will *never* run. `try_cancel` returns its ID (which tile it owned).
- **"do their work ourselves"** → the resident cluster takes that ID, decodes which output tile it maps to, and runs its main loop again for *that* tile.
- **"stay resident"** → the whole point: the resident cluster **skips the startup cost** (its TMEM is already allocated, its pipeline is already warm). Stealing a tile is cheaper than launching a fresh cluster for it. That's why CLC exists.

## Why in THEORY it's still 2 rounds

74 clusters run round 1 (74 tiles). 54 tiles remain. If each steal is spread nicely — **54 of the 74** resident clusters each steal exactly **one** tile — then round 2 runs those 54 stolen tiles in parallel, while the other 20 clusters just exit. Total time = 2 tile-times. Same as cuBLAS. Perfect.

## Why in REALITY it became 3 rounds — the RACE

`try_cancel` is **first-come-first-served against one shared queue**. All 74 resident clusters finish round 1 at *almost* the same moment and all fire cancel requests at the queue **simultaneously**. The hardware arbitrates them in whatever order they happen to arrive — **we have no control over who wins**.

The bad outcome that kept happening: a cluster that finished a hair early steals tile #2, finishes it, and *fires again* and steals tile #3 — while some slower cluster's request found the queue already empty and got nothing. End state:

```
lucky spread (the "147µs fluke"):    unlucky spread (the usual 202µs):
cluster A: ██ ██        2 tiles      cluster A: ██ ██ ██   3 tiles  ← everyone waits for HIM
cluster B: ██ ██        2 tiles      cluster B: ██ ██      2 tiles
cluster C: ██           1 tile       cluster C: ██         1 tile ─┐ finished early,
...                                  ...                          ─┘ parked at exit barrier
kernel = 2 tile-times = 147µs        kernel = 3 tile-times = 202µs
```

The kernel can't finish until the **greediest** cluster finishes — and everyone else stands parked at the exit barrier waiting for it (that's exactly the barrier+sleeping stall we measured). Since the race outcome was random, we got 147 *or* 209 randomly — the **bimodal**.

## The fix (§68b)

For grids like this (≤ 2 waves) we simply **don't arm CLC at all** — every cluster computes exactly the one tile its `blockIdx` gave it and exits; the hardware launches the queued 54 onto the freed SMs. No queue race, no greedy cluster — the hardware's distribution is trivially even: **always exactly 2 rounds, 145µs, every single run.** (That's cuBLAS's model — its kernel has zero CLC instructions.)

We keep CLC for **big grids** (>2 waves, like LMheads with ~128 tiles per SM) because there the startup-skipping is worth a lot (paid once instead of 128 times) and the race statistically evens out over that many rounds.

One honest nuance: plain-grid round 2 pays the fresh-cluster startup (~part of why we're at 145 vs cuBLAS's 137) — that startup cost is exactly the **P1 (+2.2µs fixed overhead)** target we're now hunting next. 👊

**Simple version, one para, bro:**

We had a job of 128 tiles, but the GPU can only run 74 clusters at a time — so 74 start running, and 54 wait in a queue. Our old trick (CLC) was: when a running cluster finishes its tile, instead of exiting, it "steals" a waiting tile from the queue and does that too (saving the startup cost of launching a fresh cluster). Sounds smart — but the stealing is a **race**: all 74 finish around the same time and grab from the queue at once, and whoever's fastest grabs 2-3 extra tiles while slower ones grab none. The whole kernel can't end until the greediest cluster finishes its 3 tiles, so everyone else just stands waiting at the exit — the job takes **3 rounds instead of 2** (202µs instead of ~145). Sometimes by luck the grab spread out evenly and we hit 147µs — that was our "fluke." The fix: for these grid sizes, **turn off the stealing** — every cluster does exactly its own 1 tile and exits, and the hardware launches the waiting 54 onto the freed SMs itself. Even distribution guaranteed → always 2 rounds → 145µs every time, which is how cuBLAS does it too. 👊

### CLAUDE [2026-07-18 20:04 IST]

Simple math, bro:

- **B300 has 148 SMs** (the physical compute units).
- Our kernel asks for **~227KB of shared memory per CTA** — that's basically the entire SM's shared memory budget (we deliberately max it for the deep load pipeline + big tiles). So **only 1 CTA fits per SM** — no room for a second.
- One **cluster = 2 CTAs** (the pair that shares the work of one 256-wide tile via `cta_group::2`).

So:

```
148 SMs  ×  1 CTA per SM  =  148 CTAs resident at once
148 CTAs ÷  2 CTAs per cluster  =  74 clusters at a time
```

That's the "wave" size: 74 clusters = one full wave. A 128-cluster job = 128/74 = **1.73 waves** → minimum 2 rounds no matter what. cuBLAS's kernel has the same smem appetite (1 CTA/SM too), so 74 is *their* wave size as well — same playing field, which is why the fight was purely about how evenly the 128 tiles get distributed over those 74 slots. 👊

### CLAUDE [2026-07-18 20:21 IST]

Here bro, one clean para:

When a grid is bigger than the GPU (128 clusters but only 74 slots), the extra 54 clusters sit in the hardware's launch queue waiting for a free SM. Normally, a running cluster finishes its tile, exits, and the hardware launches a queued cluster onto that freed SM — but that fresh cluster must start from zero: allocate its TMEM, run its init barrier, and fill its load pipeline from empty, which costs a few microseconds. So "stealing" just means: kill a waiting cluster in the queue and absorb its tile into yourself, because a warm, running cluster doing an extra tile is cheaper than cold-starting a new cluster for it — that saving is the entire reason CLC exists. 👊

## Does cuBLAS have this tail? YES — but theirs is ~HALF ours (bounded proof)
The tail is physically unavoidable (the last tile's epilogue has nothing to hide behind — for both of us). But the bound: our non-epilogue fixed costs are 3.94µs (init 1.04 + fill 1.60 + exit 1.03 + teardown 0.27). Even if cuBLAS paid the SAME 3.94 for those, their **total** fixed is 5.68 → their epilogue tail ≤ **1.74µs vs our 3.40µs**. The instruction dumps explain exactly why:

## The two epilogues, instruction by instruction (0.6b-K capture)
| operation | cuBLAS | OURS | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| TMEM→reg loads | 16× `LDTM.16` | 8× `LDTM` (wider) | ~equal |
| alpha scaling | **128× `FFMA2`** (2 elems/instr) | 128× `FMUL` + 64× `FFMA` (1 elem/instr) | **they scale at 2× per instruction** |
| convert | 128× `F2FP.PACK_AB` | 96× `F2FP.PACK_AB` | ~equal |
| **smem store** | **32× `STSM.16.MT88.4`** (stmatrix: 1 instr = 4 8x8 tiles, hardware layout) | 24× `STS.128` + **33× `PRMT` + ~154 integer addr ops** (`IMAD`/`IMAD.U32`/`IADD`) | **their store needs ZERO address math; our XOR-swizzle computes every address** |
| addr-math datapath | 39 ops, **uniform path** (`UIADD3`/`UIMAD` — free datapath) | 154 ops on the **main INT pipe** | theirs doesn't steal issue slots |
| **TMA store drain** | **8× `UTMASTG.3D` + 8× flush + 8× fence** (8-slice pipelined drain) | 1 `UTMASTG` site (fewer, coarser chunks) | **their drain overlaps convert of next slice 8-deep** |
| + mystery on our side | — | 32× `LDG.E.CONSTANT` in the epilogue | to investigate — possibly removable |

**Summary: our epilogue issues roughly 2× the instructions on the drain's critical path** — swizzle address arithmetic + single-width scaling + coarser TMA slicing — and with a fixed issue rate, a serial tail's length ∝ instruction count. One history note for honesty: §63's audit said our int4+swizzle store "matches CUTLASS SOTA" — that was about *throughput pattern correctness*, and it's still true; what's new is that the **tail latency** (3.4µs, 46% of fixed cost) is where the extra instructions actually bill us.

## Fix candidates (each A/B-able, ranked by evidence)
1. **`stmatrix` in the regular epilogue** — kills the PRMT + ~150 addr ops outright. Strongest candidate, and **we already have working stmatrix code in the SWAP path** (`stmatrix_x4_trans`) — porting the non-transposed form is contained.
2. **8-slice pipelined TMA drain** (match their `UTMASTG` slicing) — overlaps store-drain with conversion.
3. **float2/paired alpha scaling** → get `FFMA2` emitted (halves scaling instructions).
4. Investigate/remove the 32× `LDG.E.CONSTANT`.

## But — discipline first (one more 30-min measurement)
The 3.4µs is still one box: if it's dominated by **TMA-drain latency**, stmatrix won't help (slices would); if by **convert+store issue**, stmatrix is the winner. **Probe v2: three sub-stamps inside the epilogue** (TMEM-read done / smem staged / TMA drained) tells us which — then we implement the right one with proof, not the plausible one. ## How the big libraries actually do this
- **NVCC itself** (CUDA 11.6+) supports `-arch=native`, which detects the GPU(s) on the build machine — but it's ambiguous/unreliable whether it auto-adds the `"a"` (family-specific) suffix Hopper/Blackwell need for `wgmma`/`tcgen05`, so it's risky to lean on blindly.
- **CMake 3.24+**: `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native` — same idea, compiles a tiny probe at configure time to read the device's compute capability.
- **PyTorch**: reads `torch.cuda.get_device_capability()` at build time (or `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` env var override), but since PyTorch ships *portable* wheels, it usually falls back to baking in a whole list of architectures ("fat binary") rather than trusting single-machine detection.
- **CUTLASS**: doesn't auto-detect at all — expects you to pass `CUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS` explicitly, because it's meant to be built anywhere for any target.

**For us, the right pattern is simplest of all of these**: we always build on the *one* GPU box we're actually renting that session — no portability need, no fat binary. So: **query `nvidia-smi` directly, once, at Makefile-parse time**, and build the gencode flags from that — with the existing `make GENCODE_FLAGS=...` override staying intact for cross-compiling to a different box's queued shape.

## PyTorch's `native` detection ([torch/utils/cpp_extension.py:2609-2652](pytorch_source/torch/utils/cpp_extension.py#L2609)):
```python
capability = torch.cuda.get_device_capability(i)   # e.g. (9, 0) for H200
...

```
**PyTorch's own hardware auto-detect NEVER emits the `"a"` suffix — not even on Hopper.** It always falls back to the plain, portable form.

## CUTLASS's CMake ([CMakeLists.txt:174-206](cutlass/CMakeLists.txt#L174)):
```cmake
if (CUDA_VERSION VERSION_GREATER_EQUAL 12.0)
  list(APPEND CUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS_SUPPORTED 90a)
endif()
if (CUDA_VERSION VERSION_GREATER_EQUAL 12.9)
  list(APPEND CUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS_SUPPORTED 100f 120f 121f 103a 103f)
endif()
```
**A manually maintained, hand-typed list, gated by CUDA-toolkit-version `if` blocks** — literally the same shape as the lookup table I wrote you. NVIDIA's own engineers add a new line every time a new chip ships. No cleverer trick.

## Why — this isn't laziness, it's structural
**Whether to use `"a"` isn't a hardware fact you can query at all.** `torch.cuda.get_device_capability()` tells you the chip generation, but "does my *kernel* use `wgmma`/`tcgen05`/cluster instructions" is a property of the **source code**, not the device. A device probe can't answer "should this specific compilation use the accelerated variant" — that's a decision only the programmer (who wrote the inline PTX) can make. That's exactly why even PyTorch, with full runtime access to the device, doesn't try.

## The good news for us specifically
We don't need to solve the general problem — **our repo already answers "does this need `a`" by construction**: it's organized into `SM89/` (plain `mma.sync`, no `a`), `SM100/SM103/` (tcgen05, needs `a`), and soon `SM90/` (wgmma, needs `a`). The folder you're building from already tells you the answer — no detection needed at that level.

- H200 → compute capability **9.0** → **SM90**
- B300 → compute capability **10.3** → **SM103**
Simple mapping, that's it.

## "CUDA 13.0" is NOT a compute capability — you're mixing two different version numbers
**CUDA 13.0** = the **toolkit/compiler version** (nvcc) we just switched to. **Compute capability** = a property of the **GPU hardware itself** (9.0 for H200, 10.3 for B300). These are two completely separate numbering schemes that happen to look similar this generation — pure coincidence, not related. So "does compute capability 13.0 mean 103 or 103a" isn't quite the right question — there's no such thing as compute capability 13.0. The B300's hardware compute capability is **10.3**, and CUDA **toolkit 13.0** is simply the compiler version that's new enough to *support* compiling for it.

## 90 vs 90a, 103 vs 103a — NOT two different GPUs, one GPU, two compile targets
This is the key thing to nail down: **`sm103` and `sm103a` are the SAME physical B300 chip.** There's no separate "GPU that's sm103 without the a" — it's one piece of silicon, and you're choosing between two **compile-time feature levels** for code destined for it:
- **`sm_103`** (plain) = the portable baseline instruction set — code compiled this way is guaranteed to run on any future chip that also claims compute-cap 10.3.
- **`sm_103a`** = the SAME chip, but the compiled code is *additionally allowed* to use the family-specific accelerated instructions (`tcgen05`, `clusterlaunchcontrol`) that are exclusive to this exact chip family and not promised to survive into some hypothetical different 10.3 chip.

**B300 supports BOTH as valid compile targets** — we've just always used `103a` because our kernel needs `tcgen05`. Same exact relationship for H200: it's one chip, and `sm_90` vs `sm_90a` are just two different instruction-set opt-in levels for code you compile *for* it — not two different pieces of hardware.

I scanned every `.cu` file in the repo. Here's what actually uses Blackwell-only instructions (`tcgen05`/`clusterlaunchcontrol` — confirmed absent from Hopper's ISA entirely, not just gated):

## 1. Confirmed: on H200 it picks `90a` (not `90`); on B300 it would pick `103a` (not `103`) — and "fallback" is the wrong word
It's not a fallback ladder — it's a **superset check**. The probe tries `"a"` first because `"a"` = plain baseline **plus** the extra accelerated instructions. Since `"a"` is a strict superset, whenever the toolkit accepts it, using it is strictly better (loses nothing, gains the accelerated path). The plain form (`compute_80` fallback) only ever fires when **no GPU is detected at all** (headless/CI) — that's the one and only place it's a genuine fallback.

## 2. The mechanism, step by step, on THIS box right now
1. `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap` → `9.0` → `_GPU_CAPS = "9.0"`.
2. Probe writes a 1-line trivial kernel to a temp `.cu`, tries `nvcc -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a -c <tmp> -o /dev/null`.
3. CUDA 13.0.88 accepts it (exit 0) → `GENCODE_FLAGS = -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a`.
That's the whole mechanism — real compile test, not a lookup.

## 3. Yes — the SM89-vs-Blackwell cross-compile problem is REAL, and it's pre-existing, not something I'm introducing
I scanned every `.cu` in the repo. `BF16/SM100`, `BF16/SM103` (+`kota_addmm`), `FP8/SM103`, `FP16/B300` all use `tcgen05`/`clusterlaunchcontrol` — Blackwell-exclusive, doesn't exist on Hopper *at all*. `BF16/SM89`, `FP32/SM86`+`SM89` are clean (older, backward-compatible instructions). Since `CU_SOURCES := $(shell find $(SRCDIR) -name '*.cu')` unconditionally grabs **every** file regardless of `GENCODE_FLAGS`, and `test`/`run`/`all` all depend on `lib` (which compiles the whole tree) — **this has always been broken for any non-Blackwell box.** It just never surfaced because every session so far was on a B300, and B300's `103a` target happens to be a superset that swallows SM89's older code fine too. H200 is the first box where the asymmetry actually bites.

## 4. The BluTrain / colleague SM89-SGEMM mystery — traced to the root cause, with proof
Went through the actual dispatch chain in `BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/`:
- **`AutocastMode`** correctly defaults to `Bfloat16` and `MatrixOps.cpp::matmul()` correctly downcasts both operands before calling the real GEMM — no bug there.
- The real dispatch lives in `src/Kernels/cuda/matmul/GenMatmul.cu` (this is your **"genmatmul"** — same file, just capitalized). It's gated:
  ```cpp
  #ifdef WITH_MYBLAS
    ... dispatch_by_dtype(...) { Sgemm/Hgemm/Bgemm/Dgemm via OUR BluBLAS }   // correct per-dtype routing, no bug
  #else
    ... raw cuBLAS (cublasGemmStridedBatchedEx) + a hand-written fallback kernel ...
  #endif
  ```
- And in `Tensor-Implementations/Makefile`:
  ```makefile
  ifeq ($(WITH_BLUBLAS),1)
    BLAS_BACKEND := blublas
  else
    BLAS_BACKEND := cublas          # <-- THE DEFAULT
  endif
  ```
**`WITH_MYBLAS` (and therefore our whole BluBLAS library) only gets linked in if the training script was launched with `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` explicitly.** Default is plain cuBLAS. **So unless your colleague passed that flag, our BluBridge-BLAS was never in the binary at all** — the "SM89 SGEMM" in the nsys trace is almost certainly **cuBLAS's own internal kernel** (cuBLAS ships architecture-tagged precompiled kernels too, same naming convention as our own `nvjet_sm103_...`), completely unrelated to our repo's `SM89/` folder. Nothing to fix in our code — worth asking the colleague directly: *"did you build with `WITH_BLUBLAS=1`?"* That one flag answers it definitively.

## 5. The genuinely great discovery — BluTrain's OWN Makefile already solved our exact problem
Same file, lines 45-62 — literal code comment:
```makefile
# Fix: build fat binaries. Legacy sources compile for every supported legacy
# arch (+ a forward-compatible PTX slice); Blackwell-only sources compile only
# for the Blackwell targets they require. Selection is per source file, based
# on which directory it lives in (see GENCODE_FOR below).
GENCODE_LEGACY := -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80 \
                  -gencode arch=compute_86,code=sm_86 \
                  -gencode arch=compute_89,code=sm_89 \
                  -gencode arch=compute_90,code=sm_90 \
                  -gencode arch=compute_90,code=compute_90   # + forward-compat PTX
GENCODE_BLACKWELL := -gencode arch=compute_100a,code=sm_100a \
                     -gencode arch=compute_103a,code=sm_103a
BLACKWELL_MARKERS := SM100 SM103 B300 sm100 sm103 b300
is_blackwell_src = $(strip $(foreach m,$(BLACKWELL_MARKERS),$(findstring $(m),$(1))))
GENCODE_FOR = $(if $(call is_blackwell_src,$(1)),$(GENCODE_BLACKWELL),$(GENCODE_LEGACY))
```
**This is exactly the fix I was about to design for our BluBLAS Makefile** — per-file gencode selection by matching a marker string against the file's directory path, baking multiple `-gencode` entries into ONE nvcc invocation for the safe/legacy files (true fat binary — one `.o` works on Ampere through Hopper), and restricting the Blackwell-only files to only the archs that support them. Someone already proved this pattern works, in our own ecosystem.

## First — the vendored copy isn't a duplicate Makefile at all
Checked: `Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/` has **no Makefile** — just `include/`+`src/`+`external/`. It's pure vendored **source**, compiled directly by BluTrain's own `Tensor-Implementations/Makefile` (the smart `GENCODE_LEGACY`/`GENCODE_BLACKWELL` one). So there's no literal duplicate — but you're right that it's **the exact same underlying problem, just already solved on the BluTrain side and still unsolved on our BluBLAS side.** That's the real point, and it's correct.

## Fat binaries — exactly what you're picturing, and here's precisely how it works
Yes: when `GENCODE_LEGACY` lists `sm_80`, `sm_86`, `sm_89`, `sm_90` all in **one nvcc invocation**, nvcc compiles that **same source file** into 4 separate cubins (plus a forward-compatible PTX slice), all bundled into one `.o`/`.so` as a "fatbin" container. **At runtime**, when the kernel actually launches, the **CUDA driver itself** (not our code) inspects which GPU is present and automatically picks the matching embedded cubin — or JIT-compiles from the embedded PTX if there's no exact match. This is fully automatic; we write zero dispatch code for this layer.

## But here's the catch you already sensed: fat binaries do NOT work across incompatible families
This is the key nuance. Fat-binary-ing only works when the **same unconditional source code** is valid for every listed target. `tcgen05`/`clusterlaunchcontrol` (SM100/103) and `wgmma` (SM90) are **hardware-exclusive instructions with no equivalent on the other family** — our kernel files emit them unconditionally (no `#if __CUDA_ARCH__` guards). So you **cannot** compile `Bgemm_sm103_bf16_NN_cluster.cu` with `-gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a` in the mix — that slice of the compile would hard-fail. That's exactly why BluTrain doesn't fat-binary its SM103 files: `GENCODE_FOR` **excludes** them entirely from non-Blackwell builds (matches your instinct: "leave those higher non-compatible files... compile only for that SM" — precisely right, and it's symmetric: SM90's `wgmma` files would equally get excluded from a B300 build, since Blackwell doesn't have `wgmma` either).

## Now the part I hadn't checked — and it's genuinely good news
You asked: *"did we mention dispatching correctly to SM89 module and correct dtype, in the dispatching system?"* I went and actually read `Bgemm_dispatcher.cu` — **yes, we already have this, and it's correct**:
```cpp
int actual_sm_ver = 80;
get_gpu_info(&actual_sm_ver, &actual_sm_count);   // real runtime check
if (actual_sm_ver >= 103) {
    // call SM103 tcgen05 kernels
    ...
}
// else falls through to SM80+/SM89 (mma.sync-generation) kernel variants
```
So the **runtime routing** (which kernel *function* to call, based on the actual detected GPU) is already architecture-aware and correct — this isn't missing.

## The ONE remaining wrinkle this reveals (a real, separate problem from the Makefile)
Even with the Makefile fixed to exclude SM103 files on a Hopper build, `Bgemm_dispatcher.cu` still **declares and calls** `blublasBgemmSM103_dispatch_nn/nt/tn` as `extern "C"` functions unconditionally. If those functions' actual definitions (the excluded SM103 files) never get compiled, the **linker** will fail with "undefined symbol" — even though the runtime `if (actual_sm_ver >= 103)` would correctly never call them. The runtime check protects execution; it doesn't protect the **link step**. So the complete fix needs **two matching pieces**: (1) the Makefile excludes SM103/SM90-family files per target (BluTrain's pattern), **and** (2) `Bgemm_dispatcher.cu` (and its Sgemm/Hgemm/Dgemm siblings) wrap those `extern "C"` declarations+calls in a matching preprocessor guard (e.g. `-DBLUBLAS_HAS_SM103`, defined by the Makefile only when those files are actually in the build) — otherwise it won't link on any box that excludes them.

## The complete plan
1. Port BluTrain's `GENCODE_LEGACY`/`GENCODE_BLACKWELL`/`BLACKWELL_MARKERS`/`GENCODE_FOR` pattern into BluBLAS's own Makefile (per-file gencode selection).
2. Add a Makefile-driven define (`BLUBLAS_HAS_SM103`, `BLUBLAS_HAS_SM90`, etc.) that's set exactly when those files are included.
3. Guard the corresponding `extern "C"` forward-declarations + call sites in each dispatcher file with matching `#ifdef`s.

That's the real, complete, future-proof fix — build-level file selection **and** dispatcher-level linkage guards, working together. Want me to implement both pieces now? 👊

**That's the entire target list — just `sm_90a`. No `sm_100a`, no `sm_103a`, nothing else listed.** Compare this to `clusterlaunchcontrol`'s multicast qualifier we found earlier, which explicitly listed *multiple* valid architectures (`sm_100a`/`sm_101a`/`sm_120a`) — `wgmma` gets no such list. It's Hopper-exclusive, full stop.

## Why "higher = more compatible" breaks here — the actual hardware reason
Your instinct (newer/higher number should include everything older) is **correct for the plain baseline instruction set** — that part genuinely is a superset ladder; code compiled for plain `sm_90` will run fine on `sm_103` too. But it's **wrong for the accelerated `"a"` instructions specifically**, and here's the physical reason: Blackwell didn't *extend* `wgmma` — it **replaced the whole mechanism**.

- **Hopper's `wgmma`**: a warpgroup of 128 threads collectively issues one big async matrix-multiply, accumulating the result **directly in registers**.
- **Blackwell's `tcgen05`**: uses a **completely different hardware unit** — dedicated Tensor Memory (TMEM), physical on-chip memory that **doesn't exist on Hopper silicon at all**. The accumulator lives in TMEM, not registers, and needs an explicit read-back instruction to get it into registers afterward (that's the whole epilogue mechanism we've been optimizing all week).

So `wgmma` and `tcgen05` are **two separate, non-overlapping instruction families**, each tied to a piece of hardware that only exists on its own generation. Blackwell isn't "Hopper plus more" at this level — it's "Hopper's baseline, plus its *own new and different* accelerated mechanism." That's exactly why the PTX spec gates each to its own single architecture, with zero cross-listing.

**Practical consequence for us:** this confirms the exclusion has to run **both directions** in the Makefile fix — `SM90/` (wgmma) gets excluded from Blackwell builds exactly as symmetrically as `SM100/SM103/` (tcgen05) get excluded from Hopper builds. Neither is a subset of the other; they're siblings. 👊

## What the probe actually costs (per `make` invocation, not per file)
It runs **once**, at Makefile-parse time, before anything else: one `nvidia-smi` call (~50-100ms) + one nvcc compile of a **1-line empty kernel** (nvcc's own startup overhead dominates here, roughly ~0.5-2s, since parsing/codegen work for a trivial file is near-zero). The cost of forgetting to update a hardcoded flag (a confusing build failure, or worse, a silent wrong-arch build) is far more expensive than 1-2 seconds, especially since we're actively hopping between rented GPU boxes this campaign.

## The real gap in what I wrote
My `HAVE_BLACKWELL` check is `cc >= 100` — an **open-ended threshold**. That silently assumes: *"any future chip numbered 100 or higher automatically shares Blackwell's `tcgen05` mechanism."* But that's the **exact same wrong assumption** we just spent this whole thread disproving for `wgmma` vs `tcgen05` — being numerically higher does **not** imply instruction compatibility. If NVIDIA ships a genuinely new architecture after Blackwell (say, numbered `SM130` for whatever comes next), my `>= 100` check would **wrongly** classify it as "Blackwell-compatible" and try to compile `tcgen05` code for it — which could be **just as incompatible as Hopper is**, and we'd have zero evidence either way. You're right: that's not a permanent fix, it's the same bug wearing a disguise.

## The correct fix — enumerate only what we have actual evidence for
Instead of a threshold, use an **explicit list of the specific Blackwell cap numbers CUTLASS's own CMake confirms share the `tcgen05` family** (100, 101, 103, 110, 120, 121 — I pulled this exact list from their `CMakeLists.txt` earlier). Anything **not** in that list — including any future unknown architecture — safely falls through to "excluded," not "wrongly included." That's the only sound default: **fail safe (exclude and require an explicit update) rather than fail by silently assuming compatibility we haven't verified.** This is unavoidable for any design, including CUTLASS's own — the honest limit is: nobody can write code today that correctly handles an instruction set NVIDIA hasn't published yet. The best any Makefile can do is make the unknown-case *safe*, and require one deliberate line added once the new hardware's real compatibility is documented.

Good clarifying question — let me nail down the scope precisely, based on what's actually in the spec (not guessing beyond it):

## `wgmma` is a Hopper-**family** feature, not H200-exclusive
`sm_90a` is the family tag for **compute capability 9.0** — every chip in that family gets it, not just H200. That includes **H100** (all SKUs: SXM, PCIe, NVL), **H200**, and **GH200** (Grace Hopper Superchip) — they're all "Hopper," all report compute-cap 9.0, all support `wgmma`. H200 is just the specific chip we happen to have; it's not special within that family.

## Below Hopper (Ampere, Ada, Turing, Volta) — NOT supported, genuinely didn't exist yet
`wgmma` isn't gated-but-present on older architectures — it's a **new instruction introduced with Hopper** (PTX ISA Notes confirm: "Introduced in PTX ISA version 8.2," which lines up with Hopper's debut). Older GPUs (including our SM89/Ada, SM86/Ampere) don't have the hardware mechanism at all — they use the older `mma.sync` (warp-level) instructions instead, which is exactly what our legacy SM89 kernels rely on.

## Above Hopper (Blackwell) — confirmed NOT supported, proven from the spec
Already directly verified: the PTX spec lists `wgmma.mma_async` as "Requires sm_90a" — **only** that one arch, no `sm_100a`/`103a` etc. Blackwell replaced the mechanism with `tcgen05`/TMEM entirely.

## Beyond Blackwell (whatever comes next) — honestly, unknown
This is the one place I can't give you a hard answer, and I won't pretend to. No spec for a post-Blackwell architecture exists yet. Going by the pattern so far (each generation introduces its *own* new accelerated mechanism rather than reusing the previous one — Volta/Ampere/Ada's `mma.sync` → Hopper's `wgmma` → Blackwell's `tcgen05`), it's reasonable to expect a future chip would need its own new arch tag too, not simply "support wgmma again" — but that's an informed guess based on trend, not a documented fact. Exactly the same honest limit we discussed with the Makefile's enumerated-cap design: nobody can pre-know an unpublished ISA.

**So the summary: `wgmma` = Hopper family only (H100/H200/GH200, compute-cap 9.0), nothing older, nothing newer (confirmed through Blackwell, unknown beyond it).** 👊

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 10:56 IST]

Let me pull the actual PTX spec description rather than answer from memory alone:
> tool `Bash`: Read the actual wgmma.mma_async spec description
> tool `Bash`: Read the semantic Description section of wgmma.mma_async

Read the actual spec description — here's what `wgmma.mma_async` does, and it'll feel familiar since it's built on the same concepts as our own SM103 kernel, just wired differently:

## What it does — the core operation
`D = A*B + D` — a standard matrix multiply-accumulate, same fundamental math as everything we've built. What's different is the **scale and mechanism**:

- **Shape**: M is fixed at 64, N ranges from 8 up to 256 (in steps of 8), K is 16 for bf16/fp16 (larger for other types). But crucially — this single instruction spans a **warpgroup: 4 warps, 128 threads acting together**, not one warp (32 threads) like the older `mma.sync`. One instruction does a much bigger chunk of the tile per issue.

- **Operands read via shared-memory descriptors** — `a-desc`/`b-desc`, 64-bit encoded descriptors pointing at A/B tiles in shared memory. **This is the exact same concept as our own `make_smem_desc()`** in the SM103 kernel — same idea, ported to Hopper's version of the mechanism.

- **The accumulator `D` lives in REGISTERS, distributed across the warpgroup's 128 threads** — *this* is the single biggest structural difference from our tcgen05 kernel. Blackwell's `tcgen05.mma` writes its accumulator into TMEM (dedicated on-chip memory); Hopper's `wgmma` keeps it in the warpgroup's own registers the whole time. No TMEM alloc/dealloc, no separate read-back instruction to get the result into registers — it's already there.

- **It's asynchronous, same pattern as everything we already know**: issuing `wgmma.mma_async` returns immediately; the actual tensor-core work happens in the background. You must call `wgmma.fence` before touching related registers, and `wgmma.commit_group`/`wgmma.wait_group` to wait for completion before reading `D` — the exact same commit/wait/fence discipline as `tcgen05.commit`/`tcgen05.wait`/`tcgen05.fence` in our own kernel, just for a register-based accumulator instead of a TMEM one.

- **Precision support**: fp16, bf16, tf32, fp8 (e4m3/e5m2), int8 — same breadth as tcgen05.

## The one-line summary
`wgmma` is Hopper's warpgroup-collective, TMA-descriptor-fed, async matrix-multiply that accumulates in **registers**; `tcgen05.mma` is Blackwell's version of the same idea that accumulates in **TMEM** instead. Same job, same async discipline, different accumulator home — and that register-vs-TMEM difference is exactly why the SM90 kernel's epilogue will look structurally different from SM103's (no TMEM read-back step needed at all). 👊

I've completed the full analysis — both the existing-module survey and Kota's setup. Here's the synthesis.

## How the 3 existing modules are actually structured

They are **not** one uniform pattern — there are two distinct design families, split by hardware generation:

**Ampere-style (BF16/SM89, FP32/SM86, FP32/SM89)** — simple synchronous `mma.sync`+`ldmatrix`:
- ONE generic `*_core_template.cuh` kernel, templated on `<Config, IsAligned, SplitK, Layout>` where `Layout` is an enum `{NN, NT, TN}` handled via `if constexpr` branches inside a single kernel body.
- Thin `*_variants.cu` files instantiate that one template per tile-shape (FP32/SM89 additionally inlines alignment/splitK branching in its variants files, a bit heavier than BF16/SM89's).
- **No internal module-level dispatcher.** Shape routing lives directly in the top-level `Bgemm_dispatcher.cu`/`Sgemm_dispatcher.cu` as an if/else cascade — confirmed by grep, zero dispatcher files in any of these three directories.
- Confirmed FP32/SM86's `Sgemm_core_template.cuh` is the same struct/kernel design (~480 lines of it is actually a stale commented-out first draft sitting above the live code — harmless but worth a cleanup someday).

**Cluster/async-style (BF16/SM103)**:
- A giant shared `*_cluster_template.cuh` (2612 lines) with the actual generic kernel, but ALSO separate substantial per-layout files (`_NN.cu`, `_NN_cluster.cu`, etc., 700-870 lines each) — because TMA descriptor setup and cluster launch genuinely differ per layout, unlike Ampere's simple index-permutation approach.
- Thin `*_variants.cu` wrapper files that just call `launch_bgemm_sm103_cluster<Config, Layout>(...)`.
- **Its own internal `Bgemm_sm103_dispatcher.cu`** — alignment gate + a measured `kTnWinners[]` (N,K) winner-table for TN specifically (12+ tile-shape variants), simpler 2-variant M/N%256 check for NN/NT.
- Top-level dispatcher calls into it guarded by `#ifdef BLUBLAS_HAS_SM103` + runtime `actual_sm_ver >= 103` check, and the internal functions return true/false to signal handled-vs-decline.

So the real principle isn't "one file layout for everyone" — it's: **simple synchronous hardware gets a single generic kernel + no internal dispatcher; async/warp-collective hardware (TMA, clusters, wgmma) gets per-layout launcher files + its own internal dispatcher**, because the orchestration complexity genuinely differs.

## Kota's SM90 setup — verdict: well-designed, follow it

It correctly follows the **cluster/async-style pattern**, not the Ampere one — right call, since `wgmma` is a warp-group-collective instruction needing the same kind of pipelined staging as `tcgen05`, not simple `mma.sync`:

- `Bgemm_sm90_bf16.cuh` — public declarations, mirrors `Bgemm_sm103_bf16.cuh`'s role exactly, same true/false decline contract documented explicitly.
- `Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh` (947 lines) — the shared generic kernel.
- `Bgemm_sm90_{nn,nt,tn}_variants.cu` — thin one-line instantiation wrappers, identical style to SM103's.

## One important thing that is NOT just a "base setup detail" — flagging it clearly

Kota's `Makefile` uses a **fundamentally different, more mature build strategy** than the one we built this session, and this matters for the decision ahead:

- **Ours**: detect the GPU on the box → exclude non-matching source files entirely → one narrow .so that only runs on that GPU family. Rebuild required to move to a different GPU generation.
- **Kota's**: compile *every* file, always, but give each file only its own matching `-gencode` (via directory-marker `GENCODE_FOR`) → link all of them into ONE universal fat `.so` that runs correctly on Ampere/Ada/Hopper/Blackwell without rebuilding — the runtime dispatcher (not the build system) picks the right kernel per box.
- It also independently solves the exact toolchain problem we manually symlink-switched around: `NVCC_BLACKWELL` lets Blackwell-marked files compile with a separate, newer nvcc than the rest of the build, so you don't need CUDA 13.0 to be the box-wide active toolkit just to build Blackwell-only files.

I'm not silently folding this in — it's a real architectural fork between what we shipped and what Kota built, and worth a decision before we merge SM90 in.
> tool `AskUserQuestion`: 
> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS/Makefile

Confirmed the precise difference by re-reading our Makefile end to end (lines 48-108). Line 87's own comment is explicit about the tradeoff: *"applied here as straight inclusion/exclusion since we only ever build for the ONE GPU actually in the box (no fat-binary portability need for this repo)."* That was a deliberate, stated scope decision when we wrote it — not an oversight. But it's more specific than "SM103 excluded on H200": `GENCODE_FLAGS` (line 50-69) loops only over `_GPU_CAPS` — the compute caps physically **present on this exact box**. If the box has only H200s, `GENCODE_FLAGS` is *just* `compute_90a/sm_90a` — no fat legacy list at all. So our `.so`, copied to a *different* GPU model entirely (say an A100), wouldn't just lose Blackwell/Hopper kernels — it would have **zero matching cubin for anything**, legacy included, and CUDA would refuse to launch any kernel on it ("no kernel image available for execution on the device"). Kota's `GENCODE_LEGACY` is unconditionally `sm_80+86+89+90+90-PTX` regardless of what's attached, so his `.so` runs everywhere from Ampere up.

Honest comparison, not picking a side to match either of our instincts:

| | Ours | Kota's |
|---|---|---|
| Arch string correctness | Empirically probes if `nvcc` actually accepts `compute_XXa` before using it — genuinely more robust than his (hardcoded `compute_90a`/`compute_103a` literals; an nvcc too old to know that grammar would hard-fail ptxas with no fallback) | Hardcoded, no probe |
| Cross-GPU-model portability | None — `.so` only runs on the exact GPU model it was built on | Full — one `.so` runs on Ampere→Blackwell without rebuild |
| Mixed toolkit-version friction (the thing we manually fixed by symlinking 12.4→13.0 site-wide) | Not solved — whole box's active `nvcc` must satisfy every file | Solved independently — `NVCC_BLACKWELL` lets only Blackwell files use a newer toolkit while everything else uses the box's normal one |
| No-GPU-attached build (CI, cross-compile) | Falls back to a bare `sm_80` guess with a warning (line 71-73) — silently wrong scope, not a hard stop | `HAVE_BLACKWELL_TOOLCHAIN` gates on toolkit presence, not GPU presence — correct even with zero GPUs attached |
| Complexity | Simpler — one `NVCC`, one `CPPFLAGS` | Heavier — two parallel toolchain/flag axes keyed off the same marker function |

Given how this repo is actually used all session — always cloned fresh and built directly on the literal target box over SSH, never one artifact shipped across a fleet of mixed GPU models — the portability gap Kota's solves doesn't bite you today, so "ours is fine, don't touch it" is a defensible call, not wishful thinking. But it's a real, current limitation, not a hypothetical: the moment you ever build once on an H200 box and try to run that same `.so` on a B300 or A100 without rebuilding, ours breaks and his doesn't. And the toolkit-version friction it independently solves is one we hit for real this week.

My actual recommendation: keep our Makefile as the default now (matches actual usage, no forced change), but don't treat the comparison as closed — worth revisiting if BluBLAS is ever meant to ship as one build artifact rather than always-rebuilt-per-box.

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 12:37 IST]

Good catch — that `ptxas ... setmaxnreg ignored` note is worth digging into properly rather than hand-waving. Let me find exactly where it's used and why ptxas is rejecting it.
> tool `Bash`: Locate setmaxnreg usage and launch bounds config in the SM90 template
> tool `Bash`: Find the exact register counts requested by setmaxnreg

Found it — and it's a real, concrete bug, not just noise. Traced the exact numbers in `Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh`:

- `NUM_THREADS = 384` (1 producer warpgroup + 2 consumer warpgroups, 128 threads each)
- `PRODUCER_REGS = 72`, `CONSUMER_REGS = 240` (line 78-79)
- The kernel does `setmaxnreg_dec<72>()` for the producer warpgroup, `setmaxnreg_inc<240>()` for each consumer warpgroup

Doing the actual register-file arithmetic for what this asks the hardware to provide, for a single resident CTA (the `__launch_bounds__(384, 1)` target):

```
producer:    128 threads × 72  regs =  9,216
consumer #1: 128 threads × 240 regs = 30,720
consumer #2: 128 threads × 240 regs = 30,720
                                     --------
                                       70,656 registers
```

SM90 (H100/H200) has **65,536** 32-bit registers per SM — same figure since Volta, documented in the CUDA C++ Programming Guide's compute-capability appendix. `70,656 > 65,536` by ~7.8%. This isn't a "could be tuned better" situation — the requested split is **physically impossible to grant for even a single CTA**, regardless of occupancy target. That's exactly why ptxas silently reverts to a uniform register allocation across all three warpgroups instead: it can't do what the code asked, so it does something safe instead, and tells you via that "Potential Performance Loss" note.

**Is it harmful?** Not to correctness — the kernel still compiles, links, and (per Kota's test comments) ran correctly on H200. But the entire point of that `setmaxnreg` call — starving the TMA-issuing producer warpgroup of registers so the wgmma-heavy consumer warpgroups get a big accumulator/operand register budget, which is *the* standard Hopper warp-specialized GEMM technique — is currently a complete no-op. Whatever throughput the existing tests measured, they measured it *without* this optimization active.

**The actual bug and fix**: `PRODUCER_REGS` is set way higher than it needs to be — the producer warpgroup only issues TMA loads and waits on mbarriers, it barely touches registers. Dropping it to the documented minimum (24, which the file's own `static_assert(N >= 24)` already allows) fixes the arithmetic:
```
24×128 + 240×128 + 240×128 = 64,512 ≤ 65,536   ✓ fits, with headroom
```

That's a one-constant change (`PRODUCER_REGS = 72` → `24`, still a multiple of 8) that would actually turn the intended optimization on. I haven't touched it — this is Kota's tuning constant in code we're building on top of, and the right value might interact with things I can't verify without real hardware profiling, so figured you'd want to weigh in before I change a performance-tuning parameter in his kernel.

The real constraint is an **exact equality**, not a budget inequality like either of my two guesses:

```
CONSUMER_REGS × num_consumer_warpgroups + PRODUCER_REGS × num_producer_warpgroups  ==  baseline_regs × total_warpgroups
```

`setmaxnreg` redistributes a **fixed-size** CTA register pool — it can't create or destroy registers, only move them between warpgroups. The pool size is `baseline × total_warpgroups`, where `baseline` is whatever ptxas naturally compiles the whole (single, branching) kernel function down to. If the redistribution's total doesn't land on exactly that same pool size, ptxas can't satisfy it and silently reverts to uniform allocation — which is exactly our "ignored" message.

Now the bad news specific to Kota's kernel, which is why my two guesses both failed: our verbose ptxas output showed the natural baseline is **different per tile shape** — 126 for 128×128×64, 167 for 128×256×64 (bigger N-tile needs more accumulator registers, `CREGS = BN/2`). The exact-equality equation is:

```
128×128×64:  PRODUCER_REGS + 2×CONSUMER_REGS  must equal  126 × 3 = 378
128×256×64:  PRODUCER_REGS + 2×CONSUMER_REGS  must equal  167 × 3 = 501
```

Both tile shapes are instantiated from **one shared `Sm90WarpspecConfig` struct** with **one hardcoded `PRODUCER_REGS`/`CONSUMER_REGS` pair** — but 378 ≠ 501, so no single pair can satisfy both equations at once. - per-tile-shape register values (forcing each shape's own exact-equality N, which likely also needs its own `--maxrregcount` since both shapes currently compile in the same `.cu` translation unit and a blanket nvcc flag applies to all kernels in it), or

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 14:23 IST]

Here's exactly what we did, in plain terms:

**The problem:** Kota's SM90 kernel tries to do a performance trick called a "register split" — it splits the 384 threads in each block into 3 groups (warpgroups): 1 "producer" group that just issues memory loads, and 2 "consumer" groups that do the actual matrix-multiply math. The trick is to take registers away from the producer (it barely needs any) and give them to the consumer groups (they need a lot, for math). This is done via two special GPU instructions: `setmaxnreg.dec` (shrink producer's registers) and `setmaxnreg.inc` (grow consumer's registers).

**What was actually happening:** Every time we compiled, the GPU compiler (ptxas) printed a warning saying it was *ignoring* this trick entirely and just giving every thread the same register count instead. So the optimization Kota intended was silently never running — the code *looked* like it was doing something clever, but it wasn't.

**What we found out why:** This trick only works if a precise math equation balances exactly — how many registers you take from the producer must exactly equal how many extra registers all the consumers combined are asking for. It's not "roughly enough," it has to be exact. We confirmed this by literally reading NVIDIA's own CUTLASS library's bug tracker on GitHub, where an NVIDIA engineer explained this exact same problem. We tried several different number combinations (including NVIDIA's own official values) and none of them made the equation balance for Kota's specific kernel code — because the "right" numbers depend on exactly how much register pressure that specific kernel's code creates, which differs from file to file and even between the two tile sizes in this same file.

**What we did about it:** We checked — does any other part of this codebase (SM89, SM86, SM103/Blackwell) use this same trick? No. None of them do. And SM103 in particular already runs correctly and has been validated on real hardware without ever trying this optimization. So instead of chasing a perfect fix that even NVIDIA's own engineers struggle to nail down by trial and error, **we removed the two `setmaxnreg` calls and their leftover config lines entirely** — matching what the rest of this codebase already does successfully.

**Why that's safe, not a cop-out:** Since the trick was already being ignored by the compiler anyway, removing it changes *nothing* about how the kernel actually runs — we verified the register counts the kernel uses are essentially identical before and after (124-126 vs 126, and 167 vs 167). All we did was delete dead code that was misleadingly implying an optimization was active when it never was, and get rid of the confusing warning message. The kernel still overlaps memory loads with math (that part of the design is untouched) — we just dropped the one extra register-reshuffling layer on top that was never actually working.

End result: all 4 SM90 files now compile with zero errors and zero warnings, and nothing about the kernel's actual behavior changed from before.

watch -n 1 nvidia-smi

If ncu is actively profiling, you'll see GPU utilization flicker/pulse in bursts (it launches the kernel, stops, reads counters, relaunches — so it looks bursty, not steady, but it should be moving, not flatlined at 0%).

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 15:36 IST]

That output is actually a good sign, not a bad one — `test_h200_sm90_dispatch_path` is listed as an active process holding 702MiB of GPU memory. If it had crashed or exited, it wouldn't be there at all. The `0%` GPU-Util is expected during ncu profiling: it works by launching tiny kernel replays with real gaps in between (to read back hardware counters), so a single snapshot very often catches an idle gap — that alone doesn't mean it's stuck.

To actually tell "genuinely stuck" apart from "working but bursty," check the `ncu` process's own CPU usage in a separate terminal — a live process should be burning real CPU coordinating the replays, a frozen one wouldn't:

```bash
top -p $(pgrep -d, ncu)
```

or if `top` isn't handy:

```bash
ps -o pid,pcpu,stat,etime,cmd -C ncu
```

Look at the `%CPU` column — if it's showing meaningful, non-zero CPU usage (even 20-80%), it's actively working. Also check the `etime` (elapsed time) so you know exactly how long it's been running. If `%CPU` is sitting at 0.0 for a good stretch *and* GPU-Util in your other terminal never once ticks up over a full minute of watching, then it's actually stuck. Otherwise, this is just `--set full` being slow, as expected — let it keep going.

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 16:13 IST]

Good question, and it deserves a real answer, not just "it doesn't matter."

**The key distinction: we didn't prove the technique is useless. We proved that in THIS kernel, TODAY, it was never actually running at all — in either version.** Both the "original" and the "fixed" version have the exact same reality: ptxas rejects the redistribution and falls back to uniform allocation. Removing dead code that was already inert cannot cost you anything, because there was nothing being gained to begin with. That's a very different claim from "this technique never helps anyone."

**Why does NVIDIA use this at all — what's it actually for?**

In a warp-specialized kernel like this one, every warp in a thread block normally gets an *equal* share of the SM's register file — our kernel's uniform share was 167 registers/thread. But the roles aren't equal:
- The **producer** warpgroup just issues TMA loads and waits on barriers — extremely simple code, needs almost no registers (24-40 is plenty).
- The **consumer** warpgroups do the actual matrix multiply — they need to hold the entire accumulator tile live in registers across the whole K-loop, which can require *far* more than a uniform share, especially for large output tiles.

If the consumer doesn't get enough registers, the compiler either spills the accumulator to slow local memory, or is forced into a smaller/less efficient tile size to fit. `setmaxnreg` lets you shrink the producer's allocation and hand those freed registers to the consumers — so the consumer can carry a bigger accumulator in registers than uniform allocation would ever allow it. When it actually works, that's a real, meaningful throughput win — which is exactly why CUTLASS's own production Hopper kernels use it.

**Why is it "confusing" even for NVIDIA's own people, per that GitHub thread?**

Because the win only materializes if the exact-equality constraint balances *exactly* against whatever the compiler naturally decides for that specific kernel's code — not a value you can look up or reuse across kernels, and the compiler's own natural register count shifts depending on things you don't fully control (adding `__launch_bounds__`, a stray unused variable, anything). Get it wrong by even a handful of registers and ptxas just silently falls back to uniform allocation with a warning most people don't investigate — or in CUTLASS's own reported case, the kernel can straight-up hang. It's a real technique with a real payoff, but a narrow, fragile window to actually hit it — which is exactly the trap Kota's kernel fell into, and exactly why it took this much digging to even confirm what was happening.

**One more honest thing worth adding, from our own data:** we already proved **zero register spilling** (`STL`/`LDL`) in either version, at the uniform 167-register allocation. That's the tell that this specific kernel's accumulator already fits comfortably without the split — the classic motivating scenario for `setmaxnreg` (avoiding spills on a register-starved consumer) doesn't actually apply to these particular tile shapes (128×256, 128×128). So even if someone got the exact-equality math right for this kernel, the realistic upside might be small — this technique tends to matter more for larger tiles where the accumulator genuinely doesn't fit under uniform allocation. Worth logging as a legitimate "maybe worth revisiting for bigger future tile configs," not "we left free performance on the table today."

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 16:32 IST]

Real, sharp question — let me actually answer both parts properly.

## Can this be done "universally" (once, for all shapes)?

Not with the current 3-warpgroup design, and here's the concrete reason, not a hand-wave: CUTLASS's own kernel *looks* like it does exactly this — it hardcodes `(40, 232)` unconditionally across many different tile shapes in its catalog. But that only works because CUTLASS's tile catalog is *calibrated* to it — their kernels are built with heavier, more uniform CuTe abstraction overhead (tensor descriptors, layout metadata) that keeps the natural compiled baseline clustering tightly around ~168 registers regardless of tile size. They didn't find a universal trick; they picked tile shapes that happen to fit one register budget.

Kota's kernel is simpler and leaner, so its baseline actually *scales* with tile size — 126 registers for the 128×128 config, 167 for 128×256 (roughly tracking `CREGS = BN/2`, the accumulator size). Since the exact-equality math depends on that baseline, and the baseline itself genuinely differs per shape here, one fixed `(P, C)` literally cannot satisfy both — this isn't a tuning failure, it's arithmetic (378 vs 501, proven earlier). So yes: **each shape needs its own values**, and that only grows as more tile shapes get added later.

## Your "self-adapting fallback" question — you're actually right, mostly

You're asking: doesn't the compiler already do exactly "try the optimization, and if it doesn't fit, just use its own normal decision" — the thing we saw happen the whole time? **Yes, that's precisely what's already built in.** `setmaxnreg` is a *hint*: if the exact-equality doesn't hold, ptxas silently keeps its own uniform allocation and just emits the "ignored" warning — no crash, no wrong answer, in every case we tested. That's genuinely graceful, automatic degradation, for free.

But there's one important caveat I have to be honest about, since it directly bears on "should we try this now": **that graceful fallback is not universally guaranteed.** The CUTLASS GitHub issue we found (#2007) shows a case where a *slightly* wrong register value didn't just "get ignored" — it caused an actual **hang** at runtime (`warpgroup_reg_alloc<232>()` never returning). So the safety net has a real, documented failure mode beyond "no benefit" — it can occasionally misbehave in a way that's worse than doing nothing, and the only way to catch that is by actually *running* the kernel, not just checking that the ptxas warning disappeared.

## My honest recommendation

Doing this "correctly" now means, for each of the 2 tile shapes: isolate it into its own compile target (since they currently share a translation unit and `--maxrregcount` can't tell them apart), sweep candidate register pairs, and for every candidate that clears the ptxas warning, **actually run it on the H200** to rule out the hang failure mode — not just trust the compile log. That's several real push/pull/build/run round trips per shape, genuine iteration, not a one-shot fix.

Given that, plus the fact we already proved this specific kernel has **zero register spilling** under uniform allocation (the classic scenario this technique exists to fix doesn't clearly apply here), the realistic payoff is uncertain and possibly small — while the downside risk (a hang, if a candidate value is subtly wrong) is real and would land in code that currently works correctly and performs at 90-96% of cuBLAS.

## 3. Section 47 "B5 BENCHMARK HARNESS" (lines 4049–4213) and Section 48 "B5-MIRROR" (lines 4176–4213)

**What B5 is (§47, lines 4057–4064):** "for each of the 42 Qwen shapes (TN, batch 1): time cuBLAS (5+20 iters) then EVERY validated variant (3+10 iters), print per-variant rows + per-shape BEST + final WINNER TABLE (shape | best variant | ours | cuBLAS | %) + summary (avg best-of-all-variants %, #shapes where we BEAT cuBLAS). 17 variants benched per shape... This table IS the dispatcher's routing data."

**The two distinct test types the document actually establishes** (not verbatim "two types of tests," but this is the closest structural match to the user's recollection):
1. **§47 "Winner-table" bench** — for each shape, run *all* our variants and take the best one, regardless of what cuBLAS itself picked for that shape. This produces the dispatcher's routing table.
2. **§48 "B5-MIRROR" bench** — for each shape, build/run *only* our clone of the exact kernel strategy cuBLAS itself picked for that shape (per the §16.3 mapping), and compare head-to-head, kernel-for-kernel.

Key quote distinguishing them (§48, line 4200): "MIRROR (82.4%) &lt; WINNER-TABLE best-of (87.4%): copying cuBLAS's per-shape kernel CHOICE is ~5 points WORSE for us than routing to OUR best variant... The dispatcher must use OUR winner table, not cuBLAS's routing."

**Measurement pitfalls found and fixed, in order (this is the key methodological history for a new benchmark design):**

1. **§47.1 ORDER-BIAS (line 4068–4076):** "cuBLAS-vs-ours comparisons swing +-30% with MEASUREMENT ORDER (boost clocks: whoever runs first on a cool GPU looks faster)." Evidence: same variant measured 1630-1888T run first vs 1299T run late. **Fix:** re-time cuBLAS after the variants, use max(first, recheck), and **lock clocks**: `nvidia-smi -pm 1 &amp;&amp; nvidia-smi -lgc &lt;freq&gt;`. "STANDING RULE for all future perf claims."

2. **§47.2 POWER-CAP THROTTLE (line 4087–4099):** Locking at 1700MHz still let sustained heavy shapes throttle under the power limit (7b-LMhead drift -23.8%). Also **no warmup on the recheck pass** caused tiny shapes to read low from cold caches (-22.2% on 0.5b-K). **Fix:** "lock LOW enough that the power cap can never engage — `nvidia-smi -lgc 1400`" + added 5-iter warmup to the recheck.

3. **§47.3 OFFICIAL run at locked 1400MHz** (line 4104–4130): drift now within ±8.4%. This run retracted earlier "&gt;100% on LM-heads" claims as boost-clock bias. Diagnostic finding: our LM-head kernel scales exactly with clock (0.93 T/MHz) = compute/issue-bound; cuBLAS loses only 13% for a 31% clock cut = memory-bound (better per-SM efficiency).

4. **§47.4 THERMAL-GRADIENT / preheat bias (line 4132–4150):** Restructuring the bench variant-major exposed "a clean TIME GRADIENT, not noise: early-baseline shapes... drift -6..-13.7%, late shapes... ~0±3%." Mechanism: `-lgc` locks only the graphics clock — HBM/memory-clock thermals decay ~10% over the first ~2 minutes, so early shapes were measured cold-fast-HBM while variants measured later were not. **Fix:** 60s heavy-GEMM preheat before any measurement.

5. **§47.5 B5 FINAL (official, line 4152–4174):** "variant-major, locked 1400MHz + 60s preheat." Final protocol: idle GPU + `-lgc 1400` (+`-lmc` if supported) + 60s preheat + baseline sweep + variant sweeps + recheck sweep with max-correction + drift gate ("accept run only if worst drift within ~±3%"). Methodology convergence quote: "82.3%/1 win (run3) -&gt; 85.1%/6 (run4 variant-major) -&gt; 87.4%/8 (run5 preheated) — every fairness fix moved numbers UP (the biases were mostly against us)." Official headline: best-of-variants avg **87.4%** of cuBLAS, beat cuBLAS on **8/42** shapes.

**§48 B5-MIRROR (official):** 42 head-to-head cases, our clone of cuBLAS's exact chosen kernel per shape, "cuBLAS + clone timed back-to-back per shape (no gradient possible), locked 1400MHz + preheat." MIRROR avg **82.4%**, kernel-for-kernel wins **2/42**. Per-kernel scorecard table given (128x256_v ~96% avg and beats cuBLAS on 0.5b-LMhead 105.8%; swap160x192 worst at 47.8-50.7%; etc.).

The research came back — extremely detailed, and it changes the shape of this plan a lot. Here's the synthesis.

## What already exists (don't redo this)

The Qwen model/shape research is **already done and audited**, not something to redo from scratch:
- 8 target models (Qwen2.5: 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B, Qwen3: 0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B), configs pulled directly from HuggingFace `config.json`, cross-verified against both arxiv tech reports.
- A caught, non-obvious detail: Qwen3 decouples `head_dim` from `hidden_size`, making Q/O projections **non-square** for exactly 2 of the 4 Qwen3 models (0.6B: 1024→2048, 4B: 2560→4096) — the kind of thing that silently breaks shape coverage if missed.
- **42 unique (M,N,K) shapes**, fully enumerated with cuBLAS's actual chosen kernel per shape (extracted from real nsys traces — the exact same technique we already used this session for H200's `nvjet_sm90_*` kernel names).
- This was formally audited for completeness (§23.4) and held up — MoE correctly excluded, attention correctly excluded (fused, never hits cuBLAS as a GEMM), redundant shapes deduplicated. **One real, explicitly-flagged gap: only M=4096 was ever benchmarked** — decode (M=1-128) and larger training M (8192, 16384) were never covered. That's real, new work worth doing for H200.

Since shapes are a property of the model architecture, not the GPU, this catalog is directly reusable for H200.

## What the "confusion" actually was

Two real candidates, and I'd bet on the first:

1. **Winner-table bench vs mirror bench** — for each shape, (a) run *every* variant we have and route to whichever wins ("winner-table"), vs (b) build a clone of *cuBLAS's own* kernel choice for that shape and compare head-to-head ("mirror"). This produced a genuinely important, quantified finding: **mirror-parity average (82.4%) was worse than winner-table best-of (87.4%)** — meaning copying cuBLAS's own per-shape kernel choice is measurably worse than routing to whatever we've independently found performs best. Direct quote: "the dispatcher must use OUR winner table, not cuBLAS's routing." This is a real design principle worth carrying forward as-is.

2. **P1/P2 variant-optimization plan** — P1 = fix our clones of cuBLAS's exact per-shape kernel choices (worst-gap-first), P2 = our own bonus variants not in cuBLAS's playbook, expected to inherit P1's gains "for free" since they share template code — to be verified afterward, not assumed.

Also worth knowing: there was a genuine, explicitly-documented scope-drift mistake (§64, M1) — quoting the 42-shape *average* TFLOPS when the actual task in front of them was a specific 8-shape subset, which sent them down a wrong detour (split-K) for a day. That's likely part of what "confusion" refers to too.

## The measurement methodology is hard-won — reuse it, don't rediscover it

This is the single most valuable thing to port forward wholesale:
- **Clock-lock everything** (`nvidia-smi -lgc <freq>`) — unlocked boost clocks swing cuBLAS-vs-ours comparisons ±30% by measurement order alone.
- **Lock low enough to avoid the power cap engaging** (they landed on 1400MHz) — even locked clocks throttled under sustained load otherwise.
- **60s preheat before measuring anything** — HBM/memory clocks decay over the first ~2 minutes independent of the graphics-clock lock, creating a real thermal gradient that biased early-measured shapes.
- **Never trust static/whole-binary instruction counts** — a "6.3x more instructions" finding was fully retracted after being caught comparing the whole compiled binary (every layout's dead branches included) against cuBLAS's one specialized kernel. Always use dynamic executed counts of the *specific* kernel via ncu.
- **`ncu --set full` can *distort*, not just slow down, complex/multi-wave kernel timing** (it serializes wave-2 backfill) — we already independently hit `--set full` being slow this session; the B300 doc shows it's worse than that for some kernel shapes.
- **Stale builds from header-only changes** bit them too — `make` doesn't always rebuild `.cu` files when only a `.cuh` they include changes, exactly the same class of bug already in memory from the reduction work.
- Explicit process rule they wrote down after a same-day revert: **before touching scheduler/barrier/dispatch logic, grep the doc's own history first** — don't re-break something already validated.

## My honest opinion, as you asked

The instinct behind this plan is right — ground kernel work in real shapes, cross-check against real libraries, build a measured winner-table dispatcher, not a guessed one. But three things I'd push back on or restage before starting:

1. **"Beat or match cuBLAS on all shapes" is a very high bar that the B300 team itself didn't fully reach.** After roughly three weeks of dedicated, rigorous work on an *already mature* Blackwell kernel base, they landed at 87% best-of-variants and 82% mirror-parity average — not 100%, and several shapes stayed short even after deep root-causing. SM90 today has exactly 2 tile shapes total. Setting "beat everything across 6 libraries" as the immediate target, before even having shape coverage, sets up for a long slog with a moving goalpost. I'd stage it: **(a) get real shape+tile coverage first** (correctness across the actual 42+ shapes, which SM90 doesn't have yet at all), **(b) then run the measured winner-table campaign**, shape-by-shape, worst-gap-first — same order that worked before.

2. **Six reference libraries may be more than the signal needs.** For a given shape, PyTorch and TensorFlow's matmul almost always just *delegates* to cuBLAS/cuBLASLt or a CUTLASS-based kernel under the hood on Hopper — they're rarely a genuinely distinct kernel implementation. Worth a quick check (a few `nsys`/`torch.profiler` traces) before committing to deep separate research on both — if they're just forwarding to cuBLAS, that's redundant work, not new signal. CUTLASS and DeepGEMM are worth it (open source, can read the actual dispatch logic directly, no reverse-engineering needed). ThunderKittens is a real third opinion. I'd start with cuBLAS + CUTLASS + DeepGEMM + ThunderKittens as the core four, and only add PyTorch/TF if the quick check shows they're doing something genuinely different.

3. **The M-axis gap is real and worth closing this time**, since it was explicitly flagged and never closed for B300 — decode-regime (M=1-128) and larger training M matter for what's actually running in BluTrain, not just the M=4096 snapshot.

### CLAUDE [2026-07-21 19:31 IST]

Good, that's a big scope reduction — locks us to standard transformer architecture only, across 5 generations. Quick answer to your question, then straight into the research.

**Does the matmul actually change for MoE/hybrid, and what is hybrid architecture?**

- **MoE**: the actual matmul *math* inside each expert's up/gate/down projection is identical dense-GEMM math — no different algorithm. What changes is (a) there's an extra small router matmul (`hidden → num_experts`) to decide which expert each token goes to, and (b) each expert only processes the tokens routed to it, so its effective batch size (M) becomes small and variable instead of one big dense matmul across all tokens — this needs a different *execution strategy* (grouped/batched GEMM with variable-size groups), which is exactly what a library like DeepGEMM specializes in. Same math, genuinely different shapes and dispatch pattern.

- **Hybrid architecture** (Qwen3.5/3.6/Qwen3-Next): normal attention computes token-vs-every-other-token (`QK^T` then `softmax` then `@V`) — a fundamentally different, *recurrent-style* mechanism called linear attention (Gated DeltaNet-style) replaces most layers instead. Rather than comparing every token to every other token, it keeps a small running "state" that gets updated one token at a time via its own matrix operations — shaped completely differently from standard attention (and very differently from the QKV/O/FFN catalog we care about). Only every 4th layer keeps standard attention. It's a genuinely different computational pattern requiring its own dedicated kernels, not an extension of the dense-transformer GEMM catalog — which is exactly why deferring it is the right call.

Q:KV head ratio (GQA groups) is **not constant** across sizes, contrary to a naive assumption:
- 0.5B: 14:2 = 7:1

### Architecture confirmation (from official transformers source, v4.40.1)

Qwen2Attention (separate QKV, not fused):
```python
self.q_proj = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.num_heads * self.head_dim, bias=True)
self.k_proj = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.num_key_value_heads * self.head_dim, bias=True)
self.v_proj = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.num_key_value_heads * self.head_dim, bias=True)
self.o_proj = nn.Linear(self.num_heads * self.head_dim, self.hidden_size, bias=False)
```
Q/K/V are three independent linear layers (bias=True on all three); O has no bias.

Qwen2MLP (gated, no bias on any of the three):
```python
self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.intermediate_size, bias=False)
self.up_proj   = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.intermediate_size, bias=False)
self.down_proj = nn.Linear(self.intermediate_size, self.hidden_size, bias=False)
# forward: down_proj(act_fn(gate_proj(x)) * up_proj(x))
```

In all four sizes, `num_attention_heads * head_dim == hidden_size` exactly (896=14×64, 1536=12×128, 3584=28×128, 8192=64×128), so the O-proj input dimension and Q-proj output dimension both equal `hidden_size` cleanly — no padding/remainder oddities.

### Notable/surprising shapes flagged

- **K/V proj shapes are the narrowest matmuls in the whole network** — 7x narrower than Q/O for 0.5B and 7B (896→128, 3584→512), 6x narrower for 1.5B (1536→256), 8x narrower for 72B (8192→1024). These are the only non-square-ish projections at the attention stage; every other attention matmul (Q, O) is square (N=K=hidden_size).
- The GQA compression ratio itself is **not uniform** across the family (7:1, 6:1, 7:1, 8:1) — worth encoding per-model rather than as a fixed constant in a shape generator.
- Gate/Up proj and Down proj are the largest-N / largest-K matmuls respectively, growing to a very wide 29568 dimension at 72B — these dominate FLOPs share far more than attention projections at every size (MLP expansion ratio ≈5.4x–5.6x hidden_size across all four).
- LM head is a very wide GEMM (N=151936 or 152064) — same shape used whether or not embeddings are tied, since tying only affects whether the weight matrix is a separate parameter or shared storage, not the GEMM shape itself.
- All four models pass `hidden_size = num_attention_heads * head_dim` exactly, so there's no odd remainder/padding case to special-case in a kernel catalog for this family.

| Qwen1.5-32B | 5120 | 27392 | 64 | 40 | **8 (GQA)** | 128 | 152064 | false | 32768 |
| Qwen1.5-72B | 8192 | 24576 | 80 | 64 | **64 (MHA)** | 128 | 152064 | false | 32768 |
| Qwen1.5-110B | 8192 | 49152 | 80 | 64 | **8 (GQA)** | 128 | 152064 | false | 32768 |

**No `head_dim` field exists in any of these 8 config.json files** — confirmed by inspecting `Qwen2Attention.__init__` in `modeling_qwen2.py` (transformers v4.37.0, matching the `transformers_version` pinned in every config), where it's computed as `self.head_dim = self.hidden_size // self.num_heads`.

**GQA only appears in 32B and 110B.** 0.5B, 1.8B, 4B, 7B, 14B, and — notably — **72B are all plain MHA** (`num_key_value_heads == num_attention_heads`). This breaks a naive "bigger = more GQA" assumption; 72B sits between two GQA models (32B, 110B) but is itself full MHA.

**`tie_word_embeddings` is true only for 0.5B.** All other seven, including 1.8B, are untied — so "small ties, large doesn't" is only a 1-model phenomenon here, not a size-based cutoff.

`https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen1.5-{0.5B,1.8B,4B,7B,14B,32B,72B,110B}/raw/main/config.json`

## Architecture confirmation (from `modeling_qwen2.py`, transformers v4.37.0 — `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/huggingface/transformers/v4.37.0/src/transformers/models/qwen2/modeling_qwen2.py`)

- **MLP (`Qwen2MLP`, lines 173–185):** separate `gate_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, all `nn.Linear(..., bias=False)`. Forward: `down_proj(act_fn(gate_proj(x)) * up_proj(x))` — confirmed SwiGLU, **not fused** gate_up.
- **Attention (`Qwen2Attention`, lines 201–236):** QKV are **three separate `nn.Linear` layers**, not fused:
  - `q_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_heads*head_dim, bias=True)`
  - `k_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_key_value_heads*head_dim, bias=True)`
  - `v_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_key_value_heads*head_dim, bias=True)`
  - `o_proj = nn.Linear(num_heads*head_dim, hidden_size, bias=False)`
  - Notable detail not in config.json: **Q/K/V projections carry bias, O proj does not** (same for all 8 sizes — this is hardcoded in the model class, not config-driven).
- **LM head (`Qwen2ForCausalLM`, line 1102):** `self.lm_head = nn.Linear(hidden_size, vocab_size, bias=False)`, tied to `embed_tokens.weight` only when `tie_word_embeddings=true` (0.5B only).

So the K/V-proj rectangularity (N vs Q's N) isn't a fixed multiple across the family — don't assume a single GQA ratio applies to all 7 sizes.
- **Down proj K dimension gets very large** relative to its own N at the big end — 32B's down proj is (4096, 5120, 27648), K more than 5× N; 72B is (4096, 8192, 29568), K ~3.6× N.

| `num_attention_heads` | 16 | 32 | 40 | 64 |

**Flags:**
- `num_key_value_heads` is absent from every config **and** absent as a constructor arg in `configuration_qwen.py` — Qwen1 predates GQA, confirmed standard MHA (no default fallback field either).
- `head_dim` is not a literal config field name; it's the explicit `kv_channels` field (=128 for all 4), and independently the code derives `self.head_dim = hidden_size // num_attention_heads`, which numerically matches `kv_channels` in all four cases (2048/16, 4096/32, 5120/40, 8192/64 = 128 each) — no ambiguity, but two different code paths compute it.
- 7B and 14B have `max_position_embeddings` ≠ `seq_length` (7B: 32768 vs 8192; 14B: 8192 vs 2048 — a 4x gap). This is a genuine as-published discrepancy, not a fetch error — reported verbatim.
- `vocab_size` is **not uniform** across the generation: 151936 (1.8B, 7B) vs 152064 (14B, 72B).
- 72B alone disables dynamic NTK / logn-attn scaling and uses a 100x larger RoPE base — a real architectural difference within "Qwen1", not noise.

## Architecture verification (from `modeling_qwen.py`, identical across all 4 repos)

**QKV projection — fused, single matmul** (`class QWenAttention`, confirmed lines):
```python
self.projection_size = config.kv_channels * config.num_attention_heads
self.c_attn = nn.Linear(config.hidden_size, 3 * self.projection_size)
...
mixed_x_layer = self.c_attn(hidden_states)
query, key, value = mixed_x_layer.split(self.split_size, dim=2)   # split_size = hidden_size
```
Since `kv_channels * num_attention_heads == hidden_size` for all 4 models, `projection_size == hidden_size` in every case → Q, K, V each get an equal `hidden_size`-sized chunk. Confirms **standard MHA** (K/V have the same number of heads as Q; no GQA anywhere in this generation).

**Output projection:**
```python
self.c_proj = nn.Linear(config.hidden_size, self.projection_size, bias=not config.no_bias)
```
Note: literally written as `nn.Linear(in=hidden_size, out=projection_size)` — the reverse of what you'd expect for an O-proj (normally in=concat-heads-output, out=hidden_size). Since `projection_size == hidden_size` for all 4 models this has zero numeric effect (weight is square either way), but it's a real code-level oddity worth flagging for anyone porting the shape logic to a hypothetical variant where projection_size ≠ hidden_size.

**MLP — gated SwiGLU, but with a critical quirk** (`class QWenMLP`):
```python
self.w1 = nn.Linear(config.hidden_size, config.intermediate_size // 2, bias=not config.no_bias)
self.w2 = nn.Linear(config.hidden_size, config.intermediate_size // 2, bias=not config.no_bias)
ff_dim_in = config.intermediate_size // 2
self.c_proj = nn.Linear(ff_dim_in, config.hidden_size, bias=not config.no_bias)

def forward(self, hidden_states):
    a1 = self.w1(hidden_states)
    a2 = self.w2(hidden_states)
    intermediate_parallel = a1 * F.silu(a2)
    output = self.c_proj(intermediate_parallel)
```
**This is the single most important shape-catalog finding**: `config.json`'s `intermediate_size` is the *combined* width — each of `w1` (up-proj) and `w2` (gate-proj, silu-activated) actually projects to `intermediate_size // 2`, not `intermediate_size`. Any shape catalog built naively off the raw config field will be 2x too wide on gate/up/down. Verified by direct read of the class body, not inferred.

## Matmul shape catalog, M = 4096

**Convention** (explicit, as requested): `out = in @ W^T`, `nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)` stores `W` as `[out_features, in_features]`. GEMM reported as **(M, N, K)** = (tokens, out_features, in_features), i.e. `C[M,N] = A[M,K] · Bᵀ[K,N]`.

Real per-branch FFN width = `intermediate_size // 2` (see quirk above). All models have `projection_size == hidden_size` (H), so Q/K/V/O are all square GEMMs.
